article_title: Reading Apprenticeship — Grade 9 Literacy
citation: What Works Clearinghouse. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Reading Apprenticeship®. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. http://www.wested.org/ReadingApprenticeship
title: Making reading processes visible through teacher modeling and metacognitive classroom conversation
description: A reusable instructional pattern in which the teacher assumes the role of expert reader, modeling and guiding students' text-based problem solving to build comprehension strategies. By incorporating student/teacher discussions about the process of reading into content-area classes, the approach aims to make the teacher's and students' reading processes and knowledge visible to others in the classroom, help students understand and regulate their own reading processes, and develop strategies for overcoming obstacles while reading. Small-group and full-classroom conversations about the thinking process used while reading are fundamental components.
requirements: Teachers must be prepared to examine their own discipline-specific reading during professional development and to model it for students
constraints: The pattern is designed for content-area classes in middle school, high school, and community college settings
target_learners: adolescent learners in content-area classrooms, including struggling readers and English language learners
target_learning_goals: comprehension strategies, self-regulation of reading processes, and overcoming obstacles while reading
examples: Reading Apprenticeship® classrooms integrate the pattern through conversations about the thinking processes that students and teachers use as they read
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Reading Apprenticeship®. U.S. Department of Education, What Works Clearinghouse. http://www.wested.org/ReadingApprenticeship

article_title: Symphony Math
citation: Symphony Math. (2021). Symphony Math program description and evidence summary. https://www.symphonylearning.com
title: Require mastery of the current concept before advancing to the next in a sequenced math program
description: Symphony Math sequences mathematical concepts and does not let a student move on until the current concept is mastered. Because the time and practice students need is not uniform, the program lets students spend the time they need to master foundational concepts before progressing.
requirements: A sequenced progression of mathematical concepts with mastery assessment at each step
constraints: Requires allowing non-uniform amounts of time and practice per student
target_learning_goals: Mastery of foundational mathematical concepts
examples: A student does not move to the next concept in the Symphony Math sequence until she has mastered the current concept
key_sources: Symphony Math. (2021). Symphony Math program description and evidence summary. https://evidenceforessa.org/program/symphony-math/

article_title: Replicating Experimental Impact Estimates With Nonexperimental Methods in the Context of Control-Group Noncompliance
citation: Brian Gill, Joshua Furgeson, Hanley Chiang, Bing-Ru Teh, Joshua Haimson, Natalya Verbitsky-Savitz. (2016). Replicating Experimental Impact Estimates With Nonexperimental Methods in the Context of Control-Group Noncompliance. Statistics and Public Policy, vol. 3, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Match causal estimands when using within-study comparisons to validate nonexperimental methods
description: The article states, citing Cook, Shadish, and Wong (2008), that "WSCs require that the experimental and nonexperimental methods assess the same causal estimand." This principle guides the design of replication studies: before judging whether a nonexperimental method replicates an experimental result, researchers must ensure both approaches target the same quantity. The article operationalizes this by comparing to ITT estimates under noncompliance.
requirements: Researchers must identify and align the causal estimand of the experimental and nonexperimental analyses before conducting a replication comparison
constraints: Under control-group noncompliance, standard approaches diverge in estimand, requiring an ITT-based comparison rather than CACE
target_learners: methodologists and education researchers designing evaluation studies
target_learning_goals: valid and credible causal evidence about intervention effectiveness
examples: The article's own WSC compared nonexperimental estimates to the experimental ITT estimate to satisfy the same-estimand requirement
key_sources: Brian Gill, Joshua Furgeson, Hanley Chiang, Bing-Ru Teh, Joshua Haimson, Natalya Verbitsky-Savitz. (2016). Replicating Experimental Impact Estimates With Nonexperimental Methods in the Context of Control-Group Noncompliance. Statistics and Public Policy, vol. 3, issue 1. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/2015-replicating-experimental-impact-estimates-with-nonexperimental-methods-in-the-context

article_title: Data for Improvement and Data for Accountability: Considerations for State Boards
citation: Title as printed: Overview, State Education Standard. (2024). The Journal of the National Association of State Boards of Education. https://www.nasbe.org/the-state-education-standard/
title: Treat malleability and predictive validity as non-negotiable criteria when selecting accountability indicators
description: The article argues that when states choose indicators for accountability systems, malleability and predictive validity should function as "non-negotiable criteria". An indicator should be something schools can genuinely influence within an improvement cycle and should predict meaningful student outcomes. The article directs this principle at state boards of education evaluating proposed indicators.
requirements: State boards should seek evidence of both malleability and predictive power for any proposed indicator before adopting it.
constraints: The article warns that bringing school-level improvement data into public accountability frameworks carries risks, since pressure to perform can suppress honest inquiry and incentivize superficial fixes.
target_learners: K-12 students in states designing accountability systems
target_learning_goals: Selection of accountability and improvement indicators that support genuine school improvement
examples: The article describes examining how malleability and predictive validity should serve as criteria when selecting accountability indicators.
key_sources: Title as printed: Overview, State Education Standard. (2024). The Journal of the National Association of State Boards of Education. https://www.nasbe.org/the-state-education-standard/

article_title: Structuring Out-of-School Time to Improve Academic Achievement
citation: Beckett, M., Borman, G., Capizzano, J., Parsley, D., Ross, S., Schirm, A., & Taylor, J. (2009). Structuring out-of-school time to improve academic achievement: A practice guide (NCEE #2009-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. Retrieved from http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Maximize student participation and attendance in OST programs
description: Because students most likely to benefit from a strong academic program may be especially unlikely to enroll in or attend OST programs regularly, the panel recommends that "OST programs focus on recruiting and retaining targeted students so that they receive the dosage necessary to realize academic benefits." Program features should be designed to meet the needs and preferences of students and parents, awareness of the program should be promoted within schools and to parents, and attendance data should be used to identify students facing difficulties attending.
requirements: Program features designed around student and parent needs and preferences
Promotion of program awareness within schools and to parents
Use of attendance data to identify students facing attendance difficulties
constraints: The level of evidence for this recommendation is low
target_learners: elementary and middle school students targeted for academic assistance in OST programs
target_learning_goals: sustained attendance sufficient to receive the instructional dosage needed for academic benefits
examples: The checklist for this recommendation lists designing program features to meet needs and preferences, promoting awareness, and using attendance data to identify students facing difficulties in attending the program.

Structuring out-of-school time to improve academic achievement: A practice guide (NCEE #2009-012). article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Make data safe: build trust and conditions for hard data conversations rather than punitive judgment
description: This principle holds that data improves practice only when educators can discuss it without defensiveness, so school leaders must invest in making data safe. Many educators have primarily experienced data punitively, as a way to make harsh judgments about individual teachers or students; the goal of approaching data safely is not to make the data palatable, but to build conditions for hard conversations about current practice and improvement strategies. Trust is built through clear mission, shared values, structured protocols that instill a sense of efficacy, and by engaging in difficult data-driven conversations and reflecting on them — the paper states there is no standardized approach and the work is deeply contextual and personal. Principals and administrators must set conditions for teams to keep a lens of improvement and support rather than shame and judgment.
requirements: Strong school leadership that supports a culture of data-driven improvement
Team leaders skilled in facilitating data discussions using norms, protocols, and listening techniques
Time and intention to build social trust within teams and across the school
constraints: The paper states trust cannot be built in an off-site professional learning session and there is no standardized approach to developing it
target_learners: teacher teams and professional learning communities
target_learning_goals: using data collaboratively to interrogate and improve practice
building collective responsibility for student outcomes
examples: In high-functioning teams, educators are motivated by commitment to students and collective responsibility as peers rather than an external motivator like a rating system, which the paper links to a remarkably high level of social trust
key_sources: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/practice-driven-data-lessons-chicagos-approach-research-data-and-practice-education

article_title: Comparing Early Literacy Screening Assessment Benchmarks in Massachusetts
citation: Lemke, M., Murphy, D., Soo Ping Chow, A., Spencer, H., & Zhang, A. (2023). Comparing early literacy screening assessment benchmarks in Massachusetts. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Massachusetts DESE literacy screening assessment data collection from grantee schools and districts
description: Beginning in the 2020/21 school year, the Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education began collecting literacy screening assessment data from schools and districts participating in certain state grants, drawing on a list of state-approved commercial screener products. The analysis in this brief uses 'More than 4,000 students from the 2021/22 school year, including 28 districts and 63 schools,' with scores from DIBELS 8th Edition, FastBridge aReading, i-Ready Diagnostic, Lexia Rapid, MAP Growth, mClass, and Star Reading. The stated goal is analyzing performance patterns to inform improvement efforts and target resources.
requirements: State approval of screening assessments and grantee participation in data submission
constraints: Results described in the brief are based on grade 3 data only; the full grantee dataset includes more than 35,000 student records
target_learners: Elementary students in Massachusetts grantee districts, kindergarten through grade 3
target_learning_goals: Early identification of students at risk of reading difficulty to guide intervention and resource targeting
examples: A September 2022 amendment to state law requires elementary schools to assess each student's reading abilities a minimum of twice per year from kindergarten through at least grade 3

article_title: A First Look at Early Literacy Performance in Massachusetts: Results of Initial Analysis Based on State Grantee Literacy Screening Assessments
citation: Mariann Lemke, Dan Murphy, Aaron Soo Ping Chow, Hayley Spencer, and Angela Zhang. (2023). A First Look at Early Literacy Performance in Massachusetts: Results of Initial Analysis Based on State Grantee Literacy Screening Assessments. WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org
title: Massachusetts early literacy screening assessment longitudinal database of grantee K–3 screening, SIMS, MCAS, and ACCESS data
description: WestEd, on behalf of DESE, is building what the report calls "a longitudinal database of early literacy assessment scores" linking student-level early literacy universal screening data from state grantees with SIMS, MCAS, and ACCESS for ELLs records and publicly available school- and district-level data. For 2020/21 and 2021/22 it includes benchmark scores for just over 35,000 unique K–3 students from 43 districts and 159 schools, about 10 percent of the state's K–3 population, across 11 screening assessments.
requirements: Data come from districts receiving specific state grants (EGL, FC576, GLEAM), which were required to provide screening assessment data
constraints: The sample includes more economically disadvantaged and English learner students and fewer grade 3 students than the state overall, so the report advises "some caution may be needed in generalizing from results of these analyses to the state"
target_learners: Students in grades K–3 in Massachusetts grantee districts
target_learning_goals: Early identification of students at risk of reading difficulty, including potential dyslexia risk, to inform instructional support
examples: Benchmark levels and reading risk flags were recalculated according to vendor technical documentation, with school- or district-provided benchmark scores used in about 5% of records

citation: Lemke, M., Murphy, D., Soo Ping Chow, A., & Acuña, A. (2024). Intersections: Student background and early literacy performance. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Massachusetts early literacy screening assessment dataset, 2022/23
description: A district-provided dataset of early literacy screening assessment scores collected by the Massachusetts DESE from grantee schools and districts, covering "More than 52,000 students in grades K–3"—about 20 percent of the state's K–3 population—from 79 districts and 278 schools, with scores from 12 literacy screening assessments (e.g., Acadience Reading, DIBELS 8th Edition, i-Ready Diagnostic). Assessments are typically administered three times per year (BOY, MOY, EOY). The brief's multilevel analyses of intersecting background and school characteristics are based on these data.

examples: DESE's June 2023 Early Literacy Screening Guidance identifies which benchmark performance level, such as DIBELS 8th Edition's At Risk/Well Below Benchmark, flags students needing action

citation: Early Literacy Performance in Massachusetts: Key Findings From 2023/24 School Year Data. (2025). WestEd. https://www.wested.org

description: A statewide collection of early literacy screening assessment results from schools and districts participating in targeted state grants, with 2023/24 the first year screening was required for all kindergarten through grade 3 students statewide. The 2023/24 data cover "137,000 students" in "612 schools" across "144 districts", about 53 percent of the state's K–3 students, and screenings are "typically administered two to three times per year" to identify students at risk of reading difficulties and guide early intervention.

constraints: Data cover about half the state's K–3 population because not all schools and districts were required to report.

target_learning_goals: Early identification of students at risk of reading difficulty to guide early intervention
examples: In 2023/24 the dataset covered 137,000 students, 612 schools, and 144 districts, twice the amount of data from the prior year.

article_title: Early Literacy Performance in Massachusetts: Results of Ongoing Analysis of Literacy Screening Assessments (2023/24 Data)
citation: Lemke, M., Faulkner-Bond, M., LeBeau, B., Soo Ping Chow, A., & Quesen, S. (2025). Early literacy performance in Massachusetts: Results of ongoing analysis of literacy screening assessments (2023/24 data). WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Massachusetts K-3 early literacy screening longitudinal dataset (2020/21-2023/24)
description: A longitudinal analytic file combining early literacy universal screening benchmark scores with SIMS demographic data, MCAS scores, ACCESS for ELLs data, and school- and district-level contextual data, organized as one observation per student, per test period (BOY, MOY, EOY), per assessment, per year. In 2023/24 it includes "388,204 scores" representing "137,159 unique students across 144 districts and 612 schools," about 53 percent of the state's K-3 population, drawn from 13 screening assessments with six assessments accounting for 92 percent of the data. WestEd built and analyzes it for DESE under state grant and screening-regulation data collection.
requirements: Data depend on schools and districts participating in state grants or the statewide screening requirement sharing assessment data with DESE, with publisher data-sharing agreements for some records.
constraints: The sample overrepresents Hispanic students, students from low income backgrounds, and English learners by 6 to 8 percent relative to the state, so the report states findings may slightly underestimate overall state performance and may not be fully generalizable.

target_learning_goals: Monitoring early literacy performance and progress and identifying students at risk of reading difficulty
examples: The 2023/24 data doubled from 2022/23, with mCLASS (37%) and DIBELS 8th Edition (21%) the most commonly used assessments.

article_title: Rethinking English Learner Reclassification in California: What Research Says about the State's Criteria
citation: Faulkner-Bond, M. (2026). Rethinking English Learner reclassification in California: What research says about the state's criteria. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resource/finding-the-sweet-spot-for-english-learner-reclassification/
title: Maintain a rigorous, validated English proficiency threshold as the statewide standard for exiting English Learner status
description: The principle holds that the statewide standard for exiting EL status should be a rigorous and validated proficiency threshold rather than additional achievement-based requirements. The study found ELPAC overall PL 4 is the "sweet spot" — the most robust indicator that language is no longer the primary driver of achievement differences — and recommends maintaining it as the Criterion 1 standard. Additional criteria may be used only for specific circumstances, such as PL 3 students already demonstrating strong academic achievement.
requirements: A validated proficiency assessment threshold (ELPAC overall PL 4) established through statistical comparison against achievement outcomes
constraints: Applies to California's EL reclassification policy context and the ELPAC assessment; the brief recommends engaging the field on Criteria 2 and 3 so they do not become unnecessary barriers if Criterion 4 is removed
target_learners: English Learner students in grades 3 through 8 and 11 in California
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification of English proficiency for reclassification and equitable access to grade-level instruction
examples: The WestEd/CDE study compared ELPAC overall performance levels against SBAC English language arts performance across grades 3 through 8 and 11 using data from more than 3 million students
key_sources: Faulkner-Bond, M. (2026). Rethinking English Learner reclassification in California: What research says about the state's criteria. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resource/finding-the-sweet-spot-for-english-learner-reclassification/

article_title: Real Progress in Maryland: Student Learning Objectives and Teacher and Principal Evaluation
citation: Slotnik, W. J., Bugler, D., & Liang, G. (2014). Real progress in Maryland: Student learning objectives and teacher and principal evaluation. WestEd and Community Training and Assistance Center. http://marylandpublicschools.org/MSDE/programs/tpe/index.html
title: Maryland SLO implementation process and state support tools
description: The Maryland SLO component is an instructional process embedded in the TPE evaluation system, in which SLOs are "the predominate measure of student growth for teachers and principals" and may account for 30%-50% of the total evaluation rating, with no single SLO counting for more than 35 percent. MSDE's Guidebook outlines a nine-step implementation sequence from professional development through data review, SLO development, review and approval, mid-interval and final reviews, to integration of results and setting the attribution roster. The state also developed SLO templates and guiding questions for teachers and principals, plus review criteria in four domains: priority of standard, rigor of target, quality of measure and evidence, and action plan.
requirements: Districts must provide SLO training to local school personnel in keeping with established state guidelines and document a verification process to validate consistency, comparability, quality and rigor of SLOs
constraints: Local districts, not the state, establish processes for setting, reviewing, assessing, and aligning SLOs, under Maryland's local control structure
target_learners: K-12 teachers and principals in Maryland public school districts
target_learning_goals: Improving educator effectiveness and student achievement through data-informed goal setting and instruction
examples: MSDE released over $1.5M in mini-grants to LEAs, with the largest share for school hardware/software investments (31.4% of grants) and teacher professional development on TPE, the Danielson framework, and SLOs (8.9%)
key_sources: Slotnik, W. J., Bugler, D., & Liang, G. (2014). Real progress in Maryland: Student learning objectives and teacher and principal evaluation. WestEd and Community Training and Assistance Center. http://marylandpublicschools.org/MSDE/programs/tpe/index.html

article_title: Stay the Course: Teacher and Principal Evaluation in Maryland
citation: Slotnik, W. J., Bugler, D., & Liang, G. (2016). Stay the Course: Teacher and Principal Evaluation in Maryland. WestEd and Community Training and Assistance Center. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Stay+the+Course+Teacher+and+Principal+Evaluation+in+Maryland
title: Maryland Teacher and Principal Evaluation (TPE) system
description: Maryland's statewide educator evaluation system combines measures of professional practice and student growth. Teacher professional practice uses four Charlotte Danielson Framework domains (planning and preparation, instructional practices, classroom environment, professional responsibilities) broken into 22 components, each domain counting 12.5% of the practice score. Student Learning Objectives are the predominant growth measure. The report states "In the overall rating of teacher effectiveness, both professional practice and student growth are given equal weight."
requirements: Local evaluation models must include required criteria such as the 50/50 split between professional practice and student growth, and must be endorsed by the local bargaining unit and approved by the state.
constraints: No single SLO may count for more than 35% of the total performance score.
target_learning_goals: Teacher effectiveness evaluation
Student growth measurement
Instructional improvement
examples: Under the state model, SLOs account for 30%-50% of the total evaluation rating depending on the teacher's or principal's assignment.
key_sources: Slotnik, W. J., Bugler, D., & Liang, G. (2016). Stay the Course: Teacher and Principal Evaluation in Maryland. WestEd and Community Training and Assistance Center. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED589981

article_title: Positive Conditions for Mathematics Learning: An Overview of the Research
citation: Fitz, J. (with Price, H.). (2025). Positive conditions for mathematics learning: An overview of the research. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/967.472
title: Math anxiety mechanism: emotional threat responses divert attention and reduce working memory during mathematical engagement
description: The report describes math anxiety as prevalent psychological fear of math among students and adults, including many elementary math teachers. Neuroimaging research finds children with high math anxiety "perceive math as threatening," showing elevated neural activity in emotion-processing brain areas and lower activity in mathematical reasoning areas. Researchers hypothesize the emotional reaction diverts attention from the task, co-opting deep mathematical cognition and reducing working memory. Math anxiety is linked to reduced achievement and avoidance of math courses and careers, and may also arise from early struggles, kicking off a vicious cycle.
requirements: Classroom conditions must address students' social and emotional experiences alongside instructional quality, since anxiety can result from early math struggles
constraints: The mechanism is presented as researchers' hypothesis about neural findings, and the review notes anxiety can be a consequence as well as a cause of low achievement
target_learners: K–12 mathematics students, especially those with high math anxiety
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement
Deep cognitive engagement with math
Reduced avoidance of math courses and careers
examples: The report argues teachers can ameliorate anxiety by cultivating conditions that develop the sense of safety necessary for deep cognitive engagement with math
key_sources: Fitz, J. (with Price, H.). (2025). Positive conditions for mathematics learning: An overview of the research. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/967.472

article_title: Advancing Integration and Equity through Magnet Schools
citation: George, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2021). Advancing integration and equity through magnet schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/magnet-schools
title: Magnet schools: public schools of choice with special curricula designed to achieve voluntary desegregation
description: Magnet schools are public elementary or secondary schools that seek voluntary desegregation through parental choice rather than mandatory student assignment, by offering specialized instruction and innovative academic offerings that draw students from surrounding areas. The federal definition quoted in the report describes "a special curriculum capable of attracting substantial numbers of students of different racial backgrounds." Research cited in the report identifies distinguishing characteristics: "a distinctive school curriculum organized around a specific special theme or method of instruction," voluntary enrollment, and choice across neighborhood and sometimes district boundaries. One of the first magnet schools, McCarther-era McCarver Elementary School in Tacoma, WA, was established in 1968; recent estimates of operating magnet schools range from 3,285 to 4,340, educating over 3.5 million students.
requirements: Enrollment is completely voluntary, and students' ability to choose magnet schools depends on factors including whether the school operates on a regional basis and offers transportation.
constraints: The report notes wide variation in estimates of magnet schools highlights the necessity for a widely agreed upon definition, particularly for policy and research purposes, and that many magnet schools have departed from their integrative missions.
target_learners: families exercising voluntary school choice across attendance zones
students in urban centers and surrounding suburban districts
target_learning_goals: access to specialized, innovative academic programs
reduction of racial isolation through integrated enrollment
examples: The report describes McCarver Elementary School in Tacoma, WA, established in 1968 as part of a controlled choice program, followed in 1969 by the William Monroe Trotter School in Boston and others in Buffalo, Houston, and Minneapolis.
key_sources: George, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2021). Advancing integration and equity through magnet schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/magnet-schools

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Louisiana
citation: Educator Diversity State Profile: Louisiana. (2022). EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Make educator diversity data visible and actionable to stakeholders
description: The brief's first strategy holds that "all stakeholders must have access to useful and timely educator workforce data to set goals and chart a path forward." State education agencies, as keepers of state data systems, should publicly share school-level teacher demographics, the racial makeup of candidates entering and completing preparation programs, and retention data disaggregated by race/ethnicity, so stakeholders can make targeted workforce decisions at school, district, and state levels.
requirements: Data should be publicly available and easily accessible, e.g., in dashboards, school report cards, or state-developed reports
constraints: Louisiana was rated as not publicly posting retention data for educators of color disaggregated by race/ethnicity
target_learners: K-12 public and charter school students
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to teachers of color and same-race teachers
examples: Louisiana posts school-level racial demographics through its Educator Workforce Reports and Louisiana School Finder, earning a green rating on that criterion
key_sources: Educator Diversity State Profile: Louisiana. (2022). EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622849

article_title: State Strategies for Investing in Community Schools
citation: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402
title: Maryland Concentration of Poverty (CoP) entitlement grant program
description: Established by the Blueprint for Maryland's Future in 2020, the CoP program provides all eligible Maryland schools two complementary state funding sources: personnel grants of $248,833 annually for essential community schools staff (a community school coordinator and a licensed health care practitioner), and per-pupil grants on a sliding scale. "In 2022, the CoP grant program distributed a total of $116.7 million in state aid to 300 eligible schools (approximately 21% of all public schools in the state)." Eligibility phases in over time, starting at an 80% free or reduced-price meal threshold and decreasing by 5% each year.
requirements: Personnel grant eligibility is determined by the greater of the proportion of students receiving free or reduced-price meals, identified in a Community Eligibility Provision school, or identified through direct certification.
constraints: Per-pupil grant eligibility thresholds differ from personnel grant thresholds (80% in fiscal year 2022, declining to at least 55% starting in 2027).
target_learners: Students in high-poverty Maryland public schools
target_learning_goals: Expanded and enriched learning time, integrated student services, family and community supports, and staff professional development
examples: Per-pupil grants fund integrated student services (medical, dental, vision care, transportation, healthy food, attendance support), family supports, trauma-informed professional development, and additional support staff such as social workers and restorative practice coaches.
key_sources: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Illinois
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://edtrust.org
title: Make educator diversity data publicly visible and actionable at the school level
description: The brief argues that increasing workforce diversity requires that "all stakeholders must have access to useful and timely educator workforce data to set goals and chart a path forward." State education agencies, as keepers of state data systems, should publish school-level racial demographics of the educator workforce in dashboards, report cards, or reports so stakeholders can make targeted decisions. Illinois posts only district-level data, and the brief recommends adding school-level data and easier interpretation, citing Massachusetts' dashboard as a model.
requirements: Data should be publicly available and easily accessible, at school level, in a dashboard, report card, or state report
constraints: Illinois currently meets only some requirements: it posts district-level rather than school-level data
target_learning_goals: Data-informed state and district decisions to diversify the educator workforce
examples: Illinois' Annual Program Reporting system publicly reports racial demographics of candidates entering and completing teacher preparation programs, earning green ratings
key_sources: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622786

article_title: A study on AI-enabled course development, AI proficiency, and first-year students' academic and psychological adjustment
citation: Zhang J and Yin Y (2026). A study on AI-enabled course development, AI proficiency, and first-year students' academic and psychological adjustment. Front. Psychol. 17:1909803. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1909803
title: Manage AI-related workload in course design because excessive AI usage pressure attenuates proficiency's psychological benefits
description: Because AI usage pressure significantly attenuated the indirect pathway from course development satisfaction to psychological adjustment, the article recommends that course design attend to students' technological workload, not only tool coverage. The authors advise that "Instructors should control the number of AI-based tasks in course design, clearly define which tasks are suitable for AI use and which must be completed independently, and provide actionable guidelines," warning that excessive monitoring and task overload can turn AI from a learning support into a source of strain.
requirements: Course teams able to define which tasks are suitable for AI use and which must be completed independently
constraints: Derived from cross-sectional self-report associations in one institution; the authors note firm policy recommendations require longitudinal, multi-institution studies
target_learners: First-year university students using AI platforms for coursework
target_learning_goals: Protecting self-reported psychological adjustment while using AI learning tools
Reducing AI-related task pressure and uncertainty
examples: 66.97% of surveyed students reported additional pressure when completing tasks on AI platforms, and the moderated mediation index of −0.051 confirmed attenuation under high pressure
key_sources: Zhang J and Yin Y (2026). A study on AI-enabled course development, AI proficiency, and first-year students' academic and psychological adjustment. Front. Psychol. 17:1909803. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1909803

article_title: Warning About AI Fallibility Increases Help-Seeking in an Intelligent Tutoring System
citation: Tomohiro Nagashima, Mirella Hladký, and Vera Rief. (2026). Warning About AI Fallibility Increases Help-Seeking in an Intelligent Tutoring System. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03822
title: Give both conditions a matched popup message to isolate the effect of disclosing AI fallibility
description: When testing transparency cues about AI fallibility, the control condition should receive a comparable popup that omits only the fallibility disclosure. The authors explain that "the distinction focused on whether the warning message mentioned the possibility of hallucination or not, instead of, for example, giving no warning to students in the control condition," so the design isolates the disclosure effect rather than the general effect of any warning popup.
requirements: A control message matched in format and tone that differs only in mentioning potential mistakes
constraints: This design tests disclosure of fallibility, not the general effect of providing popup warnings
target_learners: secondary school students using AI-based tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: critical engagement with potentially fallible system output
examples: The NoMistake condition received "Please read Maddox's messages carefully!" while the Mistake condition received the fallibility warning

article_title: From Planning to Revision: How AI Writing Support at Different Stages Alters Ownership
citation: Katy Ilonka Gero, Tao Long, Carly Schnitzler, and Paramveer S. Dhillon. 2026. From Planning to Revision: How AI Writing Support at Different Stages Alters Ownership. In Designing Interactive Systems Conference (DIS '26), June 13–17, 2026, Singapore, Singapore. ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://doi.org/10.1145/3800645.3813003
title: Materialist and idealist routes to psychological ownership of writing
description: The article frames psychological ownership of writing through two routes drawn from philosophy and writing studies: a materialist route (Locke's labor theory, where mixing labor with resources makes the object one's property) and an idealist route (Hegel's embodiment of will, identity and values). It uses this framing to interpret its experiment, "investigat[ing] the various "routes" towards ownership of a piece of writing by comparing the contribution of ideas (idealist) versus text (materialist) from AI support", while noting that time reduced by AI support underlies both routes.
requirements: A writing task segmented into temporal stages so that idea versus text contribution from AI can be isolated
constraints: The article notes the routes are entangled and "it is not clear whether some routes are more effective at generating psychological ownership than others"
target_learning_goals: Maintaining feelings of ownership, agency, and cognitive engagement during AI-assisted writing
examples: The experiment compared AI support at planning, drafting, and revision stages and measured ownership, attribution of ideas and text, and essay quality
key_sources: Katy Ilonka Gero, Tao Long, Carly Schnitzler, and Paramveer S. Dhillon. 2026. From Planning to Revision: How AI Writing Support at Different Stages Alters Ownership. In Designing Interactive Systems Conference (DIS '26), June 13–17, 2026, Singapore, Singapore. ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://doi.org/10.1145/3800645.3813003

article_title: Programming Language Policy as an AI Literacy Equity Problem: A 15-Nation Comparative Analysis
citation: Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Iulia-Maria Popescu. (2026). Programming Language Policy as an AI Literacy Equity Problem: A 15-Nation Comparative Analysis. ALIT4ALL 2026, co-located with AIED 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0005-3547-5772
title: Two-dimensional framework: mandate level and governance archetype jointly determine access and depth
description: The article classifies national systems along two dimensions: Mandate Level (elective, track-mandated, or universal) and Governance Archetype, defined by "where the effective authority over the classroom programming language resides". Four archetypes are constructed inductively: sovereign-led decree, assessment-driven washback, decentralized with regional exams, and fully decentralized. The framework is applied to fifteen countries and, the authors argue, "governance archetype and mandate level jointly determine both who accesses programming education and what depth they receive".
requirements: Publicly accessible statutory curricula, examination specifications, or ministry decrees amenable to document analysis
constraints: Classifications involve interpretive judgement and the boundaries are not always sharp
Federal systems classified by dominant or nationally representative pattern where no single authoritative standard exists
target_learners: Upper secondary (ISCED 3) students across fifteen national systems
target_learning_goals: AI literacy and programming education access and depth
examples: Table 1 assigns France, China, UAE and Japan to Model A; Poland, Romania, Finland and South Korea to Model B; UK and Germany to Model C1; Switzerland (pre-2024), Norway and Netherlands to Model C2.
key_sources: Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Iulia-Maria Popescu. (2026). Programming Language Policy as an AI Literacy Equity Problem: A 15-Nation Comparative Analysis. ALIT4ALL 2026, co-located with AIED 2026. https://orcid.org/0009-0005-3547-5772

article_title: Exploring Fraction Comprehension and Interest in Elementary Education Through AI-Powered Personalized Learning
citation: Holman, Kenneth. (2024). Exploring Fraction Comprehension and Interest in Elementary Education Through AI-Powered Personalized Learning. https://stars.library.ucf.edu/etd2024/32
title: Mathbot's design framework: Constructionism combined with Reinforcement Learning Theory for adaptive AI-driven learning
description: The Mathbot intervention is grounded in a dual theoretical foundation combining Papert's Constructionism and Skinner's Reinforcement Learning Theory. The article states that "The Mathbot intervention draws from both Papert's Constructionism and Skinner's Reinforcement Learning Theory, forming a foundation for adaptive AI-driven learning environments." Constructionism contributes hands-on, active learning through interaction and reflection, with group discussions after sessions reinforcing reflection and peer-to-peer learning. Reinforcement theory contributes immediate feedback: correct answers receive positive reinforcement encouraging repetition of successful strategies, while incorrect answers prompt additional scaffolding and practice guiding students toward mastery. The author describes the two as balancing exploratory learning with behavioral reinforcement.
requirements: Immediate feedback loops that reinforce correct answers and provide scaffolding after incorrect answers
Group discussion opportunities after Mathbot sessions to support reflection and peer-to-peer learning
target_learners: elementary students with mathematical learning challenges
target_learning_goals: fraction comprehension
fraction comparison skills
examples: Students engaged directly with fraction problems in Mathbot, receiving immediate feedback and positive reinforcement, with teachers in both groups following the same fraction-comparison lesson plan over five days
key_sources: Holman, Kenneth. (2024). Exploring Fraction Comprehension and Interest in Elementary Education Through AI-Powered Personalized Learning. https://stars.library.ucf.edu/etd2024/32

article_title: Exploring Fraction Comprehension and Interest in Elementary Education Through AI-Powered Personalized Learning
citation: Holman, Kenneth. (2024). Exploring Fraction Comprehension and Interest in Elementary Education Through AI-Powered Personalized Learning. https://stars.library.ucf.edu/etd2024/32
title: Mathbot: an AI-based personalized learning platform integrating student interests into fraction problems
description: Mathbot is an AI-based personalized learning platform for elementary mathematics that dynamically adapts to individual learning patterns and integrates personal interests into fraction problems. The article describes it as exemplifying AI technology "by integrating students' interests into fraction problems, creating an engaging and customized approach to mathematics education." In the evaluated intervention, fourth and fifth graders with mathematical learning challenges used Mathbot during 40-minute sessions across five consecutive school days, receiving adaptive feedback personalized to their learning needs while teachers followed a shared lesson plan on fraction comparison. Its efficacy was assessed against business-as-usual instruction using the Fraction Comparison Assessment and a six-item Situational Interest Survey.
requirements: AI-driven adaptive feedback personalized to individual learning needs
Integration of students' personal interests into fraction problems
constraints: In the evaluated study, BAU students slightly outperformed Mathbot users on post-test fraction comprehension and situational interest changes were not statistically significant
target_learning_goals: fraction comprehension
situational interest in mathematics
examples: Used in a five-day quasi-experimental study with 22 fourth and fifth graders comparing Mathbot to business-as-usual teacher-led fraction comparison instruction

article_title: Developing Deep Learning in Science Through an Adaptive AI-Based STEM Instructional Program: Evidence From Sixth-Grade Classrooms
citation: Bin Bakheet, T., Alamri, H., & Alshaya, F. (2026). Developing deep learning in science through an adaptive AI-based STEM instructional program: evidence from sixth-grade classrooms. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00630-1
title: Mastery-based branching across micro-learning units with misconception-triggered redirection
description: Each lesson was decomposed into micro-learning units aligned with deep learning dimensions, with decision rules governing progression based on learner performance. "Mastery-based branching mechanisms were embedded at both the diagnostic entry point and within lesson-level assessments to differentiate beginner and advanced tracks." Redirection logic targeted specific misconceptions (e.g., orbital positioning, axial tilt, tide–gravity causal links) with scaffolded models, hint sequences, and worked examples, while rapid mastery unlocked enrichment challenges.
requirements: Lesson-level quizzes with automated feedback, tracked analytics indicators (accuracy, attempts, error patterns), and a defined mastery threshold (80%) to trigger branching
constraints: Adaptivity was operationalized primarily through rule-based mechanisms; machine-learning components served a supportive monitoring function only
target_learning_goals: Conceptual mastery and deep learning dimensions (explanation, interpretation, application, idea generation) in space science
examples: In the eclipses micro-lesson, incorrect alignment reasoning redirected students to an alignment simulation module, while first-attempt mastery of 90% or more activated an enrichment challenge
key_sources: Bin Bakheet, T., Alamri, H., & Alshaya, F. (2026). Developing deep learning in science through an adaptive AI-based STEM instructional program: evidence from sixth-grade classrooms. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00630-1

article_title: Learning to Grade Efficiently: A Bandit-Driven Prompt-Selection Framework for Low-Cost LLM Essay Scoring
citation: Olga Manakina, Igor Bogdanov. (2026). Learning to Grade Efficiently: A Bandit-Driven Prompt-Selection Framework for Low-Cost LLM Essay Scoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23814v1
title: Cost-aware multi-armed bandit framework for adaptive prompt selection in automated essay scoring
description: The framework treats each prompt-model combination as an arm in a multi-armed bandit (MAB) controller that adaptively selects prompting strategies during inference. The agent "observes a reward signal based on the agreement between the LLM's predicted score and the examiner's ground-truth score", using an epsilon-greedy algorithm whose reward incorporates prediction accuracy (negative absolute error) and optionally penalizes token usage. This transforms prompt selection from offline hyperparameter optimization into an online learning task, claimed as the first application of online control mechanisms to AES.
requirements: A reward signal based on agreement between LLM-predicted scores and ground-truth human scores
A set of distinct prompt recipes implemented as arms, with a prompt library separating templates from dynamic instantiation
constraints: Implemented and tested with only one LLM (Gemini 2.5) on IELTS Task 2 essays
The epsilon-greedy implementation used a constant exploration rate (ϵ = 0.2), which the authors say could be further refined
target_learners: IELTS Writing Task 2 candidates whose essays are scored
target_learning_goals: Accurate, cost-efficient automated scoring of argumentative essays against official band-score criteria
examples: The system dynamically assembles prompts from a template library, injecting essay question and text, and sequentially generates criterion-specific prompts for multi-step recipes before programmatically calculating the overall score.
key_sources: Olga Manakina, Igor Bogdanov. (2026). Learning to Grade Efficiently: A Bandit-Driven Prompt-Selection Framework for Low-Cost LLM Essay Scoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23814

description: Math Mysteries is the artifact created by the teacher team during the workshop: "a storytelling-based, AI-powered, gamified platform designed to support middle school mathematics learning". Teachers prototyped it using Google's AI Studio, chosen because it is free for educators, browser-based, and supports multimodal generation including text, images, video, audio, and code through Gemini-family models. article_title: Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues
citation: Zhangqi Duan, Shuyan Huang, Alexander Scarlatos, Jaewook Lee, Simon Woodhead, Andrew Lan. (2026). Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30051
title: First-of-its-kind real-world dataset of student dialogues and question responses from a math learning platform
description: A dataset built from a real-world online math learning platform where students practice multiple-choice questions and can initiate on-demand chat conversations with human tutors grounded in the question. After processing it "contains 1,775 dialogues and 66,705 question-answering records from 670 students", spanning topics including Algebra, Geometry, and Number. Dialogues average 12.95 turns, 84.8% are tutor-initiated, and turn-level dialogue acts and correctness labels were annotated with GPT-4.1. The authors state they are in the process of publicly releasing it after PII removal.
requirements: Turn-level dialogue act and correctness annotations, produced via GPT-4.1 annotation following prior work
constraints: The data is fully anonymized, so demographic information about individual students and tutors is not available
target_learners: K-12 math students on an online learning platform
target_learning_goals: Mathematics question answering and tutoring dialogue behavior
examples: Questions span Algebra, Geometry, and Number; interactions include 31 tutors and five dialogue-act labels such as Math Answer and Not Understanding

article_title: Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought
citation: Sora Kang. (2026). Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought. In Proceedings of CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24751v1
title: Maieutic Partner / Generative Refusal framework for Tools for Thought
description: The paper proposes shifting GenAI from a "Co-author" role to a "Maieutic Partner" that facilitates inquiry by strategically withholding text generation. Generative Refusal treats refusal "not as a lack of functionality, but as a core mechanic for Tools for Thought": the AI creates "a structured gap that demands user input, rather than filling that gap with synthetic text", shifting interaction from delegation to activation. The framework draws on desirable difficulties and scaffolding within the Zone of Proximal Development, and is operationalized in Actor's Note, which refuses to generate text and instead asks context-aware questions.
requirements: The domain must be one where the mental effort of articulation and interpretation is central to learning, such as artistic training
constraints: The paper argues the efficiency-first paradigm is detrimental specifically in educational and training contexts, not universally
target_learners: professional and student actors in artistic training
target_learning_goals: internalizing character roles through first-person reflective journaling
critical articulation rather than cognitive offloading
examples: Actor's Note analyzes the uploaded script, role, and performance date to generate three context-specific questions daily, framed in the second person to elicit first-person reflection
key_sources: Sora Kang. (2026). Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought. In Proceedings of CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24751

article_title: MathBuddy: Affective Math Tutoring
citation: Debanjana Kar, Leopold Böss, Dacia Braca, Sebastian Dennerlein, Nina Hubig, Philipp Wintersberger, and Yufang Hou. (2025). MathBuddy: A Multimodal System for Affective Math Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19993
title: MathBuddy: multimodal emotion-aware LLM math tutoring system
description: MathBuddy is an emotionally aware LLM-powered math tutor that, per the authors, "dynamically models the student's emotions and maps them to relevant pedagogical strategies, making the tutor-student conversation a more empathetic one." It captures emotions from conversational text (a fine-tuned DistilBERT classifier) and from webcam facial expressions (face-api.js, reporting 76% accuracy and 71% F1 on its test set), aggregates both modalities into Positive/Neutral/Negative, and prompts the LLM tutor accordingly. The system has a TypeScript frontend with chat interface, webcam input, and visual workspace, and a Python REST backend for inference. Code, dataset, and demo video are publicly released.
requirements: Webcam access and conversational text input for multimodal emotion capture
A backend LLM tutor model (e.g., LearnLM) prompted with the aggregated emotional state
constraints: The authors state the current text- and face-based modalities "may not be informative enough to accurately capture a user's emotional state" in technical education contexts
Handwritten-note submission is reserved for future research owing to implementation constraints
target_learners: Learners solving mathematics problems (study participants aged 15-55)
target_learning_goals: Geometry and probability problem solving with scaffolded, emotionally adaptive tutoring
examples: In the user study, each participant completed two tutoring sessions (one geometry, one probability problem) in Emotion ON and OFF conditions with randomized order, webcam capture, and pre/post multiple-choice tests
key_sources: Debanjana Kar, Leopold Böss, Dacia Braca, Sebastian Dennerlein, Nina Hubig, Philipp Wintersberger, and Yufang Hou. (2025). MathBuddy: A Multimodal System for Affective Math Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19993

article_title: MathBuddy: Affective Math Tutoring
citation: Debanjana Kar, Leopold Böss, Dacia Braca, Sebastian Dennerlein, Nina Hubig, Philipp Wintersberger, and Yufang Hou. (2025). MathBuddy: A Multimodal System for Affective Math Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19993
title: Annotated student-utterance emotion dataset (224 turns) for text-based emotion recognition in math tutoring
description: The authors annotated student turns in the hard version of the MathDial-Bridge dataset to support developing emotion recognition models from text. Emotion extraction was modeled as multi-label classification over three target states — Boredom, Engagement, and Neutral — with a polarity score from 0 to 2 capturing intensity as an arousal indicator. "Finally, 224 unique student turns were annotated ensuring an equal distribution across the labels." The manually annotated set serves as a test set, while a noisy silver-labeled dataset generated with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B serves as training data for fine-tuning BERT-based models.
requirements: Annotated student-tutor conversational data; the authors note the lack of such an annotated dataset was a major bottleneck they addressed by annotating MathDial-Bridge student turns
constraints: The authors state the dataset "currently contains coarse-grain emotion labels for student utterances" and that finer emotion labels capturing micro facial expressions are left for future work
target_learners: Students interacting in text-based math tutoring dialogues
target_learning_goals: Recognition of student affective states (boredom, engagement, neutral) to support emotionally aware tutoring
examples: Four annotators aged 27-38 labeled the data; after an initial round yielding 40% Cohen's Kappa agreement, three annotators adjudicated conflicts, and the best fine-tuned model (DistilBERT) reached 61.8% accuracy and 57.9% F1
key_sources: Debanjana Kar, Leopold Böss, Dacia Braca, Sebastian Dennerlein, Nina Hubig, Philipp Wintersberger, and Yufang Hou. (2025). MathBuddy: A Multimodal System for Affective Math Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19993

article_title: From MOOC to MAIC: Reshaping Online Teaching and Learning through LLM-driven Agents
citation: Jifan Yu, Zheyuan Zhang, Daniel Zhang-li, Shangqing Tu, Zhanxin Hao, Ruimiao Li, Haoxuan Li, Yuanchun Wang, Hanming Li, Linlu Gong, Jie Cao, Jiayin Lin, Jinchang Zhou, Fei Qin, Haohua Wang, Jianxiao Jiang, Lijun Deng, Yisi Zhan, Chaojun Xiao, Xusheng Dai, Xuan Yan, Nianyi Lin, Nan Zhang, Ruixin Ni, Yang Dang, Lei Hou, Yu Zhang, Xu Han, Manli Li, Juanzi Li, Zhiyuan Liu, Huiqin Liu, Maosong Sun. title: MAIC: an LLM-driven multi-agent online course framework balancing scalability and adaptivity
description: MAIC (Massive AI-empowered Course) is a proposed form of online education in which instructors upload slides and LLM-driven agents prepare structured lecture resources, then deliver classes through a teacher agent, teaching assistant agent, and customizable classmate agents. The article frames it as balancing the scalability of MOOCs with adaptivity: 'a new form of online education that leverages LLM-driven multi-agent systems to construct an AI-augmented classroom, balancing scalability with adaptivity.' Classroom interactions are organized around four behavior categories — Teaching and Initiation, In-depth Discussion, Emotional Companionship, and Classroom Management — orchestrated by a Session Controller with a Class State Receptor and Manager Agent.

constraints: The authors state the reported assessments 'provide only an initial view of specific aspects of MAIC rather than its overall effectiveness'

personalized adaptive learning
student engagement
examples: A three-month pilot deployed MAIC in the courses 'Towards Artificial General Intelligence' and 'How to Study in the University' with over 500 student volunteers

In LAK 2026: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK 2026). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://doi.org/10.1145/3785022.3785113
title: Marked Pedagogies: systematic shifts in LLM feedback language that reveal pedagogical orientations changing with prompted student characteristics
description: Marked Pedagogies is the article's framework, grounded in the sociolinguistic notion of markedness, in which "dominant groups (e.g., White and male identities in the U.S.) function as institutional norms while nondominant groups are socially and linguistically marked." The framework defines Marked Pedagogies as "systematic shifts in feedback language that reveal how LLMs' underlying pedagogical orientations change in response to prompted student characteristics." It is operationalized through contrastive prompting, Marked Words log-odds lexical analysis, and a concentration metric, and names named pedagogies of disapproval, language inadequacy, lowered expectations, cultural stereotypes, emotional connection, and enthusiasm.
requirements: Contrastive prompt conditions (marked, comparative, baseline) over the same essays to isolate the effect of student attributes
A lexical-difference method (log-odds ratios with Dirichlet prior, |z| > 1.96, minimum frequency 30) to identify distinctive words
constraints: Findings draw on two writing assignments from a single dataset of middle school persuasive essays; generalization to other genres, grade levels, and assignments is untested
Only four LLMs were evaluated; model-level differences were not quantified
Attributes were examined singularly and independently, though intersectional in real-world settings; analyses drew on U.S. stereotypes
target_learners: middle school (eighth-grade) students in English Language Arts
target_learning_goals: writing feedback and revision in persuasive/argumentative writing
examples: The article identifies a Marked Pedagogy of disapproval in which high achievers are positioned as capable writers with expanding potential while lower achievers are positioned as error-prone and in need of correction
The article identifies a Marked Pedagogy of enthusiasm in which unmotivated students are met with enthusiasm whereas motivated students receive direct, higher-level critique
key_sources: Mei Tan, Lena Phalen, and Dorottya Demszky. 2026. Marked Pedagogies: Examining Linguistic Biases in Personalized Automated Writing Feedback. In LAK 2026: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK 2026). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://doi.org/10.1145/3785022.3785113

article_title: Misconception Acquisition Dynamics in Large Language Models
citation: Naiming Liu, Xinghe Chen, Richard Baraniuk, Mrinmaya Sachan, and Shashank Sonkar. (2026). Misconception Acquisition Dynamics in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00818
title: MalAlgoLib: graph-based library generating algebra problems with correct and misconception-specific step-by-step solution traces
description: MalAlgoLib (Mal-Algorithm Library) operationalizes the mal-rule view of misconceptions by representing equation solving as a directed acyclic graph of problem types, where each misconception is an alternative transition yielding an erroneous trace. It "covers 16 linear-equation problem types and 20 misconceptions drawn from established taxonomies", enabling scalable generation of paired correct and misconception-driven traces. Its design principles are extensibility across equation types, modularity in misconception modeling, and faithful representation of cognitive error patterns.
requirements: New problem types are added by implementing a reduce() method linking to an existing type; new misconceptions are added as alternative transitions without modifying existing problem-type implementations.
constraints: The library handles linear equations with one variable, including forms with parentheses and multiple terms.
target_learners: Algebra learners whose misconceptions are being modeled
target_learning_goals: Linear equation solving with correct and erroneous step-by-step reasoning traces
examples: The library generated the controlled training data for the student-model, tutor-model, and no-steps ablation experiments in Section 5.
key_sources: Naiming Liu, Xinghe Chen, Richard Baraniuk, Mrinmaya Sachan, and Shashank Sonkar. (2026). Misconception Acquisition Dynamics in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00818

article_title: Modularizing Educational LLM-Agency for Fostering Responsible Learning Assistance
citation: Gabelmann, J., Jahn, F., Baum, K., van Rossum, S., Wuenscher, E., Gros, T. P., Wolf, V. (2026). Modularizing Educational LLM-Agency for Fostering Responsible Learning Assistance. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30187
title: MALA: a modular agentic AI chatbot architecture for exercise-solving assistance
description: MALA (Modular Artificial Learning Assistance) decomposes tutoring into a two-stage process of intent classification and task-specific execution. A central classifier routes each student message to one of four specialized modules: a hint module that handles requests where students ask for 'a starting point, the next step, or a nudge toward the solution', an explanation module constrained to short structured messages, a feedback module with a reasoning-then-evaluation-then-output workflow, and a fallback/safety module deflecting prompt-injection attempts. It was prototyped with GPT-4o for guiding students through problem-solving exercises and optionally generating new exercises.
requirements: Each module is governed by a dedicated system prompt aligned with its educational goal; a sample solution is provided in the feedback prompt to mitigate hallucinated corrections
constraints: It does not serve as a general-purpose tutor or study planner
target_learning_goals: exercise solving with preserved epistemic agency
examples: In an adversarial test, the hint module consistently refused to give the full solution despite escalating urgency claims, offering guiding questions instead

article_title: Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning
citation: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Janne Rotter, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20047
title: MAI-AI: Metacognitive Awareness Inventory for Artificial Intelligence
description: The MAI-AI is an AI-centered adaptation of the shortened Metacognitive Awareness Inventory and the MSLQ, used to assess students' metacognitive awareness of AI-assisted learning. As the article states, "the MAI-AI questionnaire consists of 29 questions (28 in post), divided into 6 constructs": Attitudes towards AI, AI Engagement, AI Literacy, Metacognitive Knowledge of Cognition, Metacognitive Regulation of Cognition, and Autonomy & Control. All questions use a five-point Likert scale with subscale averages as scores ranging from 1 to 5. It was administered at pre-test, post-test, and five-week follow-up.
requirements: Administered as repeated self-report; the article notes the instrument is still awaiting validation.
constraints: The article notes self-report limitations including social desirability bias and possible familiarity effects from repeated exposure to the same instrument.
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness of AI-assisted learning (knowledge and regulation of cognition)
examples: Used at three time points (T0, T1, T5) in the quasi-experiment with 126 students.
key_sources: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Janne Rotter, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20047

article_title: Beyond Problem Solving: Large Language Models for Emotional and Reflective Support in Mathematics Learning
citation: Rief, V., Hladký, M., Yoo, M., Heel, S., Sato, S., Nagashima, T. (2026). Beyond Problem Solving: Large Language Models for Emotional and Reflective Support in Mathematics Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02611
title: Math with Matt: an LLM-enhanced algebra ITS with a mindful pedagogical agent
description: Math with Matt is an ITS for linear systems of equations built in CTAT, offering three math units (substitution, elimination, equalization) with three-level hints and immediate feedback, plus mindfulness components: an LLM-based mindful chat (GPT-4o-mini), a 60-second guided breathing exercise, and mindful hint/feedback language. The system "leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to provide both cognitive and emotional support in algebra learning" through "a fox-shaped pedagogical agent called 'Matt'" who converses in first- and second-person language.
requirements: An LLM API connection for the dynamic chat units, with prompts constrained by CTAT's interface design and behavior graph logic
Interaction guidelines in the system prompt for handling inappropriate language, nonsensical answers and off-topic responses
constraints: Dynamic LLM hints and feedback were avoided during problem solving due to potential hallucinations; generated mindful messages were hard-coded after accuracy checking
In the classroom setting, self-paced mindfulness practices were vulnerable to peer influence and students' limited English proficiency required translation tools that disrupted the workflow
target_learning_goals: Solving linear systems of equations via substitution, elimination, and equalization methods
Emotional regulation of state math anxiety during problem solving
examples: In the classroom evaluation, students in each class were randomly assigned to the Mindful or Cognitive condition and used the ITS across two 50-minute sessions with pretest and posttest

article_title: Can students identify AI? – A cross-sectional quantitative study about AI recognition in tablet-based MCQ assessment among fifth-year undergraduate medical students at Saarland University, Germany
citation: Vogt P, Wolf N, Jordan S, Volz-Willems S, Jäger J, Dupont F. (2026). Can students identify AI? – A cross-sectional quantitative study about AI recognition in tablet-based MCQ assessment among fifth-year undergraduate medical students at Saarland University, Germany. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10410-8
title: Maintain structured human expert oversight when integrating AI-generated MCQs into assessment
description: The article recommends that AI-generated MCQs enter assessment only within a structured review process in which "humans remain responsible for quality control". Because AI output can be indistinguishable from human-written items, undetected errors or biases could pass uncritically into exams; the authors state the findings "suggest maintaining human oversight to minimize AI mistakes and avoid a possible specialty bias". Reviewing, rather than drafting, is where educator effort shifts.
requirements: An expert panel reviews and validates every AI-generated item before exam use
Items requiring substantial content or structural revision are excluded rather than rewritten
constraints: Non-recognition of AI content "could lead to uncritical use on both sides"
AI output can carry structural biases from training data, such as the observed bias underestimating Family Medicine competency
target_learning_goals: valid and curriculum-aligned summative assessment of clinical decision-making
examples: In the study's exam, the expert panel eliminated 18.2% of initially generated MCQs and refined retained items to the German primary care and guideline context before use

article_title: Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics
citation: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703
title: MAESTRO v3.0.0 pretraining corpus and custom 4,320-recording student dataset
description: The study used two data sources. For initial pretraining of the CMT's feature extraction layers it used the MAESTRO v3.0.0 dataset (https://magenta.tensorflow.org/datasets/maestro, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), containing "approximately 200 h of solo piano performances (1,276 MIDI-aligned audio recordings)"; the authors argue solo-piano pretraining transfers to other tonal instruments because the CMT learns cross-modal alignment at the score-feature level. For the educational study it built a custom repository of approximately 4,320 audio recordings (120 participants × 12 weeks × 3 excerpts) totaling 2,160 minutes, annotated by two expert instructors with inter-annotator agreement κ = 0.87.
requirements: Participant-level split into training (70%, N = 84), validation (15%, N = 18) and test (15%, N = 18) partitions with no within-participant cross-partition leakage
Feature normalization using only training-set statistics to prevent information leakage
constraints: No participant, session, or musical excerpt overlap between the pretraining corpus and the student dataset; MAESTRO samples were used solely to initialize foundational layers
All model components were finalized before the 12-week intervention; the system operated solely in fixed-policy inference mode with no online learning
target_learners: undergraduate music majors with ≥ 3 years of formal training on piano, violin, flute or guitar
target_learning_goals: model pretraining for cross-modal audio-score alignment
evaluation of adaptive feedback in instrumental practice
examples: Repertoire covered Baroque (30%), Classical (35%), Romantic (20%), and Contemporary (15%) styles, with instruments distributed piano n = 48, violin n = 32, flute n = 24, guitar n = 16

article_title: Evidence and Theory for why the Best Example-Problem Ratio To Optimize Learning Gain Depends on Knowledge Content
citation: Rachatasumrit, N., Koedinger, K. R., & Carvalho, P. F. (2023). Evidence and theory for why the best example-problem ratio to optimize learning gain depends on knowledge content. https://osf.io/29wpe
title: Match the example-problem ratio to the knowledge content: favor practice testing for verbatim facts and example-integrated practice for general skills
description: This principle holds that the best mixture of worked examples and practice problems depends on the type of knowledge being learned. Because retrieval practice strengthens memory processes suited to constant-condition, constant-response content, while example study supports the inductive processes needed for variable-condition, variable-response skills, instruction should allocate more retrieval practice when teaching verbatim facts and more example study when teaching generalizable skills. The article demonstrates this cross-over empirically and computationally.
requirements: A classification of the target content as verbatim fact versus general skill, per the KLI taxonomy
constraints: The evidence comes from a short geometry-area task with a brief retention interval; the article notes testing gains may not extend to novel tasks per prior work it cites
target_learners: Adult learners (Mechanical Turk participants) learning geometry facts and skills
target_learning_goals: Verbatim fact retention
General skill acquisition and application
examples: Experiment 1 assigned participants to EPPP (one example then three practice trials) or EPEP (alternating example and practice trials) for facts or skills and measured pre-post gains
key_sources: Rachatasumrit, N., Koedinger, K. R., & Carvalho, P. F. (2023). Evidence and theory for why the best example-problem ratio to optimize learning gain depends on knowledge content. https://osf.io/29wpe

article_title: The care-full craft of feedback in an age of generative AI
citation: Winstone, N. E., Gravett, K., Bearman, M., Noble, C., Jensen, L. X., Jones, A., & Nicola-Richmond, K. (2026). The care-full craft of feedback in an age of generative AI. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 51(5), 911-927. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2643333
title: Manifesto for Feedback in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence (ten principles)
description: A manifesto produced by the author team (Winstone et al. 2025), summarised in Box 1 of the paper, comprising ten principles for feedback in the age of GenAI. It asserts, among others, that "Feedback is a process not corrective comments", that feedback is a relational practice and an ethical practice, that "Feedback can be enhanced by digital technologies, but digital technologies do not always enhance feedback", and that more feedback is not necessarily better for learning. The paper's four core values were identified in writing these principles.
requirements: Feedback engagement requires time and care; learning, not technological efficiency or compliance, should drive decision-making about feedback processes
constraints: The authors state the manifesto principles are not exhaustive
target_learning_goals: learning over time through feedback processes
examples: Principle 6 states feedback and associated technologies should be designed in conversation with learners and educators; principle 10 states more feedback is not necessarily better for learning

citation: Bin Liu, Xiaoli Sun, Jia Song. (2026). A hybrid collaborative filtering and knowledge graph-based cross-domain recommendation method for multimodal teaching resources. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100678
title: Preprocessed English subset of the MARS dataset for multimodal teaching resource recommendation
description: The evaluation corpus is the English-language subset of the publicly available MARS dataset, containing multimodal teaching resources (primarily videos with text descriptions, tags, and transcripts) plus user interaction logs. After preprocessing (users with fewer than five interactions removed, invalid logs filtered, engagement-based retention), "the final experimental subset contains 4,800 users, 14,200 teaching resources, and 132,000 interaction records collected over a 14-month period", including 6,200 text, 6,800 video, and 1,200 interactive resources, with interaction matrix sparsity of 0.9981.
requirements: Users with fewer than five interactions removed and invalid logs filtered before modeling
constraints: High sparsity (0.9981) means behavioral evidence alone is limited
Resource counts are reported by modality after preprocessing
target_learners: Learners of English interacting with multimodal teaching resources on the platform
target_learning_goals: Personalized recommendation of English teaching resources aligned with learner behavior and instructional needs
examples: Implicit positive feedback derived from interactions with view duration exceeding a predefined threshold or high completion ratio
