article_title: Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators.
citation: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209
title: Massing-aids-induction hypothesis (blocking advantage account)
description: The massing-aids-induction hypothesis, coined by Kornell and Bjork (2008) who do not advocate it, holds that "blocking enhances inductive learning by facilitating the recognition of similarities among nonidentical items within a category." It cannot explain positive interleaving effects but addresses the advantage of blocked over interleaved presentation, and may help interpret studies in which interleaving failed, such as word-material studies showing a blocking effect. The meta-analysis's negative effect for words is consistent with this account.
requirements: Applies when successful inductive learning depends on identifying features shared by exemplars within a category
constraints: Cannot explain positive interleaving effects; addresses only blocking advantages
target_learning_goals: inductive learning of concepts defined by shared features
examples: Sorensen and Woltz (2016) found interleaving led to poorer outcomes than blocking when items of different conceptual categories were words, a condition the article cites as consistent with this hypothesis.
key_sources: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209

article_title: Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis.
citation: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed Practice in Verbal Recall Tasks: A Review and Quantitative Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354
title: Choose the interstudy interval in relation to the intended retention interval
description: Because the ISI producing maximal retention increases as the retention interval increases, instruction should not fix one universally optimal spacing gap. The article states the practical stakes directly: "One can hardly select an ISI that optimizes instruction unless one knows how learning depends upon ISI; if that function varies with retention interval, this too must be considered in designing the most efficient procedures for pedagogy or training." Designers should therefore estimate how long learners will need to retain material and set spacing accordingly, keeping in mind that very long lags can produce smaller effects.
requirements: Knowledge of the target retention interval before selecting the ISI
constraints: The literature poorly represents combinations of long ISIs with long retention intervals, so precise optimal values for long delays remain uncertain
target_learners: learners of verbal information in instructional or training settings
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied verbal material
examples: The review's lag analyses found the optimal ISI bin increased as retention interval increased, and within-study studies (e.g., Cepeda et al., 2005; Gordon, 1925) showed subday ISIs optimal at subday retention intervals and supraday ISIs optimal at supraday retention intervals
key_sources: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed Practice in Verbal Recall Tasks: A Review and Quantitative Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354

article_title: Video improves learning in higher education: A systematic review
citation: Noetel, M., Griffith, S., Delaney, O., Sanders, T., Parker, P., del Pozo Cruz, B., & Lonsdale, C. (2021). Video Improves Learning in Higher Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research, 91(2), 204–236. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654321990713
title: Maintain or increase interactivity when moving teaching content to video
description: The review's discussion recommends that shifting didactic content onto video should not reduce the interactive opportunities students receive. It reports that "moving content to video is more effective when teachers maintain, or even increase, the level of active learning offered to students", and suggests online discussions and embedded questions (e.g., using H5p or EdPuzzle) can raise interactivity in multimedia. This frees face-to-face time for discussion and other dynamic interactions.
requirements: Video-based instruction must offer interactivity at least equivalent to the teaching it replaces, e.g., embedded questions or online discussion.
constraints: The review could not quantify effects of combined designs because they involve more than one independent variable; the interactivity moderation rested on a small subgroup (k = 8) for the most-interactive condition.
target_learning_goals: knowledge and skill acquisition in higher education courses
examples: The review found videos were effective when both conditions had equivalent interactivity (g = 0.33) and particularly effective when video conditions added interactivity such as co-viewing with a peer (g = 0.62), but showed no benefit when the control condition was more interactive.

article_title: Mad City Mystery: Developing Scientific Argumentation Skills with a Place-based Augmented Reality Game on Handheld Computers
citation: Squire, K.D., Jan, M. (2007). Mad City Mystery: Developing Scientific Argumentation Skills with a Place-based Augmented Reality Game on Handheld Computers. J Sci Educ Technol 16, 5–29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-006-9037-z
title: Mad City Mystery: a place-based augmented reality curriculum on handheld computers for environmental science
description: Mad City Mystery is an Augmented Reality curriculum used on handheld computers to support learning in environmental science, investigated across three cases in a design-based research study. The game places students in an environmental mystery (involving possible contamination, e.g. mercury and PCBs) where they interpret readings and build arguments. The authors investigate "whether augmented reality games on handhelds can be used to engage students in scientific thinking (particularly argumentation), how game structures affect students' thinking, the impact of role playing on learning, and the role of the physical environment in shaping learning."
requirements: Handheld computers running the augmented reality platform and a physical location to play in
constraints: The authors acknowledge that time constraints alone might disqualify the game from being considered authentic in any meaningful respect
target_learners: students in environmental science (roughly 28 students across three cases)
target_learning_goals: scientific argumentation
environmental science reasoning
examples: Students interpreted a marginally high mercury reading as evidence in the environment; the authors note the group was probably justified in that interpretation but not in throwing out their hypothesis altogether

article_title: When is PBL More Effective? A Meta-synthesis of Meta-analyses Comparing PBL to Conventional Classrooms
citation: Strobel, J., & van Barneveld, A. (2009). When is PBL More Effective? A Meta-synthesis of Meta-analyses Comparing PBL to Conventional Classrooms. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-Based Learning, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1046
title: Match the choice between PBL and conventional instruction to the targeted retention horizon and outcome
description: Because the meta-analytic evidence shows divergent advantages by outcome type, instructional designers should choose PBL when the goal is long-term retention, skill development, or learner and teacher satisfaction, and conventional instruction when the goal is short-term retention on standardized board exams. The synthesis found "PBL was superior when it comes to long-term retention, skill development and satisfaction of students and teachers, while traditional approaches were more effective for short-term retention as measured by standardized board exams."
requirements: Clarity about which outcome matters for the program: long-term retention and skills versus short-term standardized exam performance
constraints: The short-term retention evidence is specific to standardized board exams as the outcome measure
target_learners: students in higher education and professional programs using PBL
target_learning_goals: long-term retention, skill development, satisfaction, standardized exam performance
examples: The meta-synthesis compared PBL with traditional instruction across meta-analyses and found the advantage flips depending on whether the outcome is long-term retention and skills or short-term board-exam performance.

article_title: ONE SIZE FITS ALL?: Recasts, Prompts, and L2 Learning
citation: Ahlem Ammar and Nina Spada. (2006). ONE SIZE FITS ALL?: Recasts, Prompts, and L2 Learning. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 28, Issue 4. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060268
title: Match corrective feedback technique to learner proficiency: prefer prompts for lower-proficiency learners
description: The article's proficiency-moderated findings support tailoring oral corrective feedback to learner proficiency rather than applying one technique to all learners. Because "low-proficiency learners benefited significantly more from prompts than recasts," while high-proficiency learners benefited equally from both, prompts are the safer default for lower-proficiency learners, and recasts remain a viable option for higher-proficiency learners.
requirements: Teachers must be able to assess or distinguish learner proficiency levels when choosing feedback techniques
constraints: Evidence concerns one grammatical structure (his and her) with young Francophone ESL learners in intensive grade 6 classes; the article's available text does not establish generalization to other structures or populations
target_learners: Grade 6 intensive ESL learners of varying proficiency
target_learning_goals: Improving grammatical accuracy through oral corrective feedback
examples: In the study, prompts and recasts were embedded in instruction on his and her across three intact grade 6 classes over 4 weeks
key_sources: Ahlem Ammar and Nina Spada. (2006). ONE SIZE FITS ALL?: Recasts, Prompts, and L2 Learning. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 28, Issue 4. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060268

article_title: Studying Visual Displays: How to Instructionally Support Learning
citation: Renkl, A., & Scheiter, K. (2017). Studying Visual Displays: How to Instructionally Support Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9340-4
title: Taxonomy of instructional support for visual displays: material-oriented versus learner-oriented interventions
description: The review organizes empirically tested support procedures for learning from visual displays along one axis: whether the intervention changes the learning material or the learner. Material-oriented interventions modify the displays themselves, "for example, reducing the visual displays' complexity, cueing/signaling, or physically integrating text and pictures." Learner-oriented interventions instead target the person, referring to "the training of learning prerequisites, pre-training, and prompting." This two-branch taxonomy structures the review's overview of effectiveness evidence.
requirements: Applies to learning from visual displays in learning materials, where support procedures have been empirically tested
target_learners: Learners working with visual displays in learning materials
target_learning_goals: Learning from pictures and multimedia materials
Comprehension of multiple representations
examples: The review's overview of effectiveness evidence is structured by this distinction, with material-oriented examples such as cueing/signaling and learner-oriented examples such as pre-training and prompting.
key_sources: Renkl, A., & Scheiter, K. (2017). Studying Visual Displays: How to Instructionally Support Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9340-4

article_title: Peer Assessment Enhances Student Learning: The Results of a Matched Randomized Crossover Experiment in a College Statistics Class
citation: Sun DL, Harris N, Walther G, Baiocchi M (2015) Peer Assessment Enhances Student Learning: The Results of a Matched Randomized Crossover Experiment in a College Statistics Class. PLoS ONE 10(12): e0143177. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0143177
title: Matched randomized crossover design for within-student comparison of an instructional treatment
description: A course-level experimental pattern in which each student serves as their own control across units of a course. Students are assigned to treatment and control in different orders over the units (e.g., TCTC, CTCT, TCCT, CTTC), which, as the authors note, "eliminates what is arguably the largest source of variability in educational studies: variation between students." Matching students on covariates before assigning complementary treatments further guards against baseline differences.
requirements: A course with multiple parallel units so each student can experience both treatment and control; covariate information (e.g., class year, previous statistics experience) for matched-pairs randomization; blinded grading of assessments.
constraints: Excluding non-compliers estimates the effect on the subpopulation of students who would be affected by the intervention, as the authors state.
target_learners: students in multi-unit courses, such as large college classes
target_learning_goals: estimating the causal effect of an instructional treatment on achievement
examples: In the study, each student participated in peer assessment for exactly two of four main units and control for the other two, with matched-pairs randomization on covariates.

article_title: HOW DOES PRIOR WORD KNOWLEDGE AFFECT VOCABULARY LEARNING PROGRESS IN AN EXTENSIVE READING PROGRAM?
citation: Stuart Webb and Anna C.-S. Chang. (2015). HOW DOES PRIOR WORD KNOWLEDGE AFFECT VOCABULARY LEARNING PROGRESS IN AN EXTENSIVE READING PROGRAM? Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 37, Issue 4, pp. 651-675. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263114000606
title: Match extensive reading materials to learners' prior vocabulary knowledge, because prior word knowledge shapes vocabulary learning progress
description: The article's results indicate that "prior vocabulary knowledge may have a large impact on the amount of vocabulary learning made through extensive reading": learners with higher prior knowledge gained more (63.18%) than lower-knowledge learners (28.12%). This supports matching graded reader difficulty and vocabulary demands to learners' existing vocabulary size so that extensive reading yields vocabulary growth for all proficiency levels.
requirements: Assessment of learners' prior vocabulary knowledge (e.g., pretests of target vocabulary and Vocabulary Levels Test scores) before selecting reading materials
constraints: Evidence comes from EFL learners reading Level 1 and Level 2 graded readers; the abstract reports relative gains without effect sizes or significance tests
target_learners: English as a foreign language learners at high, intermediate, and low vocabulary levels
target_learning_goals: Incidental vocabulary learning and retention through extensive reading
examples: In the study, learners were divided into high-, intermediate-, and low-level groups based on pretest and Vocabulary Levels Test scores before reading graded readers.

article_title: A Systematic Review Mapping of AI Literacy Progression in K–12
citation: National Science and Technology Council, Committee on Technology. (2016). Preparing for the Future of Artificial Intelligence. Executive Office of the President. https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp
title: Machine learning as statistical learning from data, contrasted with expert systems
description: The report defines modern machine learning as "a statistical process that starts with a body of data and tries to derive a rule or procedure that explains the data or can predict future data." This learning-from-data approach contrasts with the older expert-system approach, in which programmers translate human experts' rules into code. The report describes training (adjusting model parameters to maximize an objective function), test-set evaluation, and generalization to unseen cases as the core workflow.
requirements: Applying machine learning requires a historical data set divided into training and test sets, a chosen model with adjustable parameters, and a defined objective function
constraints: The report states it is typically not possible to extract a straightforward explanation for why a trained model is effective, and even the best models can fail in unpredictable ways, such as on adversarial images
target_learners: students learning AI or data science
target_learning_goals: understanding how machine learning differs from rule-based expert systems
understanding training, evaluation, and generalization
examples: The report's fraud-detection example: a company uses a labeled data set of past login attempts to derive a rule predicting which future attempts are likely fraudulent

article_title: Knowledge as a formative construct: A good alpha is not always better
citation: Stadler, Matthias, Michael Sailer, and Frank Fischer. 2021. “Knowledge as a formative construct: a good alpha is not always better.” New Ideas in Psychology 60: 100832. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.newideapsych.2020.100832.
title: Match a knowledge assessment's measurement model to the construct's theoretical conceptualization before applying scale-quality criteria
description: The article argues researchers should check whether their theoretical conceptualization of a construct is represented in its empirical operationalization before applying reflective scale-development criteria. It concludes with the hope that researchers "review their assessments of domain knowledge" and consider whether conceptualization matches operationalization, since a mismatch "can lead to critical misrepresentation and misinterpretation".
requirements: A clear theoretical construct definition, including arguments for and against each indicator, is pivotal for formative models.
constraints: The article notes other, more general issues with Cronbach's alpha exist that it could not discuss, referring readers to Trizano-Hermosilla and Alvarado (2016).
target_learners: students whose knowledge is measured in educational and psychological research
target_learning_goals: valid measurement and modeling of domain knowledge
examples: The article's illustrative case is biology knowledge defined as five distinct disciplines, where choosing different disciplines would change the assumed latent construct.
key_sources: Stadler, Matthias, Michael Sailer, and Frank Fischer. 2021. “Knowledge as a formative construct: a good alpha is not always better.” New Ideas in Psychology 60: 100832. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.newideapsych.2020.100832.

article_title: The effects of hypertext glosses on L2 vocabulary acquisition: a meta-analysis
citation: Yun, J. H. (2008). The Effects of Hypertext Glosses on L2 Vocabulary Acquisition: A Meta-Analysis. Doctoral dissertation, University of Kansas. https://kuscholarworks.ku.edu
title: Mayer's Generative Theory of Multimedia Learning as the theoretical basis for hypertext gloss effects on L2 vocabulary
description: The dissertation adopts Mayer's Generative Theory of Multimedia Learning, built on Paivio's dual coding theory, as its organizing framework. It holds that the brain has separate visual and verbal coding systems, and that "both pictorial and written input collaboratively enhance L2 readers' reading comprehension and vocabulary learning" when learners integrate the two representations. Learners must select relevant verbal and visual information, build coherent verbal and visual mental representations, and connect them. The framework motivates the text + visual versus text-only comparison tested in the meta-analysis.
requirements: Learners must be cognitively capable of dealing with both written and pictorial information at the same time, as the article states better vocabulary learning with multimedia input is more likely under that condition.
constraints: The article notes low-proficiency learners are less likely to take advantage of multimedia learning environments due to high cognitive load when given two types of annotations, so multimedia input does not always enhance all learners' vocabulary performance.
target_learners: L2 learners (ESL/EFL, SFL, JFL, GFL) at university or college level reading computerized texts
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary acquisition during computerized reading
Reading comprehension of authentic L2 texts
examples: The dissertation's meta-analysis of text-only versus text + visual gloss conditions was framed as a test of this theory's prediction that combined verbal and pictorial input benefits vocabulary learning.
key_sources: Yun, J. H. (2008). The Effects of Hypertext Glosses on L2 Vocabulary Acquisition: A Meta-Analysis. Doctoral dissertation, University of Kansas. https://kuscholarworks.ku.edu

article_title: Cognitive and emotional math problems largely dissociate: Prevalence of developmental dyscalculia and mathematics anxiety.
citation: Devine, A., Hill, F., Carey, E., & Szűcs, D. (2017). Cognitive and Emotional Math Problems Largely Dissociate: Prevalence of Developmental Dyscalculia and Mathematics Anxiety.
title: Competing accounts of the MA–performance relationship: the Deficit Theory, the Debilitating Anxiety Model, and the Reciprocal Theory
description: The article reviews three explanatory accounts of the negative MA–performance association. The Deficit Theory "claims that anxiety emerges a result of an awareness of poor mathematics performance in the past". The Debilitating Anxiety Model posits that high anxiety interferes with performance via disruption of pre-processing, processing and retrieval, and via avoidance of mathematics-related situations. The Reciprocal Theory holds the relationship functions bidirectionally as a vicious circle. The article argues the two models may operate simultaneously and that its comorbidity findings qualify the Deficit Theory.
requirements: Distinguishing the models requires study designs sensitive to their different time courses: longitudinal studies for the Deficit Theory, experimental studies for the Debilitating Anxiety Model.
constraints: The article states the evidence supporting the two models is in conflict and that its own cross-sectional design could not determine the direction of the association.
target_learners: primary and secondary school children (8- to 13-year-olds)
target_learning_goals: mathematics performance
mathematics anxiety
examples: The article cites longitudinal data (Luo et al., 2014; Cargnelutti et al., 2016) suggesting the MA–performance relationship functions reciprocally.
key_sources: Devine, A., Hill, F., Carey, E., & Szűcs, D. (2017). Cognitive and Emotional Math Problems Largely Dissociate: Prevalence of Developmental Dyscalculia and Mathematics Anxiety. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000222

article_title: Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition?
citation: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0
title: Macrocognition: cognition in naturalistic, ill-defined decision settings, complementary to microcognition
description: The article presents macrocognition, introduced by Cacciabue and Hollnagel and elaborated by Klein et al., as a descriptor for cognitive activities in natural decision-making settings. Klein et al. "mention phenomena like the following: planning and problem detection using leverage points to construct options, attention management, and uncertainty management." The author argues the key difference from microcognition is "the ill-defined conditions of the tasks and problems under consideration", and that the two approaches are complementary; he contends lab research is not necessarily restricted to microcognition.
requirements: Study settings with ill-defined tasks, whether in the field or in high-external-validity labs and simulators
constraints: The article argues against the belief that macrocognition can only be analyzed outside the lab
target_learners: experienced professionals making decisions in dynamic environments
target_learning_goals: situation assessment, decision making, attention and uncertainty management
examples: Naturalistic Decision Making studies experienced people in dynamic, uncertain, fast-paced environments
key_sources: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0

article_title: A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology.:
citation: Ellen P. Hall, Sherrie P. Gott, Robert A. Pokorny. (1995). A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology. Armstrong Laboratory, Human Resources Directorate, Brooks AFB, Texas. AL/HR-TR-1995-0108
title: Make the reasons for task performance (conceptual support knowledge) explicit for teaching
description: Instruction for complex problem solving should go beyond teaching observable procedure steps and explicitly teach the conceptual support knowledge — why procedures work, when they apply, and what results mean — that underlies adaptive performance. The report states "Making the reasons for task performance explicit (i.e., specifying this conceptual support knowledge) is therefore a central goal of the PARI approach." Such knowledge gives meaning to procedure steps, enables invention of new procedures, and supports reconstruction of forgotten ones in novel situations.
requirements: Task analysis must capture declarative and strategic knowledge, not only procedural knowledge, which requires situated rather than decontextualized elicitation
constraints: The report notes routinized-procedure training remains appropriate for some stable tasks; the principle targets dynamic, unstable task environments where novel situations are frequently encountered
target_learners: Technical trainees preparing for adaptive troubleshooting in complex systems
target_learning_goals: Adaptive application of procedures to novel problem situations
examples: PARI interviews probe experts for the reasons behind actions and interpretations of results during situated problem-solving sessions, and the resulting models guide instruction targeting all three knowledge components

article_title: Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles
citation: Wang, M. & Shen, R. (2012). Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles. British Journal of Educational Technology, 43(4), 561-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2011.01214.x
title: Mayer's multimedia message design principles as a framework for mLearning message design
description: The article presents Mayer and Moreno's theory of multimedia learning as the most widely cited approach to message design, drawing on dual-coding theory, working memory, cognitive load theory and the SOI model. It states that the theory "generates principles for overcoming common types of cognitive overload by building coherence, providing learning cues, creating spatial and temporal contiguity, and reducing redundancy". The article argues these principles are applicable to mLearning, citing the Multiple Modality principle as a guideline for mobile content.
requirements: Designers need a deep understanding of how people learn and how cognition works in realistic settings to organize learning messages appropriately
constraints: Mayer's principles were developed for online and computer-based learning and had not been tested for mobile learning at the time of writing
target_learners: mobile learners in formal and informal settings
target_learning_goals: effective design of instructional messages for mobile devices
examples: The article applies the Multiple Modality principle, advocating explanations in pictures with annotated graphics and related audio, as a guideline for designing mobile content

article_title: Math Mindsets and Academic Grit: How Are They Related to Primary Math Achievement?
citation: Kaya, S., & Karakoc, D. (2022). Math Mindsets and Academic Grit: How Are They Related to Primary Math Achievement?. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 10(3), 298-309. https://doi.org/10.30935/scimath/11881
title: Domain-specific math mindset framework (fixed vs growth math mindsets)
description: The article applies Dweck's self-theories to mathematics: students hold either a "fixed math mindset", believing math capability "is innate and fixed", or a "growth math mindset", believing capability "can be developed with practice or instruction". Mindsets are treated as domain-specific, so a person can hold a growth mindset in one field and a fixed one in another. The study measures both with an adapted 6-item scale and models their direct and grit-mediated effects on achievement.
requirements: Domain-specific measurement, since general mindset instruments are argued to explain school achievement less well
constraints: Mindsets tend to be domain-specific and exist independently across domains
target_learning_goals: math achievement
motivational beliefs about math intelligence
examples: Adapted Dweck items such as: you can change your math intelligence a lot (growth) versus you have a certain amount of math intelligence you cannot change (fixed)

article_title: The role of domain-general cognitive abilities and decimal labels in at-risk fourth-grade students' decimal magnitude understanding
citation: Malone Amelia S., Loehr Abbey M., Fuchs Lynn S. (2017). The Role of Domain-General Cognitive Abilities and Decimal Labels in At-Risk Fourth-Grade Students' Decimal Magnitude Understanding. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2017.05.007
title: Use magnitude language (place value labels) when defining decimals to reduce whole-number misconceptions
description: The article recommends that decimal instruction always use place value labels (e.g., reading 0.12 as "twelve hundredths") because such magnitude language supports students' decimal magnitude understanding and reduces misconceptions that decimals behave like whole numbers. The recommendation draws on the study's label correlations and prior label research. The authors caution that "more work is needed to assess the tenability of these recommendations."
requirements: Instruction must consistently use place value labels when naming decimals
constraints: Very little research exists on improving at-risk students' decimal magnitude understanding; tenability not yet assessed
target_learning_goals: decimal magnitude understanding
rational number reasoning
examples: The study correlated students' spontaneous decimal label use with their accuracy on three magnitude tasks

article_title: Math Anxiety in Students With and Without Math Learning Difficulties
citation: Yılmaz Mutlu. (2019). Math Anxiety in Students With and Without Math Learning Difficulties. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 11(5), 471-475. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2019553343
title: Reciprocal relationship model among math anxiety, poor math performance, and working memory
description: The article presents a model (Figure 1) depicting reciprocal relationships among math anxiety, poor math performance, and lack of working memory. It is generally accepted that "the math anxiety affects negatively the mathematical performance by distorting sources of working memory," and learning difficulties in mathematics relate to deficiencies in the central executive of working memory. The model draws on studies the article reviews.
requirements: The model presumes tasks whose performance depends on working memory resources
constraints: The article states it is not clear to what extent math anxiety affects mathematical difficulties and how much the experience of difficulties causes anxiety
target_learners: elementary school students, especially third graders
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement and reduction of math anxiety
examples: Figure 1 in the article depicts the reciprocal relationships among math anxiety, poor math performance, and lack of working memory

article_title: Working memory, math performance, and math anxiety
citation: Mark H. Ashcraft and Jeremy A. Krause. (2007). Working memory, math performance, and math anxiety. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 14(2), 243-248.
title: Math anxiety functions like a resource-demanding secondary task that compromises working memory during math processing
description: The article proposes that "High math anxiety works much like a dual task setting: Preoccupation with one’s math fears and anxieties functions like a resource-demanding secondary task". This account explains why math anxiety harms performance only when the anxiety is actually aroused, why computation-based span tasks reveal compromised working memory while verbal span tasks do not, and why highly anxious participants suffer most when a secondary task occupies working memory during demanding math. It frames math anxiety as a malleable individual difference with measurable cognitive consequences.
requirements: The anxiety must be actually aroused by the task, as in span tasks that involve computations, for working memory resources to be drained
constraints: The article notes this account is being refined, stating they are currently exploring other ways in which this diversion of working memory affects the outcomes of mental processing
target_learners: high school and college students in math coursework
target_learning_goals: arithmetic and mathematics performance
math achievement on standardized tests
working memory capacity during computation
examples: The dual-task addition experiment in which highly anxious participants, already wasting working memory resources by attending to their own anxiety, suffered the most in the six-letter load condition with carry problems
key_sources: Mark H. Ashcraft and Jeremy A. Krause. (2007). Working memory, math performance, and math anxiety. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 14(2), 243-248. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03194059

article_title: A Longitudinal Investigation of the Role of Quantity and Quality of Child-Directed Speech in Vocabulary Development
citation: Rowe Meredith L. (2012). A longitudinal investigation of the role of quantity and quality of child-directed speech in vocabulary development. Child development. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3440540/
title: Match input type to child age: quantity for toddlers, diverse and sophisticated vocabulary for two-and-a-half-year-olds, decontextualized talk for preschoolers
description: The article recommends that parents concentrate on the quality of their talk in age-appropriate ways. As the authors conclude, "it would also be helpful for parents to concentrate on the quality of their talk, incorporating a diverse and sophisticated vocabulary with toddlers and engaging their preschool children in conversations about past or future events." This principle follows from the finding that different input dimensions predicted later vocabulary at different ages with SES and quantity controlled.
requirements: Knowledge of the child's current age and language ability
Caregiver capacity to produce diverse vocabulary and decontextualized talk
constraints: Evidence base is one longitudinal study of 50 dyads
SES confounded with race in the sample
target_learners: parents and caregivers of children aged 18 to 54 months
target_learning_goals: receptive vocabulary development
examples: Parents who used more different words or rare words with 30-month-olds had children with larger vocabularies one year later
Parents who produced more narrative utterances with 42-month-olds had children with larger vocabularies one year later

article_title: Math Circles: A Tool for Promoting Engagement Among Middle School Minority Males
citation: Eugene Kennedy & Lawrence Smolinsky (2016). Math Circles: A Tool for Promoting Engagement among Middle School Minority Males. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 12(4), 717-732. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2016.1223a
title: Math circles as enculturation into the community of professional mathematicians
description: The article frames a math circle as "a social structure where participants engage in the depths and intricacies of mathematical thinking, propagate the culture of doing mathematics, and create knowledge." Rooted in Eastern European practice, a professional mathematician inducts youth into the culture of mathematics—its games, talk, reasoning, heroes, myths and values—often in the mathematicians' own workplace. Participation is theorized as enculturation: appropriating the language, values, and habits of mind of the discipline and developing a personal mathematical identity, drawing on a socio-cultural, constructivist view of mathematical learning.
requirements: A professional mathematician willing to spend time with youth and lead the induction into mathematical culture
constraints: The article notes there is only limited research on math circle dynamics, especially for minorities and under-represented groups
target_learning_goals: mathematical thinking and reasoning
positive mathematical identity
appreciation of mathematical culture
examples: The circle met in the mathematics department lounge, where students encountered artifacts such as a Rubik's Cube, a chess set, and blackboards with complex equations left by graduate students

article_title: Tracking Grade 10 learners’ geometric reasoning through folding back
citation: Mabotja, S., Chuene, K., Maoto, S., & Kibirige, I. (2018). Tracking Grade 10 learners' geometric reasoning through folding back. Pythagoras, 39(1), a371. https://doi.org/10.4102/pythagoras.v39i1.371
title: Martin's elaborated framework for describing folding back: source, form and outcome
description: Martin (2008) expands Pirie and Kieren's notion of folding back with three key elements: 'source of intervention, form of actions that leads to folding back and outcome of folding back'. Sources can be teacher, material, peer or self, and are intentional or unintentional, explicit or unfocused. Forms include working at an inner layer using existing understanding, collecting at an inner layer, moving out of topic and working there, and causing a discontinuity. Outcomes are effective or ineffective depending on whether folding back enables further understanding at an outer layer. The study adopted these elements to guide both data analysis and the tracking of learners' geometric reasoning.
requirements: Analysis requires identifying, in learners' conversations, the source of the intervention, the form of folding back, and the outcome of folding back.
constraints: Forms that cause a discontinuity do not result in thickening or enriched understanding of the existing concept.
target_learning_goals: Geometric reasoning through folding back
examples: In Extract 3 the teacher's intentional, explicit intervention directed learners to collect at an inner layer using co-interior angles, an effective form of folding back.

citation: Powell, S. R., Fuchs, L. S., Fuchs, D., Cirino, P. T., & Fletcher, J. M. (2009). title: Math Flash computer-assisted instruction for math fact practice
description: Math Flash is the computer-assisted instruction program used in both fact retrieval tutoring conditions. "In Math Flash, the student was presented with an addition or subtraction math fact with the answer; the math fact flashed on the screen for a second or two," after which the student typed the fact from memory while a number line shaded to represent addends or minuend and subtrahend. Correct answers earned sparkling numbers and applause; incorrect facts reappeared until typed correctly, and flashing speed adapted to performance, with treasure rewards for each five correct facts.
requirements: Tutor supervision during the 7.5-minute computer session
target_learning_goals: Automatic retrieval of addition and subtraction facts
examples: Used 7.5 minutes per session within FR-P and FR-C/P tutoring, three sessions per week over 15 weeks.

article_title: Enriching Mathematics Education with Visual Arts: Effects on Elementary School Students’ Ability in Geometry and Visual Arts
citation: Eveline M. Schoevers & Paul P. M. Leseman & Evelyn H. Kroesbergen. (2019). Enriching Mathematics Education with Visual Arts: Effects on Elementary School Students' Ability in Geometry and Visual Arts. International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10763-019-10018-z
title: The MACE pedagogy: five key features for integrating geometry and visual arts
description: The MACE pedagogy is an explanatory framework for integrated geometry and visual arts instruction built on five features the article names: "visual arts perception, open activities, reflection, communication with peers, and a specific role of the teacher". Artworks are discussed whole-class with visual thinking strategies; open activities invite artwork production at the boundary of the two disciplines without predetermined solutions; lessons end with reflection making implicit knowledge explicit; peer communication supports creative thinking and geometrical language; and teachers act as facilitators asking open, activating questions. The framework underpins the MACE lesson series and PD program evaluated in the study.

Whole-class discussion of artworks, e.g. with an interactive whiteboard and visual thinking strategies
constraints: The article's evaluation found the PD component added no measurable student outcome effect beyond the lesson series and manual

target_learning_goals: geometrical ability (understanding and explaining geometric phenomena, geometrical vocabulary, creative geometrical problem solving)
visual arts perception
examples: In the lesson Playing with perspective, students discussed six artworks on perspective and viewpoints, then made photos creating visual illusions in groups of 3-4 students, followed by whole-class reflection

article_title: Enriching Mathematics Education with Visual Arts: Effects on Elementary School Students’ Ability in Geometry and Visual Arts
citation: Eveline M. Schoevers & Paul P. M. Leseman & Evelyn H. Kroesbergen. (2019). Enriching Mathematics Education with Visual Arts: Effects on Elementary School Students' Ability in Geometry and Visual Arts. International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10763-019-10018-z
title: MACE program: nine integrated geometry-visual-arts lessons plus a five-session teacher professional development program
description: The MACE program is an instructional program consisting of "a lesson series for fourth, fifth, and sixth grade students in which geometry and visual arts education were integrated along with a PD program for teachers". The lesson series comprised nine lessons of 60-90 minutes each (five on the theme space, four on patterns), each with a whole-class introduction discussing artworks, an open activity in which students create an artwork in small groups, and a whole-class reflection. The PD program consisted of five 2.5-hour expert-guided sessions with interactive methods, with teachers teaching one or two MACE lessons after each session. It was evaluated in a quasi-experiment with 2909 students in 121 classes and 57 schools.
requirements: Teachers deliver the lesson series; the PD program is optional but was designed to assist implementation
constraints: Schools had to be within traveling distance of PD training locations, so random assignment of schools was not fully possible
target_learners: fourth, fifth, and sixth grade elementary students in the Netherlands
target_learning_goals: geometry curriculum goals
visual arts perception
creative skills in both disciplines
examples: A pilot study with 15 teachers formatively evaluated an initial version of the program before the main study

article_title: Material syntonicity: Examining computational performance and its materiality through weaving and sewing crafts
citation: Anna Keune (2022). Material syntonicity: Examining computational performance and its materiality through weaving and sewing crafts. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2022.2100704
title: Material syntonicity: ongoing physical intra-action with materials shapes what can be learned computationally
description: Material syntonicity extends Papert's body syntonicity with posthumanist perspectives, shifting attention to the ongoing physical aspects of domain learning. The article theorizes "this ongoing intra-action as material syntonicity, which shifts attention to the ongoing physical aspects of domain learning," capturing how students and craft materials come together and move apart to produce disciplinary phenomena. It disrupts assumptions about the neutrality of dominant notions of computing such as computing as automation, since what counts as computation was contingent on the material: weaving drove automation while fabric manipulation drove speculative 3D modeling.
requirements: Materials must be manipulable tangible media with which learners bodily intra-act during domain performance, as in the matrix-based fiber crafts studied.
constraints: The theory was developed from two matrix-based fiber crafts (weaving and fabric manipulation) in one middle school design studio setting; the article presents it as a material direction for computing education rather than a tested intervention.
target_learning_goals: computational concepts (variables, conditionals, functions)
broadening what counts as computing
examples: Devanie's weaving moved from irregular skip patterns to regular hourglass patterns as she and the loom repeated intra-actions; Aki's sewing produced folds that counteracted one another through knot-stitch functions on the fabric matrix.

article_title: The mechanics of CSCL macro scripts
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg, Fabrice Hong. (2008). The mechanics of CSCL macro scripts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://hal.science/hal-00692019
title: Macro scripts as a lesson-level pattern structuring collaborative learning
description: Macro scripts are a reusable unit-level design for collaborative activities: "Macro scripts structure collaborative learning and foster the emergence of knowledge-productive interactions such as argumentation, explanations and mutual regulation". The pattern operates at the level of whole activity sequences (phases) rather than moment-to-moment prompts, shaping who works with whom, with what resources, toward what products.
requirements: A collaborative task and a phased script structure that can perturb team convergence
target_learners: student teams in computer-supported collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: argumentation, explanations and mutual regulation among team members
examples: Three scripts are used in the article to illustrate the model

article_title: Bringing maker practices to school: tracing discursive and materially mediated aspects of student teams’ collaborative making processes
citation: Riikonen, S., Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, P., & Hakkarainen, K. (2020). Bringing maker practices to school: tracing discursive and materially mediated aspects of student teams' collaborative making processes. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09330-6
title: Making-Process-Rug video-analysis method
description: The Making-Process-Rug is a visual video-analysis method developed by the authors to trace "social-discursive, materially mediated, individual, and collaborative making processes" across a longitudinal co-invention project. Video is coded in fixed three-minute segments in ELAN using a sociomaterialgetCode template, then converted into layered, color-coded diagrams resembling woven rag rugs that show how verbal and embodied actions intertwine over time. It enables macro-level overview and later zooming to micro-level events such as process organizing, and quantitative comparison of action proportions.
requirements: a systematic coding template adapted to the study's purpose
fixed three-minute segmentation of video data in the ELAN multimedia annotator
constraints: segments with no analyzable action are removed, so rugs reflect adjusted usable video data
target_learners: student teams of adolescents in collaborative making projects
target_learning_goals: characterizing how collaborative invention processes unfold over time
examples: Applied to five seventh-grade teams' roughly 65 h of usable video; rugs revealed model making as the most prominent activity in the four successful teams.
Two teams were independently coded by two investigators to check coding reliability.
key_sources: Riikonen, S., Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, P., & Hakkarainen, K. (2020). Bringing maker practices to school: tracing discursive and materially mediated aspects of student teams' collaborative making processes. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. article_title: Self-efficacy and behavior patterns of learners using a real-time collaboration system developed for group programming
citation: Ting-Chia Hsu, Hal Abelson, Evan Patton, Shih-Chu Chen, Hsuan-Ning Chang. (2021). Self-efficacy and behavior patterns of learners using a real-time collaboration system developed for group programming. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09357-3
title: MAI real-time collaboration platform for synchronous multi-user block-based programming
description: The article extended MIT App Inventor with a real-time collaboration mode that "allows users to co-edit their blocks in the program", like a Google Document, while sharing components and notes. The current version added "a chat room for each group and an annotation function for each block" so collaborators can discuss changes in real time, making instant co-creation at a distance feasible in the block-based programming environment.
requirements: Users work on the web-based MAI platform, which has Designer and Blocks environments, during the programming task
constraints: The study does not investigate effects on learning of programming or production of high quality software; CPSE is the main success variable
target_learners: adult learners in higher education, both CS majors and non-CS majors
target_learning_goals: computational thinking through collaborative block-based app development
examples: Thirteen adult learners in six groups used the RTC platform for two collaborative projects of approximately 50 minutes in a half-day workshop

article_title: Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects
citation: Sini Davies, Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, Kai Hakkarainen. (2024). Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09427-2
title: Making-Process-Rug video analysis framework for co-invention processes
description: A video analysis framework for tracing situationally interleaving social and material aspects of maker-centered collaborative learning. It provides "a systematic approach to examine situationally interleaving social and material aspects of knowledge-creating learning from video data" through pre-defined coding schemes, 3-min segment coding in ELAN, and graphical timeline charts (co-invention process rugs) that render patterns across design-process, computing, product-design, and science practices and teacher/tutor engagement visible.
requirements: Video data of the collaborative process, a pre-defined coding scheme with analytic themes and coding categories, and coding software (ELAN)
constraints: The 3-min segmentation is described by the authors as relatively coarse but as having provided a good overall insight into the teams' design and making processes
target_learners: researchers and educators analyzing maker-centered and materially mediated collaborative learning
target_learning_goals: portraying temporal trajectories of collaborative learning and epistemic practices in artifact making
examples: Applied to the three teams' co-invention process rugs; inter-rater reliability on the first two SleepSound sessions yielded Cohen's kappa of 0.865 with a standard error of 0.063, 'indicating almost perfect agreement'

article_title: How gaze and proxemics shape and signal shared regulatory processes during AI-supported collaborative learning
citation: Ridwan Whitehead · Andy Nguyen · Sanna Järvelä. (2026). How gaze and proxemics shape and signal shared regulatory processes during AI-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09478-7
title: MAI metacognitive AI agent, adaptive and static support conditions
description: Metacognitive Artificial Intelligence (MAI) (Edwards et al., 2024) is an experimental AI agent integrated into the classroom to support students' metacognitive engagement during group problem solving. In the adaptive condition it "delivered adaptive, real-time feedback contingent on the groups' ongoing activities, with prompts triggered by live transcript analysis that detected specific regulatory challenge categories." Four comparison groups received static support: "the MAI provided a fixed sequence of three prompts at predetermined intervals that were not responsive to the groups' immediate actions," scheduled at 5–8, 10–20, and 20–30 min.
requirements: Live transcript analysis capable of detecting regulatory challenge categories for adaptive triggering
constraints: Static prompts at predetermined intervals were evaluated as nonresponsive to groups' immediate actions; one static-condition episode recorded a disengaged response
target_learners: secondary school students aged 12–14 in groups of 3–4
target_learning_goals: metacognitive engagement and shared regulation during collaborative group problem solving
examples: In one adaptive-condition episode around 53 min into the task, MAI detected a cognitive challenge and asked "Do you understand all the key concepts of the task?", after which the group converged gaze and shifted closer before enacting a strategy
key_sources: Ridwan Whitehead · Andy Nguyen · Sanna Järvelä. (2026). How gaze and proxemics shape and signal shared regulatory processes during AI-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09478-7

article_title: It matters how to recall – task differences in retrieval practice
citation: Tino Endres, Lena Kranzdorf, Vivien Schneider, Alexander Renkl. (2020). It matters how to recall – task differences in retrieval practice. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09526-1
title: Match the type of retrieval-practice task to the educational goal and the breadth of the learning content
description: The article recommends that teachers choose recall tasks according to their goals: "when teachers decide on a task type for retrieval practice, they should also take the nature of the learning contents into account". Specific short-answer tasks suit materials with a few central content units and foster retention of targeted information plus accurate metacognition; unspecific free-recall tasks suit materials with many important information units and foster broader retention, self-efficacy and situational interest.
requirements: The learning content must be classifiable as containing a few central content units or a wider range of important information
constraints: The holistic-retrieval advantage for non-targeted information was confirmed only on the free-recall posttest, not the short-answer posttest
target_learning_goals: retention of expository text content
accurate metacognitive judgments
self-efficacy
situational interest
examples: For a text about three crucial factors of climate change with illustrative examples, the authors would use specific short-answer tasks; for a text on the Gulf Stream with many important points, unspecific free-recall
key_sources: Tino Endres, Lena Kranzdorf, Vivien Schneider, Alexander Renkl. (2020). It matters how to recall – task differences in retrieval practice. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09526-1

article_title: Which events can cause iteration in instructional design? An empirical study of the design process
citation: Verstegen, D.M.L., Barnard, Y.F. & Pilot, A. (2006). Which events can cause iteration in instructional design? An empirical study of the design process. Instructional Science 34, 481–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-3346-0
title: MASTER-TPD prototype tool for training program design
description: A prototype tool implementing the Training Program Design phase of the MASTER method, customised from Designer's Edge (DE 2.0, 1997). It guides users through six main steps with sub-steps and Notepads, logs user actions, and 'supports iteration because intermediate results (including the subjects’ notes) remain available'. 'A small number of warnings appears automatically when an event that is a likely cause for iteration can be measured.'
requirements: Implements the middle MASTER-TPD phase of the MASTER method for specifying training simulators; guidelines provide information about relations between design activities, strategic advice, and indications for taking notes.
constraints: Subjects reported that in later steps the tool does not show all training activities but only those taking place with the simulator, and sequencing information can get lost when the tool is not used as intended.
target_learning_goals: designing functional specifications for training simulators
training program design
examples: The tool logged time-stamped actions from which iteration counts were derived, and stored final and intermediate designs and Notepad notes.
key_sources: Verstegen, D.M.L., Barnard, Y.F. & Pilot, A. (2006). Which events can cause iteration in instructional design? An empirical study of the design process. Instructional Science 34, 481–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-3346-0

article_title: How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach
citation: Sarah von der Mühlen, Tobias Richter, Sebastian Schmid, Kirsten Berthold. (2019). How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach. Instructional Science 47:215–237. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9471-3
title: Design argumentation interventions to match learners' ability level and include complex, atypical arguments
description: The article concludes that argumentation training should be integrated into curricula but tailored to learners' ability: benefits concentrated among high-achieving students and those with high pretest accuracy, while low performers showed no gains. It also argues interventions should use "a variety of argument types, including arguments with a more typical and arguments with a less typical structure", since training effects emerged specifically for warrants and atypical full-fledged arguments rather than for simple three-component arguments.
requirements: Training materials must include both typical and atypical, complex and less complex arguments
learners' prior ability should be assessed and matched
constraints: Effects were limited to posttest and did not persist at the 4-week follow-up; low-performing students did not benefit
target_learning_goals: argument structure knowledge
argument comprehension
examples: In the experiment, only students 1 SD above the mean in study performance clearly outperformed controls after argument structure training, while low performers did not differ from the speed-reading group
key_sources: Sarah von der Mühlen, Tobias Richter, Sebastian Schmid, Kirsten Berthold. (2019). How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach. Instructional Science 47:215–237. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9471-3

article_title: How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language
citation: Palladino, P., Trotta, E., Bonvino, A., Carlucci, L., & Cottini, M. (2025). How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09414-4
title: MASRL and control-value theory as a joint framework for metacognition and achievement emotions in early L2 learning
description: The study grounds its design in two complementary models: Efklides' metacognitive and affective model of self-regulated learning (MASRL) for metacognitive competence, and Pekrun's control-value theory (CVT) for achievement emotions. The article states: "our study refers to the MASRL model by Efklides for metacognitive competence and the CVT by Pekrun for achievement emotions." Both models treat task characteristics via subjective experiences at the person level, with task monitoring information gaining importance at the Task × Person level. CVT holds that achievement emotions arise from perceived controllability and value, while MASRL explains how metacognitive, motivational and affective competence interact for self-regulated learning.
requirements: Both models focus on learning and evaluate task characteristics on the basis of students' subjective experiences, so tasks must be meaningful enough to trigger control and value appraisals.
constraints: The MASRL model does not explicitly explain the role of the distal environment, unlike CVT, which the authors note as a difference between the models.
target_learners: primary school children (grades 2–3, ages 6–9) learning English as a second language
target_learning_goals: second language (English) vocabulary acquisition
self-regulated learning
examples: The study measured procedural metacognition (confidence judgments, relative monitoring accuracy, withdrawal/maintenance control) alongside enjoyment, anxiety and boredom on an English vocabulary test at two time points.
key_sources: Palladino, P., Trotta, E., Bonvino, A., Carlucci, L., & Cottini, M. (2025). How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09414-4

article_title: Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach
citation: Mark Feng Teng, Mei Yue. (2022). Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09328-5
title: MAWSQ: Metacognitive Academic Writing Strategies Questionnaire (43 items, eight strategies)
description: The MAWSQ is a self-report questionnaire developed and validated by Teng et al. (2022b) to measure metacognitive strategies in academic writing. It includes 43 items on a 7-point Likert scale, with 13 assessing knowledge of metacognition (declarative, procedural, conditional) and 30 assessing regulation (planning, monitoring, evaluating, information management, debugging). In this study Cronbach's alpha values "for the eight strategies ranged from 0.792 to 0.872". Validation evidence included EFA and CFA supporting an eight-factor correlated model and a one-factor second-order model, with the second-order model preferred.
requirements: Respondents must be engaged in academic writing in higher education for items to reflect their awareness and use of metacognitive strategies in writing situations
constraints: The article notes criticism that metacognitive strategy use cannot be adequately assessed by questionnaires (Veenman & Van Cleef, 2019), which the authors address by designing the instrument specifically for academic writing contexts
target_learners: EFL university students in academic writing courses
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive knowledge and regulation strategies for academic writing
examples: Applied to 644 third-year students at a Chinese university; completed online within 30 minutes during the last two lessons of the writing course
key_sources: Mark Feng Teng, Mei Yue. (2022). Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09328-5

article_title: Metacognition and motivation in creativity: examining the roles of self-efficacy and values as cues for metacognitive judgments
citation: Kamila Urban, Marek Urban. (2025). Metacognition and motivation in creativity: examining the roles of self-efficacy and values as cues for metacognitive judgments. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09421-5
title: Foster creative self-efficacy through mastery experiences with repeated practice and feedback to support accurate creative self-evaluation
description: The article argues that because creative self-efficacy acts as a direct heuristic cue for how individuals evaluate their creative performance, well-calibrated self-efficacy matters for accurate self-evaluations. It observes that interventions have enhanced self-efficacy in domains like reading and mathematics but "similar interventions targeting creative self-efficacy are notably absent." It recommends adapting the most common strategies, namely "mastery experiences through repeated practice and feedback," to foster creative self-efficacy in educational and workplace settings.
requirements: Interventions must build well-calibrated self-efficacy, since miscalibrated self-efficacy could bias metacognitive judgments
constraints: The article notes the recommendation is extrapolated from intervention evidence in other domains such as reading and mathematics, not from tested creativity-domain interventions
target_learning_goals: accurate self-evaluation of creative performance
sustained engagement in creative tasks
examples: The study measured creative self-efficacy with a 3-item scale and modeled its direct and indirect effects on expectancies and judgments across two creativity tasks
key_sources: Kamila Urban, Marek Urban. (2025). Metacognition and motivation in creativity: examining the roles of self-efficacy and values as cues for metacognitive judgments. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09421-5

article_title: The meta-attention knowledge questionnaire (MAKQ): a new instrument for investigating meta-attention in a young adolescent sample
citation: Mulvihill, A., Matthews, N., Chidley, K., Macmahon, S., Armitage, K. L., Sherlock, D., Dux, P. E., & Carroll, A. (2025). The meta-attention knowledge questionnaire (MAKQ): a new instrument for investigating meta-attention in a young adolescent sample. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09433-1
title: The Meta-Attention Knowledge Questionnaire (MAKQ): a dual-component self-report instrument for adolescent meta-attention knowledge
description: The MAKQ is a self-report questionnaire measuring adolescent metacognitive knowledge in the domain of attention, built on Posner's attention network model and Efklides' metacognitive knowledge framework. It combines 20 self-knowledge Likert items with 12 open-ended strategy questions whose responses are coded and scored, so that "a comparison between student responses on these two components provides a novel means to investigate the interaction between self-perceived skill and researcher coded and quantified strategy knowledge within a simple questionnaire format."
requirements: Requires students to complete 20 Likert self-knowledge items and 12 open-ended strategy questions, completed online in a median time of 15.54 min in Study One
constraints: Designed for and validated in typically developing early adolescents (grades 7-8, ages 11-15) in Australian high schools
target_learning_goals: metacognitive knowledge of attention: self-perceived attentional control and monitoring, and declarative strategies to self-regulate attention
examples: Study One administered the MAKQ online via Qualtrics to 293 students; Study Two administered it pen-and-paper to 83 students at the opening of an intervention session
key_sources: Mulvihill, A., Matthews, N., Chidley, K., Macmahon, S., Armitage, K. L., Sherlock, D., Dux, P. E., & Carroll, A. (2025). The meta-attention knowledge questionnaire (MAKQ): a new instrument for investigating meta-attention in a young adolescent sample. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09433-1

article_title: The meta-attention knowledge questionnaire (MAKQ): a new instrument for investigating meta-attention in a young adolescent sample
citation: Mulvihill, A., Matthews, N., Chidley, K., Macmahon, S., Armitage, K. L., Sherlock, D., Dux, P. E., & Carroll, A. (2025). The meta-attention knowledge questionnaire (MAKQ): a new instrument for investigating meta-attention in a young adolescent sample. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09433-1
title: Fourteen strategy types for adolescent self-regulation of attention, identified via inductive automated content analysis
description: Inductive automated content analysis (Leximancer 4.5) of student responses to the 12 MAKQ open-ended strategy questions identified "14 dominant themes" of strategies students use to self-manage alerting, orienting and executive attention, ranging from physical movement and meeting physiological needs to goal setting, planning, time management, and phone-specific management tools (reported by 6% of students). The most frequently reported was blocking distractions (87% of students). These themes inform the scoring of the strategy knowledge dimension.
requirements: Strategy responses are scored by frequency of mentioned strategies per the Table 3 taxonomy, requiring the coded strategy list as a scoring rubric
constraints: Strategy taxonomy derived from typically developing Australian grade 7-8 students; the least common strategy (phone-specific tools) was reported by only 6% of students
target_learning_goals: declarative knowledge of strategies to self-regulate attention-related behaviours in daily learning contexts
examples: Sample strategies students reported include "Sit away from friends in order to have no one to distract me" and "Put it in order of priority, so I get what is most important done first"
key_sources: Mulvihill, A., Matthews, N., Chidley, K., Macmahon, S., Armitage, K. L., Sherlock, D., Dux, P. E., & Carroll, A. (2025). The meta-attention knowledge questionnaire (MAKQ): a new instrument for investigating meta-attention in a young adolescent sample.
