article_title: Publisher Correction to: Metamotivational Processes in Self-regulated Learning: Exploring the Implications for Research, Theory, and Educational Practice
citation: Anastasia Efklides, Eleftheria N. Gonida, Eve Kikas. (2026). Publisher Correction to: Metamotivational Processes in Self-regulated Learning: Exploring the Implications for Research, Theory, and Educational Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10165-0
title: The MASRL model, adopted from Efklides (2011), is presented in Fig. 1 of the metamotivational processes in self-regulated learning article
description: The MASRL model is a figure-presented model of self-regulated learning used in the corrected article, adopted from Efklides (2011). The correction restores the figure's caption and legend, which define three abbreviated components: "ME = metacognitive experiences; MK = metacognitive knowledge; MS = metacognitive skills". The model thus serves as the organizing figure for the article's treatment of metamotivational processes in self-regulated learning.
requirements: The figure requires its caption and legend to be present, as the correction states these were "inadvertently missing during the production processed" and restores them.
constraints: This correction concerns only the caption and legend of Fig. 1; it states no substantive change to the article's arguments or findings.
target_learners: learners studied in self-regulated learning research
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning, including metacognitive experiences, metacognitive knowledge, and metacognitive skills
examples: The corrected caption reads: "The MASRL model. Adopted from Efklides (2011). Note. ME = metacognitive experiences; MK = metacognitive knowledge; MS = metacognitive skills".
key_sources: Anastasia Efklides, Eleftheria N. Gonida, Eve Kikas. (2026). Publisher Correction to: Metamotivational Processes in Self-regulated Learning: Exploring the Implications for Research, Theory, and Educational Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10165-0

article_title: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis to Support Power Analyses for Randomized Intervention Studies in Preschool: Cognitive and Socio-Emotional Learning Outcomes
citation: Martin Brunner, Sophie E. Stallasch, Cordula Artelt, Oliver Lüdtke. (2025). An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis to Support Power Analyses for Randomized Intervention Studies in Preschool: Cognitive and Socio-Emotional Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09981-z
title: Match design parameters to the key characteristics of the planned intervention study when conducting a priori power analyses
description: This principle holds that a priori power analyses should strive for an ideal match between the selected design parameters and the planned study's characteristics: the clustering structure (single-, two-, or three-level), the target outcome domain, the assessment method, and the target age group. The article urges selecting "design parameters that offer the best match to the assumptions of how the data of the planned study will be clustered" and, given heterogeneity, using estimates from the same or a very similar target measure and age group.
requirements: Design parameters must be available for the target population, outcome, and assessment method of the planned study
constraints: Suitable estimates may be unavailable for a specific data structure, measure, age group, or covariate set
target_learners: preschool children aged two to six attending daycare centers
target_learning_goals: cognitive outcomes (math/science, verbal, general cognitive, psychomotor skills)
socio-emotional learning outcomes (self-, other-, and task-orientation)
examples: The article illustrates matching two-level parameters (ρCenter, R2Child, R2Center) to a two-level CRT and notes that when ρGroup and R2Group are missing, relevant two-level parameters can be used because between-group differences were often smaller than between-center differences
key_sources: Martin Brunner, Sophie E. Stallasch, Cordula Artelt, Oliver Lüdtke. (2025). An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis to Support Power Analyses for Randomized Intervention Studies in Preschool: Cognitive and Socio-Emotional Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09981-z

article_title: Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data
citation: Dumas, D., Goecke, B., Kagan, S., & Weiss, S. (2026). Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10110-7
title: Matrix sampling with planned missingness in large-scale assessments (e.g., PISA testlets counterbalanced across students)
description: Large-scale assessments organize items into testlets counterbalanced across students within a sampling frame, so that 'no student ever takes the entire battery of assessments, or even all the items on any one test'. In PISA, 'each student participates for 2 h, seeing only a fraction of the total set of test items', and for optional domains many students see no items yet still receive PVs. This design makes individual-level scoring from item responses impossible and necessitates the PV methodology.
requirements: A scoring methodology that models population distributions rather than individual item-response-based scores
constraints: Planned missingness primarily affects performance testing; background questionnaires are typically more completely responded to, though PISA has begun incorporating planned missingness there too
target_learners: students participating in population-level educational monitoring
target_learning_goals: monitoring educational systems at the population level
examples: PISA 2022 used a balanced incomplete block design; a full battery would take up to 15 hours, so students respond for 2 hours
key_sources: Dumas, D., Goecke, B., Kagan, S., & Weiss, S. (2026). Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10110-7

article_title: Text Generation Benefits Learning: a Meta-Analytic Review
citation: Julia Schindler · Tobias Richter. (2023). Text Generation Benefits Learning: a Meta-Analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09758-w
title: Material appropriate processing / contextual framework of desirable difficulties
description: The contextual framework by McDaniel and Butler, incorporating material appropriate processing (MAP) and transfer appropriate processing (TAP), describes desirable difficulties such as text generation as "the result of a complex interaction of learning material, difficulty intervention, learning assessment tasks, and learner characteristics." It predicts generation benefits learning only when the generation task stimulates cognitive processes relevant to the learning test that are not already stimulated by the material. It distinguishes individual-item (propositional) processing from relational (integrative) processing and holds that narratives foster relational processing while expository texts draw attention to individual propositions, so letter completion should complement narratives and sentence unscrambling should complement expository texts.
requirements: The generation task must stimulate cognitive processes relevant for the specific learning test that are not already stimulated by the learning material or initiated by the learners themselves
constraints: The article reports the framework's genre-by-task predictions received only partial support in the meta-analysis: the expository-text contrast was significant but the narrative-text contrast was not
target_learners: learners studying narrative or expository texts, including university students and other populations such as high-school students
target_learning_goals: text comprehension and memory for text content at text-base and situation-model levels
examples: The meta-analysis tested the framework's predicted genre-by-generation-task interaction across 129 effect sizes, finding sentence unscrambling (g = 0.77) significantly stronger than letter completion (g = 0.23) in expository texts
key_sources: Julia Schindler · Tobias Richter. (2023). Text Generation Benefits Learning: a Meta-Analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09758-w

article_title: Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape
citation: Julia Chatain, Charlotte Müller, Keny Chatain, Leon Calabrese, Manu Kapur. (2025). Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10073-9
title: Mapping-level axes of concreteness are objective properties of how a representation maps to a concept
description: The taxonomy identifies six mapping-level axes between representation and concept: "situatedness between idealized and real life, experientiality between symbolic and enacted, speciﬁcity between universal and speciﬁc, informality between formal and informal, approximation between rigorous and approximate, and physicality between virtual and physical." These axes are objective because they depend only on the designer's decisions about how the representation is defined in relation to the concept, not on the learner.
requirements: Axes at the mapping level depend only on the representation and the represented concept, so they are fully under the designer's control
constraints: Mapping-level axes may relate to interaction-level axes: making certain design decisions along one axis may impact another
target_learners: Mathematics learners in high school and higher education
target_learning_goals: Making deliberate design choices about how representations map to mathematical concepts
examples: A designer may decide to use real-world examples (situatedness) or to design an experiential representation of the concept, independent of the learner
key_sources: Julia Chatain, Charlotte Müller, Keny Chatain, Leon Calabrese, Manu Kapur. (2025). Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10073-9

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: Make domain connections explicit for students rather than relying on self-discovery
description: This principle holds that the connections among core concepts, key representations, and the world must be explicitly pointed out during instruction, because learners often fail to recognize structural relatedness on their own. The authors implement it in two ways: structuring the textbook so connections are visible and stated (e.g., every concept tied to DATA = MODEL + ERROR), and repeatedly asking questions whose answers are the target connections. They also use R to reduce extraneous load, leaving resources for reflection on connections, consistent with cognitive load theory's distinction of intrinsic, germane, and extraneous load.
requirements: Instructional materials must be structured so the targeted connections recur and are named in the text
Questions must repeatedly ask students to articulate the connections themselves
constraints: The article notes effort alone is usually not enough; explicitness must be combined with productive struggle rather than replacing learner effort
target_learners: Novice learners in complex academic domains, especially those who get stuck on surface features
target_learning_goals: Recognizing structural relatedness across problems and contexts
Building coherent domain knowledge
examples: When the mean is introduced, the text explicitly identifies it as a function that fills the MODEL slot in DATA = MODEL + ERROR; residuals, sum of squares, variance, and standard deviation are explicitly connected to ERROR.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: Let's talk evidence – The case for combining inquiry-based and direct instruction
citation: de Jong, T., Lazonder, A. W., Chinn, C. A., Fischer, F., Gobert, J., Hmelo-Silver, C. H., Koedinger, K. R., Krajcik, J. S., Kyza, E. A., Linn, M. C., Pedaste, M., Scheiter, K., & Zacharia, Z. C. (2023). Let's talk evidence – The case for combining inquiry-based and direct instruction. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100536
title: Match instructional approach to learning goal: inquiry for deep, transferable understanding of ill-structured topics; direct instruction for foundational surface knowledge
description: The article's first design recommendation is to "employ inquiry-based methods if the instructional goal requires students to develop deep and transferrable conceptual understanding of topics that are open-ended or susceptible to misconceptions." Direct instruction is described as generally more appropriate and probably more efficient for acquiring well-structured and foundational (surface) knowledge. The recommendation draws on early instructional design theories and on Frey et al. (2017), who observed that inquiry-based methods were used effectively in lessons beyond the surface learning phase.
requirements: Teachers and curriculum designers should align instructional and assessment methods with the kind of learning outcomes they expect from students.
constraints: The article states direct instruction will not necessarily lead to deep conceptual understanding in less-well-structured domains.
target_learners: Science and STEM students in classroom settings
target_learning_goals: Deep and transferable conceptual understanding of science topics
Acquisition of well-structured foundational (surface) knowledge
examples: The article recommends inquiry for topics susceptible to misconceptions, such as how water's boiling point changes with altitude, and direct instruction for factual information such as the chemical formula of water.
key_sources: de Jong, T., Lazonder, A. W., Chinn, C. A., Fischer, F., Gobert, J., Hmelo-Silver, C. H., Koedinger, K. R., Krajcik, J. S., Kyza, E. A., Linn, M. C., Pedaste, M., Scheiter, K., & Zacharia, Z. C. (2023). Let's talk evidence – The case for combining inquiry-based and direct instruction. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100536

article_title: Educational Inequalities at the Intersection of Multiple Social Categories: A﻿n Introduction and Systematic Review of the Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA) Approach
citation: Keller, L., Lüdtke, O., Preckel, F., & Brunner, M. (2023). Educational Inequalities at the Intersection of Multiple Social Categories: An Introduction and Systematic Review of the Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA) Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09733-5
title: The MAIHDA approach models individuals nested within intersectional strata to quantify intersectional effects and discriminatory accuracy
description: MAIHDA (Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy) is a statistical framework in which individuals are nested within intersectional strata defined by combinations of social categories. It partitions variance within and between strata, yielding global measures (VPC, adjusted VPC, PCV) and specific measures (strata means and strata-level residuals) of intersectionality. The article introduces it to educational psychology, noting that 'the intersectional MAIHDA approach is considered the "new gold standard" for studying social inequalities in epidemiology (Merlo, 2018)'.
requirements: Very large and diverse samples are required to apply the intersectional MAIHDA approach for reliably estimating effects, so that strata have sufficient sample sizes
constraints: Meaningful cut points must be chosen when transforming continuous variables into categories or collapsing categories to reduce the number of strata
target_learning_goals: Understanding and quantifying educational inequalities in achievement outcomes across intersecting social categories
examples: The article demonstrates the approach with PISA 2018 German data, assigning each student to one of 40 strata combining gender, immigrant background, parental education, and parental occupational status
key_sources: Keller, L., Lüdtke, O., Preckel, F., & Brunner, M. (2023). Educational Inequalities at the Intersection of Multiple Social Categories: An Introduction and Systematic Review of the Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA) Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09733-5

article_title: Educational Inequalities at the Intersection of Multiple Social Categories: A﻿n Introduction and Systematic Review of the Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA) Approach
citation: Keller, L., Lüdtke, O., Preckel, F., & Brunner, M. (2023). Educational Inequalities at the Intersection of Multiple Social Categories: An Introduction and Systematic Review of the Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA) Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09733-5
title: Annotated R syntax and OSF repository for replicating MAIHDA analyses
description: The article provides a hands-on tutorial consisting of a step-by-step table of analytical steps with corresponding R code (using brms via the brm function) and a thoroughly annotated R syntax released with supplemental materials. The authors state: "The supplemental materials and R code for reproducing the results and figures from the present study can be accessed via https:// osf. io/ qdcna/." The tutorial covers strata formation, both multilevel models, VPC/PCV calculation, and predicted strata values.
requirements: Analyses were conducted in R (version 4.1.2); in principle MAIHDA can be conducted with any statistical software supporting multilevel analyses
constraints: If missing data are imputed using multiple imputation techniques, each preprocessing step needs to be repeated for each multiply-imputed data set
target_learners: Educational psychology researchers learning to apply MAIHDA
target_learning_goals: Replicating and applying intersectional MAIHDA analyses to educational inequality data
examples: The article's Table 2 maps each analytical step (forming strata, variance decomposition, VPC, predicted values, PCV) to R code using dplyr and brm
key_sources: Keller, L., Lüdtke, O., Preckel, F., & Brunner, M. (2023). Educational Inequalities at the Intersection of Multiple Social Categories: An Introduction and Systematic Review of the Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA) Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09733-5

article_title: Toward Synergizing Educational Research and Movement Sciences: a Dialogue on Learning as Developing Perception for Action
citation: Dor Abrahamson · Franz Mechsner. (2022). Toward Synergizing Educational Research and Movement Sciences: a Dialogue on Learning as Developing Perception for Action. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09668-3
title: Mathematics Imagery Trainer: a technologically enabled activity architecture for embodied mathematics learning
description: The Mathematics Imagery Trainer is a technologically enabled activity architecture in which students manipulate a geometrical figure, such as a rectangle, with both hands along orthogonal axes while color feedback signals a target ratio. The student is "tasked first to make the rectangle green and, once that is accomplished, to keep moving the two vertices while keeping the rectangle green". After a performance criterion is met, a human or virtual tutor introduces grids and numerals, and activities then move to paper-and-pen tasks formalizing the attentional anchor.
requirements: Real-time color feedback tied to the target quantitative relation; supplementary inscriptions (grid, numerals) introduced only after a pre-specified minimal performance criterion
constraints: Reported studies are cross-sectional rather than longitudinal; the program has focused primarily on extremity (hand) actions without explicit regard to whole-body sub-movements
target_learning_goals: proportionality and ratio; trigonometry graphs; parabolas; quantitative reasoning grounded in movement
examples: The Orthogonal Proportion task with a 1:2 height-to-width green rectangle; grid and numeral overlays; paper-and-pen generation of further green triangles using hand-gauge and unit-counting techniques
key_sources: Dor Abrahamson · Franz Mechsner. (2022). Toward Synergizing Educational Research and Movement Sciences: a Dialogue on Learning as Developing Perception for Action. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09668-3

article_title: Learning Styles, Preferences, or Strategies? An Explanation for the Resurgence of Styles Across Many Meta-analyses
citation: John Hattie, Timothy O'Leary. (2025). Learning Styles, Preferences, or Strategies? An Explanation for the Resurgence of Styles Across Many Meta-analyses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10002-w
title: Two-stories framework: matching-hypothesis (d) studies versus correlational (r) studies of learning styles
description: The article's central organizing framework distinguishes two types of learning styles meta-analyses that "effectively measure different things": d-studies testing whether "students do better when taught to their preferred learning style" and r-studies correlating learning style inventory scores with achievement. The framework explains the apparent resurgence of learning styles: the higher correlational average (r = 0.24) is mistaken for support of matching, which itself shows d = 0.04. The review uses this distinction to argue that correlational evidence cannot establish causation nor support the matching hypothesis.
requirements: Meta-analyses must be classified by whether they randomly assign learners within style groups to different teaching methods, per Pashler et al.'s design criteria
constraints: Correlational studies fail Pashler et al.'s criteria because they do not divide learners into groups or randomly assign methods, so they cannot support matching claims
target_learners: all school and higher education students
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
examples: The review classifies the 17 MetaX meta-analyses in Table 1 into four matching studies (pooled d = 0.04) and thirteen correlational studies (pooled r = 0.24)
key_sources: John Hattie, Timothy O'Leary. (2025). Learning Styles, Preferences, or Strategies? An Explanation for the Resurgence of Styles Across Many Meta-analyses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10002-w

article_title: Not New, but Nearly Forgotten: the Testing Effect Decreases or even Disappears as the Complexity of Learning Materials Increases
citation: van Gog, T., & Sweller, J. (2015). Not New, but Nearly Forgotten: the Testing Effect Decreases or even Disappears as the Complexity of Learning Materials Increases. Educational Psychology Review, 27, 247–264. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9310-x
title: Consider the complexity of learning materials when deciding between practice testing and further study
description: Because the testing effect shrinks or vanishes for high element interactivity materials, teachers and instructional designers should weigh material complexity when choosing between practice tests and restudy. The review argues that research on complexity as a boundary condition "would help teachers and instructional designers to know for which learning tasks they can and cannot expect benefits of having their students take practice tests instead of engage in further study".
requirements: Judgement of the element interactivity of learning tasks and test items before assigning practice testing
constraints: In several special-issue studies, other known boundary conditions such as test format, retrieval success on the initial test, feedback, or test spacing "cannot be ruled out entirely as an alternative explanation"
target_learning_goals: choosing between practice testing and restudy for complex learning tasks
examples: Worked example studies in the special issue found no testing effect for problem-solving tasks, while scrambled sentences and word lists showed benefits on delayed tests
key_sources: van Gog, T., & Sweller, J. (2015). Not New, but Nearly Forgotten: the Testing Effect Decreases or even Disappears as the Complexity of Learning Materials Increases. Educational Psychology Review, 27, 247–264. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9310-x

article_title: What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis
citation: Emma C. Burns · Penny Van Bergen. (2025). What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09998-y
title: Match the level of analysis to the referents used in relationship measurement items, using multilevel analyses for plural or averaged referents
description: Because relationship items differ in their referents — dyadic ("I like my teacher"), plural ("this teacher likes us"), or averaged ("I like my teachers") — the referent should determine the level at which analysis takes place. The review states that "Where referents are plural or averaged, analyses should be multilevel to account for shared group-level variance and ensure appropriate interpretation". This matters because implications for practice and intervention differ depending on whether individual relationships, multiple relationships, or classroom culture is being addressed.
requirements: Researchers must identify the referent of each measurement item before selecting an analytic level
constraints: The review notes it is unclear how frequently multilevel analyses are in fact used for plural or averaged configuration types
target_learning_goals: Accurate inference about relationships and motivation at the dyadic, plural, or classroom level
examples: The review cites Marsh et al. (2012) and Stapleton and Johnson (2019) on referent-driven levels of analysis
key_sources: Emma C. Burns · Penny Van Bergen. (2025). What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09998-y

article_title: Null and Void? Errors in Meta-analysis on Perceptual Disfluency and Recommendations to Improve Meta-analytical Reproducibility
citation: Sophia C. Weissgerber, Matthias Brunmair & Ralf Rummer. (2021). Null and Void? Errors in Meta-analysis on Perceptual Disfluency and Recommendations to Improve Meta-analytical Reproducibility. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09579-1
title: Meta-analyses should mandatorily publish their dataset and complete analysis code prior to publication
description: The article argues that open-science practices should be mandatory rather than voluntary for meta-analyses: "it should thus be mandatory (and not voluntary) to publish the data set as a separate file alongside the manuscript", and it should be mandatory prior to publication to provide the complete analysis code via a repository such as OSF. This enables independent researchers to exactly recreate reported results and supports future re-analysis as statistical tools evolve. The principle rests on the TOP-guidelines and the Reproducibility Enhancement Principles.
requirements: Data files must include all relevant texts from primary studies underlying coding decisions, statistical raw values, and a link to data files directly analyzable with statistical software
constraints: The article notes existing guidelines such as PRISMA are not always formulated specifically enough for reproducibility
target_learning_goals: ensuring meta-analytical results about learning effects can be independently verified and re-analyzed
examples: The commentary could not apply Level 1 checks as outlined because Xie et al. provided no data or code files, illustrating the consequence of non-compliance
key_sources: Sophia C. Weissgerber, Matthias Brunmair & Ralf Rummer. (2021). Null and Void? Errors in Meta-analysis on Perceptual Disfluency and Recommendations to Improve Meta-analytical Reproducibility. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09579-1

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno
citation: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2
title: Mayer and Moreno's 1998 split-attention effect study as the first of nine joint Journal of Educational Psychology articles
description: This element is the 1998 Journal of Educational Psychology study by Mayer and Moreno, which the reference list titles "A split-attention effect in multimedia learning: Evidence for dual processing systems in working memory." Mayer's tribute describes it as based on work Moreno started in her first years of graduate study at UCSB, and reports it "was the first of what was to become a string of nine research articles we published together in the Journal of Educational Psychology." The editorial characterizes it as a significant contribution to cognitive theories of how people learn from words and pictures.
requirements: The study used the lightning-formation multimedia lesson developed by Moreno during her graduate work at UCSB
target_learning_goals: learning from words and pictures under split-attention conditions
examples: The editorial reports the lightning passage from this study was subsequently used in more than a dozen published experiments at UCSB and around the world
key_sources: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2

article_title: Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach
citation: Tetzlaff, L., Edelsbrunner, P., Schmitterer, A., Hartmann, U., & Brod, G. (2023). Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09830-5
title: Match instructional focus to learners' multivariate reading profiles rather than to single characteristics
description: The article argues that individualized instruction requires knowing for whom which instruction works, per Hunt's definition of differential effectiveness: "Given this kind of person, which of these approaches is more effective for a given objective?" Because learner characteristics interact (aptitude complexes), teachers and researchers should consider constellations of characteristics rather than one variable at a time. The study's findings illustrate this: vocabulary focus benefited good readers but not poor decoders or poor comprehenders, while advanced reading focus benefited poor comprehenders.
requirements: Learner profiles must be diagnosed on multiple relevant characteristics, and instructional foci must be measurable and variable across classrooms
constraints: Findings are exploratory, from German third-grade reading instruction, with teacher self-reported foci; the article notes self-reports showed a tendency to report the presence rather than absence of foci
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
examples: Teachers' aggregated self-reported emphasis on vocabulary, advanced reading abilities, and reading motivation was related to profile-specific reading-comprehension gains over one school year
key_sources: Tetzlaff, L., Edelsbrunner, P., Schmitterer, A., Hartmann, U., & Brod, G. (2023). Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09830-5

article_title: On Model Interpretability and Time-Reversal Testing in Analyses of Reciprocal Effects: Clarifying Modeling Issues in Sorjonen et al.’s (2025a, 2025b) Commentaries
citation: Núñez-Regueiro, F., Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Guo, J. (2026). On Model Interpretability and Time-Reversal Testing in Analyses of Reciprocal Effects: Clarifying Modeling Issues in Sorjonen et al.'s (2025a, 2025b) Commentaries. Educational Psychology Review, 38(80). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10179-8
title: Make modeling assumptions fully explicit when comparing alternative longitudinal models, so differences reflect substantive mechanisms rather than specification issues
description: This principle holds that debates over alternative longitudinal models should distinguish defensible modeling choices from specification errors that depart from SEM logic. The authors argue that "what appeared to be contradictory results from alternative models ... are better understood as consequences of specification issues that, once resolved, yield results consistent with the REM". Explicit assumptions ensure interpretability of reciprocal-effect estimates.
requirements: Model comparisons must state temporal ordering, identification, and parameter-interpretability assumptions explicitly
constraints: Improper solutions (non-positive definite matrices) invalidate interpretation of parameters under standard SEM principles
target_learners: researchers analyzing longitudinal data on academic self-concept and achievement
target_learning_goals: valid causal interpretation of reciprocal effects between academic self-concept and achievement
examples: The commentary restates the LCSM, STARTS, and ESDM misspecifications in Table 1 and shows corrected versions yield proper solutions corroborating Marsh et al. (2024)
key_sources: Núñez-Regueiro, F., Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Lüdtke, O., & Guo, J. (2026). On Model Interpretability and Time-Reversal Testing in Analyses of Reciprocal Effects: Clarifying Modeling Issues in Sorjonen et al.'s (2025a, 2025b) Commentaries. Educational Psychology Review, 38(80). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10179-8

article_title: Multi-Level Meta-Analysis of Physical Activity Interventions During Childhood: Effects of Physical Activity on Cognition and Academic Achievement
citation: Vasilopoulos, F., Jeffrey, H., Wu, Y., & Dumontheil, I. (2023). Multi-Level Meta-Analysis of Physical Activity Interventions During Childhood: Effects of Physical Activity on Cognition and Academic Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09760-2
title: Match the type of physical activity integration to the targeted outcome: embed PA in academic instruction for mathematics and use enriched PA for language
description: This principle recommends selecting the form of school-based physical activity according to the outcome a designer wants to improve, because the meta-analysis found outcome-specific moderator patterns. PA combined with academic instruction — for example children answering a sum by moving as many times as the answer — showed significant mathematics benefits (g = 0.32), while enriched PA programmes benefited language outcomes. The article's own conclusion is that "These results therefore suggest differential mechanisms of impact of different types of PA on different aspects of cognition", so a single PA format cannot be assumed to serve all academic goals.
requirements: Interventions need at least three sessions over more than one week, as single bouts were excluded from the evidence base
constraints: The mathematics benefit was observed for 6–10-week interventions of moderate or moderate-to-vigorous intensity; moderator analyses were exploratory with high heterogeneity
target_learners: Typically developing primary-school children aged 5–12 years
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement
Language achievement
examples: Close integration examples in the article include giving the answer to a sum by star jumps or jumping on letters to spell a word; the moderator analysis found PA with academic instruction constituted 67% of AA effect sizes
key_sources: Vasilopoulos, F., Jeffrey, H., Wu, Y., & Dumontheil, I. (2023). Multi-Level Meta-Analysis of Physical Activity Interventions During Childhood: Effects of Physical Activity on Cognition and Academic Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09760-2

article_title: A consideration of racial/ethnic diversity conceptualization and measurement: Clarifying ambiguities and advancing scholarship
citation: Chan, M.-k., & Benner, A. D. (2023). A Consideration of Racial/Ethnic Diversity Conceptualization and Measurement: Clarifying Ambiguities and Advancing Scholarship. Educational Psychologist (accepted manuscript). https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6451-2417
title: Match the diversity measure to the diversity conceptualization: researchers should explicitly define which aspect of diversity they intend to assess before selecting a measure
description: The article's central methodological recommendation is that measure selection follow conceptualization. "The selection of a given diversity measure should be driven by the diversity conceptualization researchers intend to assess." Because different measures operationalize different frameworks (normic, dual-concept, representative), a study that defines diversity one way but measures it another produces inappropriate or misleading conclusions. The review found many studies did not explicitly delineate their diversity definition, obscuring what aspect of diversity was studied and hindering cross-study comparison.
requirements: Studies should explicitly state their definition of school racial/ethnic diversity and specify diversity terminology, since using "diversity" without specification makes results hard to interpret and compare
constraints: The review documents that current practice frequently violates this principle, with the same term used for different concepts and different terms for the same construct
target_learning_goals: valid operationalization of school racial/ethnic diversity in research on student outcomes
examples: The review shows bullying-victimization studies using minority proportion versus dual-concept indices support fundamentally different claims about how diversity relates to victimization
key_sources: Chan, M.-k., & Benner, A. D. (2023). A Consideration of Racial/Ethnic Diversity Conceptualization and Measurement: Clarifying Ambiguities and Advancing Scholarship. Educational Psychologist (accepted manuscript). https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6451-2417

article_title: Solving graphics tasks: Gender differences in middle-school students
citation: Lowrie, Tom and Diezmann, Carmel. (2010). Solving graphics tasks: Gender differences in middle-school students. Learning and Instruction. http://eprints.qut.edu.au/
title: Mackinlay's six graphical languages framework for classifying graphics tasks
description: The study adopts Mackinlay's (1999) model, derived from Bertin (1967/1983), in which graphics are categorised into six "graphical languages" that "represent mathematical relationships among perceptual elements and use particular encoding techniques": Axis, Apposed-position, Map, Retinal-list, Connection, and Miscellaneous. Each language is defined by its encoding technique — Axis encodes by mark position on one axis, Apposed-position by marks on both x and y axes, Map by fixed positions and map-specific techniques, Connection by linking node and link objects, Retinal-list without position encoding, and Miscellaneous by conventions of particular graphics. The framework provides the perceptual basis for analysing students' decoding performance on the GLIM test.
requirements: Items must be classifiable by expert panels into the six graphical-language categories (the GLIM categorisation achieved Cronbach's alpha 0.9)
constraints: Miscellaneous languages can have various graphical structures, whereas the other languages each have a unique graphical structure
target_learners: primary school students in the last three years of primary education (ages 9-12)
target_learning_goals: decoding and interpreting mathematical information represented in graphs, maps, diagrams and number lines
examples: The GLIM test comprised six items from each of the six language categories, with items drawn from state, national and international year-level mathematics and science tests
key_sources: Lowrie, Tom and Diezmann, Carmel. (2010). Solving graphics tasks: Gender differences in middle-school students. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2009.11.005

article_title: Relations between the worked example and generation effects on immediate and delayed tests
citation: Relations Between the Worked Example and Generation Effects on Immediate and Delayed Tests. (2016). Submitted 29/01/2016.
title: Match the level of instructional guidance to the element interactivity of the material and the expertise of the learners
description: The article's central design recommendation is that guidance must be calibrated to material complexity and learner knowledge. It states that "the required level of instructional guidance cannot be determined without considering the level of complexity of learning materials which is dependent on the level of element interactivity". For novices facing complex, high element interactivity content, explicit worked examples are recommended; for simple content, or complex content handled by more expert learners, self-generation is recommended, especially for longer-term retention. The recommendation rests on the delayed- and immediate-test findings of the trigonometry experiment reported in this article.
requirements: Learner expertise and the element interactivity of the materials must be assessable so guidance can be matched to them.
constraints: The delayed worked-example effect for novices on high element interactivity material only approached significance on a 2-tailed test (p = .06), and the Year 11 delayed test had low internal reliability, so replications are required.
target_learners: Secondary school mathematics students (Year 10 novices and Year 11 more knowledgeable learners)
target_learning_goals: Learning to simplify trigonometry expressions and memorising trigonometry formulae
examples: Year 10 novices studying worked examples for high element interactivity simplification problems while generating low element interactivity formulae from name cues
key_sources: Relations Between the Worked Example and Generation Effects on Immediate and Delayed Tests. (2016). Submitted 29/01/2016. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2016.06.007

article_title: Elementary tests in psychology.
citation: Seashore, C. E. (1922). Elementary tests in psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Before attributing a developmental trait to a subject, ascertain the test of capacity has been made elemental
description: Seashore draws a practical implication for educational psychology and mental testing: the findings "constitute a challenge to a large part of current systems of mental tests". Before attributing a developmental trait to a subject, the tester must ascertain that the measured variable is not an artifact of failing to make the test of capacity elemental, since a non-elemental test can reflect training, age-related apperceptive skill, or cognitive difficulty rather than native capacity.
requirements: Tests intended to measure capacity must be reduced to simple, direct impressions requiring no skill in action, so that training cannot improve the record.
constraints: The article states no test can be made absolute, because even the most elemental test involves some acquired power of observation.
target_learners: all subjects of mental and sensory testing, including school children
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of capacity versus developmental or trained traits
examples: The Iowa laboratory's two experiment lines — comparing blind and seeing pupils, and prolonged training on intensity-of-sound discrimination — were undertaken to verify the principle before applying it to test design.
key_sources: Seashore, C. E. (1922). Elementary tests in psychology. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org

article_title: Correlation of excellence in different school subjects based on a study of school grades.
citation: L. E. Frailey and C. M. Crane. (1912). Correlation of Excellence in Different School Subjects Based on a Study of School Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Control instructional conditions by studying a cohort with identical instructors, subjects and years before comparing grade-based ability correlations
description: The article's method is to first establish constancy of conditions, then compare standings. The authors write that "in order to make our investigations as constant as possible it was necessary that we should select from the many students a certain group which had passed through the same conditions in respect to time of studying the subjects investigated, years of schooling, instructors, etc." This makes grade-based group comparisons interpretable as reflecting pupil ability rather than differing instruction.
requirements: Access to multi-year pupil records allowing selection of pupils whose study experiences were identical in instructors, subjects, and years of schooling.
constraints: The authors note the unequal numbers of boys (14) and girls (18), saying the difference is so slight as to have little or no effect on general conclusions.
target_learning_goals: measuring consistency of academic achievement
examples: The study secured 32 pupils who all entered in fall 1908, graduated spring 1912, and studied algebra, civics, American history, geometry, Latin and English together under the same instructors.
key_sources: L. E. Frailey and C. M. Crane. (1912). Correlation of Excellence in Different School Subjects Based on a Study of School Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology

article_title: Understanding instructions.
citation: Marcus, N. (1998). Understanding Instructions. PhD thesis, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/70247
title: Five-experiment instructional materials: resistor problems and angle construction tasks
description: The empirical core of the thesis is a series of five experiments using electrical resistor problems and angle construction tasks, comparing instruction presented as diagrams that cue pre-existing schemas against text, and in Experiment 5 also against diagrams unlikely to cue pre-existing schemas. The abstract states: "In Experiments 1 to 4, three different electrical resistor problems were given to students to complete, with instructions presented using diagrams (which cue pre-existing schemas) or text." Subjective rating scales were used in Experiments 4 and 5 (Appendix D).
requirements: Instructions must be presentable in both diagrammatic and textual modes for comparison
target_learners: primary and high school students from the participating Sydney schools
target_learning_goals: understanding instructions for electrical resistor and angle construction problems
examples: Experiment 5 presented four different angle construction tasks under three presentation conditions: schema-cueing diagrams, non-cueing diagrams, or text.
key_sources: Marcus, N. (1998). Understanding Instructions. PhD thesis, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/70247

article_title: The child's speech. I. The impulse to speech.
citation: Robert MacDougall. (1912). The Child's Speech. I. The Impulse to Speech. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=none-in-text
title: MacDougall's account of the impulse to speech as arising from inherited developmental factors plus external social-practical demands
description: The article presents a theory in which the incentives to speech are internal and external: they 'spring from the new forces which are growing up within his own nature' as well as 'in the world about the child'. Speech appears as a spontaneous product of maturation, driven by expressive and social instincts, imitation, and play, and sustained by the practical need to make wants known and secure social mediation.
requirements: the child must have reached a phase of organic development in which brain and organs of speech are sufficiently matured for articulation and understanding
constraints: the account is a theoretical argument rather than an empirical test; it is the first in a series of papers, with imitation's later role deferred to subsequent installments
target_learning_goals: early language acquisition and articulate expression
examples: the article describes the infant's widening activity — looking, listening, reaching, handling — as the developmental context in which the craving for expression arises
key_sources: Robert MacDougall. (1912). The Child's Speech. I. The Impulse to Speech. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=none-in-text

article_title: Zur Erkennung jugendlichen Schwachsinns.
citation: Paul Wilhelm Knuth. (1909). Zur Erkennung jugendlichen Schwachsinns [review of Gustav Major's monograph]. Zeitschrift für Experimentelle Pädagogik, 9, 425. none in text
title: Major's three-class taxonomy of feeble-mindedness: debility, imbecility, and idiocy
description: The review reports that Major classifies the feeble-minded by severity: "The feeble-minded are grouped into three classes,debility.imbecihtv and idiocy, corresponding to light, medium and severe cases." The organizing axis is defect type as well as severity: "The leading characteristic of the first class is their ethical defect, that of the last two intellectual defect." This taxonomy structures Major's discussion of teachability, moral treatment, and diagnosis throughout the monograph.
requirements: Diagnosis must first distinguish the severity class, since the leading defect differs by class: ethical defect in the light cases and intellectual defect in the medium and severe cases
target_learners: children identified as feeble-minded (debility, imbecility, idiocy)
target_learning_goals: identification and classification of degree of mental weakness to guide educational placement and treatment
examples: Major's diagnostic outline assigns children to debility, imbecility, or idiocy corresponding to light, medium, and severe cases
key_sources: Paul Wilhelm Knuth. (1909). Zur Erkennung jugendlichen Schwachsinns [review of Gustav Major's monograph]. Zeitschrift für Experimentelle Pädagogik, 9, 425. none in text. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0063874

article_title: Zur Erkennung jugendlichen Schwachsinns.
citation: Paul Wilhelm Knuth. (1909). Zur Erkennung jugendlichen Schwachsinns [review of Gustav Major's monograph]. Zeitschrift für Experimentelle Pädagogik, 9, 425. none in text
title: Major's diagnostic procedure for detecting mental debility in youth
description: The element is Major's full diagnostic outline for detecting mental debility, described as "fairly simple and can be applied by the capable parent and teacher." It consists of "the chief tests being (1) mathematical problems; (2) questions involving discrimination; (3) tests of school learning, and (4) various tests by the psychoanalytic method" such as association reactions, mental imagery tests, and story analysis, plus "an elaborate outline for medical examination."
requirements: Application by a capable parent or teacher, per the review's statement that the method is simple enough for lay use
target_learning_goals: detection and diagnosis of mental debility to inform educational decisions
examples: Test components include mathematical problems, discrimination questions, tests of school learning, association reactions, tests of mental imagery, and analysis of stories

article_title: A Further Criterion for the Selection of Mental Test Elements.
citation: Chapman, J. Crosby and Dale, A. Barbara. (1921). A Further Criterion for the Selection of Mental Test Elements. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=A+Further+Criterion+for+the+Selection+of+Mental+Test+Elements
title: The matched-groups criterion: ranking test elements by their weight on hereditary brightness versus environmental training
description: The article proposes "A new criterion ... which will rank tests with reference to the weight placed on hereditary brightness rather than on environmental training." It works by selecting two groups of children matched in total intelligence-test score but differing widely in chronological age, then comparing their average scores on each test element. Elements on which the Young Bright group exceeds the Old Dull group are judged to favor native intelligence; the reverse order ranks elements by dependence on training. This loads age and training factors in opposite directions, unlike the usual criteria of age-increase and coherence.
requirements: A large sample of complete intelligence-test administrations from which two total-score-matched groups of differing chronological age can be selected
constraints: Where ratios differ only slightly from unity, nothing can be inferred; the criterion yields order of merit, not absolute quantitative estimates
target_learners: school-age children in elementary grades being assessed with group intelligence tests
target_learning_goals: distinguishing native intellectual endowment from environmentally trained performance in test-element selection
examples: Applied to the National Intelligence Test Series A with 50 matched pairs from Mount Vernon, N. Y. elementary schools, using the five subtests arithmetical reasoning, sentence completion, logical sequence, opposites, and symbol-digit substitution
key_sources: Chapman, J. Crosby and Dale, A. Barbara. (1921). A Further Criterion for the Selection of Mental Test Elements. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=A+Further+Criterion+for+the+Selection+of+Mental+Test+Elements

article_title: Cognitive training enhances growth mindset in children through plasticity of cortico-striatal circuits
citation: Lang Chen, Hyesang Chang, Jeremy Rudoler, Eydis Arnardottir, Yuan Zhang, Carlo de los Angeles and Vinod Menon. (2022). Cognitive training enhances growth mindset in children through plasticity of cortico-striatal circuits. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00146-7
title: Design cognitive training as mastery-oriented learning experiences to enhance both skills and growth mindset
description: The article's tutoring program deliberately promoted mastery-oriented rather than performance-oriented learning: "children were encouraged to learn and received positive feedback upon completion of activities, rather than being evaluated for their performance levels." Because this design was aligned with growth mindset's core concept, the training enhanced growth mindset alongside number knowledge. The authors suggest "a supportive learning environment can lead to simultaneous improvements in academic performance and growth mindset."
requirements: Tutoring must focus on learning to improve skills rather than demonstrating ability, with positive feedback on completion rather than performance evaluation
constraints: Effects demonstrated in a four-week one-on-one tutoring program for 7–10-year-old children focused on number knowledge
target_learners: early elementary school children ages 7–10, including children with math learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: foundational number knowledge (counting, comparing, ordering numbers)
growth mindset
examples: A one-on-one tutoring program (3 days/week, ~60 min/day, 4 weeks) using non-symbolic dot arrays and symbolic Arabic numerals, with positive feedback upon completion of activities
key_sources: Lang Chen, Hyesang Chang, Jeremy Rudoler, Eydis Arnardottir, Yuan Zhang, Carlo de los Angeles and Vinod Menon. (2022). Cognitive training enhances growth mindset in children through plasticity of cortico-striatal circuits. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00146-7

article_title: Enhancing senior high school student engagement and academic performance using an inclusive and scalable inquiry-based program
citation: Davenport Huyer, L., Callaghan, N. I., Dicks, S., Scherer, E., Shukalyuk, A. I., Jou, M. & Kilkenny, D. (2020). Enhancing senior high school student engagement and academic performance using an inclusive and scalable inquiry-based program. npj Science of Learning 5:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00076-2
title: Mandatory whole-class participation in partnered inquiry programming to reach reluctant high-ability students
description: Discovery's design pattern is whole-class, mandatory participation in a term-long partnered inquiry project, chosen deliberately for inclusivity: "The mandatory nature of program participation was established to reach highly capable students who may be reluctant to engage on their own initiative, as a means of enhancing the inclusivity and impact of the program." Students work as full class cohorts with their teacher and graduate mentors rather than as self-selected volunteers, which the article links to building a relevant learning community and to capturing under-engaged students.
requirements: A post-secondary partner able to provide facilities, graduate student mentors, and co-developed curriculum with teachers 1–2 months before each term
constraints: Requires institutional investment and accessible post-secondary collaboration; the second-school replication had only two terms, and the authors call for larger collections to separate SES and cohort effects
target_learners: All students in a senior science class cohort, including capable students reluctant to opt in voluntarily
target_learning_goals: STEM persistence and interest
Critical thinking and problem-solving practice within curriculum subjects
examples: Students were enrolled regardless of volunteering; teachers assessed deliverables against consistent rubrics, and the program was a mandatory course component representing 10–15% of the final grade
key_sources: Davenport Huyer, L., Callaghan, N. I., Dicks, S., Scherer, E., Shukalyuk, A. I., Jou, M. & Kilkenny, D. (2020). article_title: A systematic review of AI literacy scales
citation: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4
title: MAILS: a modular meta AI literacy scale in which creating AI emerged as a separate factor from AI literacy
description: MAILS is a 34-item general-population scale built on Ng et al.'s four AI literacy areas plus psychological competencies (self-efficacy, self-perceived competency). Its CFA found that "creating AI was found to be a separate factor", so the authors made the scale modular: AI literacy (18 items), create AI (4 items), AI self-efficacy (6 items), and AI self-competency (6 items) can each be measured independently. The review found high evidence for structural validity, internal consistency, and construct validity, and reports it is the only scale with evidence for minimal floor and ceiling effects.
requirements: Content validity on the general population still needs to be checked, per the review
constraints: Available in German and English, although the English version has not yet been revalidated
target_learning_goals: knowing and understanding AI
using and applying AI
detecting AI
AI ethics
AI self-efficacy
examples: Most participants completed the scale within 20 minutes (mean 16:05, SD 5:46 in Table 4)
key_sources: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4

article_title: What we learned from creating one of the world’s most popular MOOCs
citation: Barbara A. Oakley and Terrence J. Sejnowski. (2019). What we learned from creating one of the world's most popular MOOCs. npj Science of Learning 4:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0046-0
title: Mayer's principles of multimedia learning as a foundation for effective instructional video
description: Mayer's framework comprises some 30 principles describing how to convey ideas while respecting the limits of working memory, defined as learning "from both pictures and words". The article reproduces the video-relevant subset in Table 1, including multimedia, coherence, signaling, spatial and temporal contiguity, pre-training, segmenting, modality, personalization, voice, embodiment, animation, and the image principle. The authors treat these principles as the theoretical basis explaining LHTL's video design choices and its popularity.
requirements: Application to video requires attending to working-memory limitations when combining words and pictures
constraints: The principles are presented as "technologically agnostic," applying regardless of the technology used to convey information
target_learners: online learners in MOOCs, predominantly 25-34-year-old working adults
target_learning_goals: effective conveyance of learning concepts through video while managing cognitive load
examples: LHTL's videos were designed to satisfy the signaling, segmenting, coherence, personalization, voice, and embodiment principles via green-screen integration, pre-planned scripts, and motion
key_sources: Barbara A. Oakley and Terrence J. Sejnowski. (2019). What we learned from creating one of the world's most popular MOOCs. npj Science of Learning 4:7. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0046-0

article_title: First-year students’ math anxiety predicts STEM avoidance and underperformance throughout university, independently of math ability
citation: Daker, R.J., Gattas, S.U., Sokolowski, H.M., Green, A.E., & Lyons, I.M. (2021). First-year students' math anxiety predicts STEM avoidance and underperformance throughout university, independently of math ability. npj Science of Learning 6:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00095-7
title: Macro-avoidance vs. micro-avoidance framework for math anxiety's academic consequences
description: The authors propose distinguishing two forms of math avoidance: macro-avoidance, the high-level decision to avoid STEM courses, majors, and careers, and micro-avoidance, "small-scale decisions about how much attention to pay in math class, how much effort to exert on math homework, and so on". Because their models controlled for % STEM Courses, macro-avoidance could not explain the grades effect, so they propose micro-avoidance as a candidate mechanism linking math anxiety to STEM achievement independently of math ability. The framework extends Ashcraft and colleagues' local vs. global avoidance distinction to academic behaviors like paying less attention in class, skipping class, and studying less.
requirements: Future research must directly measure micro-avoidance behaviors in real educational contexts to test the hypothesis
constraints: The micro-avoidance mechanism is a hypothesis the present data cannot directly confirm; the article states its data cannot fully rule out the in-the-moment working-memory account either
target_learning_goals: STEM participation
STEM achievement
examples: The study showed math anxiety predicted STEM Grades even with % STEM Courses as a covariate, ruling out macro-avoidance as the explanation for the grades effect
key_sources: Daker, R.J., Gattas, S.U., Sokolowski, H.M., Green, A.E., & Lyons, I.M. (2021). First-year students' math anxiety predicts STEM avoidance and underperformance throughout university, independently of math ability. npj Science of Learning 6:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00095-7

article_title: Neurophysiological prediction of competitive orientation via EEG during outcome evaluation in gamified learning
citation: Hiroki Watanabe, Ayato Tabata, Chikara Ishii & Yasushi Naruse. (2026). Neurophysiological prediction of competitive orientation via EEG during outcome evaluation in gamified learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00420-y
title: Match competitive gamification elements to learners' competitive orientation instead of implementing them uniformly
description: This principle holds that competitive game elements in gamified learning should be selected flexibly according to individual differences in competitive orientation, because the article finds these elements "can undermine motivation for individuals with low competitive orientation". The article argues results "highlight the importance of considering individual differences among learners and designing competitive elements flexibly according to competitive orientation, rather than implementing them uniformly for all learners", and proposes EEG-based assessment during learning as an objective complement to self-report questionnaires such as BrainHex.
requirements: An objective or subjective measure of learners' competitive orientation, such as the BrainHex questionnaire or EEG-derived ERP features, must be available before or during learning.
constraints: The article states its sample of 28 adults was small, limiting statistical power and generalizability, and that prediction performance was moderate; the motivation incongruence effect was detected for low-COS learners while task performance showed no congruence effect.
target_learners: adult learners in gamified digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: sustaining motivation and engagement in goal-structured gamified learning tasks
examples: Twenty-eight adults completed a gamified mental arithmetic task under competitive and self-referential goal conditions while P300, FRN and RewP responses to outcome feedback were recorded.
key_sources: Hiroki Watanabe, Ayato Tabata, Chikara Ishii & Yasushi Naruse. (2026). Neurophysiological prediction of competitive orientation via EEG during outcome evaluation in gamified learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00420-y

article_title: Design of generative AI-powered pedagogy for virtual reality environments in higher education
citation: Ulla Hemminki-Reijonen, Noha M. A. M. Hassan, Minna Huotilainen, Jaana-Maija Koivisto & Benjamin Ultan Cowley. (2025). Design of generative AI-powered pedagogy for virtual reality environments in higher education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00326-1
title: Madida: a fictional GAI learning companion supporting the backcasting exercise
description: Madida is a fictional GAI character serving Use case 2 as a learning companion for the values-thinking backcasting exercise; "Its role includes helping the student prepare their backcasting presentation by engaging in a sparring session about their backcasting exercise." Madida's sparring approach "was prompt-engineered based on the backcasting questions formulated according to the I SEE project," and the character offers emotional support while helping students accomplish the task. Domain experts described Madida's interaction as natural and its nature as encouraging, supportive, and approachable.
requirements: Prompt engineering based on structured backcasting questions, iterated through multiple testing rounds
constraints: The associated exercise includes a limited number of structured questions, which is why testing required fewer questions than Tero
target_learners: higher education students in sustainability education
target_learning_goals: values-thinking competency: creating visions guided by sustainability values via backcasting
examples: A domain expert expressed interest in using Madida for backcasting exercises with her students, and noted Madida could give diplomatic answers on sensitive topics

article_title: Understanding the effects of education through the lens of biology
citation: H. Moriah Sokolowski and Daniel Ansari. (2018). Understanding the effects of education through the lens of biology. npj Science of Learning 3:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0032-y
title: Aim educational interventions at maximizing each child's individual potential across many outcome measures rather than equalizing performance
description: The article recommends abandoning the twin goals of shifting the mean and narrowing the distribution of a single attainment measure, because biological mechanisms generate individual differences even under equitable conditions. It argues "the goal of educational interventions should be to maximize potential at the individual level" across "a kaleidoscope of educational outcomes" on which individuals occupy different rank positions. Policy should offer diverse educational opportunities so children find niches fitting their predispositions.
requirements: Educational attainment must be reconceptualized as an umbrella term spanning many distinct measurable outcome distributions
constraints: True equity in the sense of equal outcomes is described as unattainable even in a perfectly equitable system
target_learners: all children across development, including those from impoverished environments
target_learning_goals: maximizing individual potential across cognitive and emotional educational outcome measures
examples: The Abecedarian follow-up showed mean gains of 5–7 points with unchanged variance, illustrating why mean-shift goals should replace gap-narrowing goals
key_sources: H. Moriah Sokolowski and Daniel Ansari. (2018). Understanding the effects of education through the lens of biology. npj Science of Learning 3:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0032-y

article_title: Intelligent Augmented Reality Training for Motherboard Assembly
citation: Giles Westerfield, Antonija Mitrovic & Mark Billinghurst. (2015). Intelligent Augmented Reality Training for Motherboard Assembly. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:157–172. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0032-x
title: MAT: Motherboard Assembly Tutor combining a constraint-based ITS with a spatially-registered AR interface
description: MAT is an intelligent AR system that trains users to identify and install components (memory, processor, graphics card, TV tuner card, heatsink) on a computer motherboard. A communication module relays information between the AR interface and the ITS over "XML remote procedure calls over a TCP/IP network connection"; the AR interface uses a head-mounted display, camera-based marker tracking, spatially-registered 3D models, animations, and a screen-aligned HUD with color-coded text and text-to-speech. The architecture is designed to be modular so it can be adapted to new assembly and maintenance tasks.
requirements: The display elements and the domain model must be customized for each type of task, while the underlying architecture and scaffolding algorithms remain the same
constraints: The fiducial marker-based tracking approach has limited accuracy, poor resistance to occlusion and obtrusive markers
target_learners: novice users with minimal computer hardware assembly experience
target_learning_goals: identifying motherboard components and installing memory, processors, and heat sinks
examples: A prototype taught 16 university students to install five motherboard components through an HMD, with tracking via eight markers around the motherboard and ARToolkit marker tracking
key_sources: Giles Westerfield, Antonija Mitrovic & Mark Billinghurst. (2015). Intelligent Augmented Reality Training for Motherboard Assembly. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:157–172. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0032-x

article_title: Preschoolers’ Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study
citation: Gulz, Agneta; Londos, Ludvig & Haake, Magnus. (2020). Preschoolers' Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2020) 30:38–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00193-4
title: Magical Garden: a teachable agent-based play-&-learn game for early math with a state-machine adaptation logic
description: Magical Garden is a research-based play-&-learn game for 4- to 6-year-olds targeting number sense and basic math skills within the number range 1–9. It comprises "60 scenarios, ordered by difficulty defined by number range (1–4, 1–6, or 1–9), representation (none, fingers, dots, dice, number symbols) and method (counting, proto-addition/subtraction, 'true' addition/subtraction)". A state machine tracks each child's progress, steering different paths: children who master a scenario move on, while children who struggle repeat scenarios through varying sub-games or drop back half or entire difficulty levels.
requirements: Children play individually on their own tablet with a personal log-in and their own digital friend (the TA)
constraints: The game deliberately keeps each child working just beyond current mastery, so repetition amounts differ substantially among individual children
target_learning_goals: number sense: connecting number words, magnitudes, and iconic, semi-symbolic and symbolic number representations
examples: Sub-games feature distinct narratives, e.g., a nearsighted bumblebee needing help finding the right flower or a treasure hunter reaching a cave by attaching balloons to her basket
key_sources: Gulz, Agneta; Londos, Ludvig & Haake, Magnus. (2020). Preschoolers' Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2020) 30:38–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00193-4

article_title: Preschoolers’ Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study
citation: Gulz, Agneta; Londos, Ludvig & Haake, Magnus. (2020). Preschoolers' Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2020) 30:38–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00193-4
title: Dynamic assessment in a game: state-machine steering toward the zone of proximal development
description: Magical Garden integrates assessment and instruction through its state-machine progression logic. The article states that "Magical Garden relies on dynamic assessment, i.e., integrating assessment and instruction (Vygotskij 1978), to address a 'potential for learning' rather than a 'static levels of achievement'", with the goal of keeping each child working at a level just beyond current mastery — the zone of proximal development — to maximize learning. Repetition is embedded without monotony by varying the sub-game narrative while keeping the pedagogical challenge constant.
requirements: Continuous logging of each child's performance to decide progression, repetition, or stepping back in difficulty
constraints: The amount and placement of repetition vary among individual children, so different children receive substantially different amounts of training on the same task type
target_learning_goals: number sense and basic math skills
examples: When a child's performance remains low, the system goes back a half or entire level in difficulty so the child can practice and prepare for a new attempt on the higher level

Preschoolers' Understanding of a Teachable Agent-Based Game in Early Mathematics as Reflected in their Gaze Behaviors – an Experimental Study.
