article_title: Adaptive Learning is Hard: Challenges, Nuances, and Trade-offs in Modeling
citation: Pelánek, R. (2025). Adaptive Learning is Hard: Challenges, Nuances, and Trade-offs in Modeling. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00400-6
title: Make design trade-offs in adaptive learning environments explicit, and favor easily realizable approaches when gains are small
description: The article argues designers must weigh cost-effectiveness under limited time, money, and people, since "it is not possible to avoid the issue of trade-offs" and making them explicit is beneficial. Because published research asks only whether an approach improves learning, it cannot tell designers that a slightly weaker but far more easily realizable approach Y should often get priority over X. The principle calls for research that explicitly takes trade-offs into account and for developers to state their compromises openly.
requirements: Awareness of resource constraints (time, money, people) and of the relative realizability of candidate approaches.
constraints: Existing research on whether an approach improves learning does not by itself provide guidance for practical trade-off decisions.
target_learners: designers and developers of adaptive learning environments
target_learning_goals: realistic design decisions for adaptive behavior in practical learning environments
examples: The article contrasts approach X with a smaller-improvement but much more easily realizable approach Y that should often get priority.
The article recommends more research explicitly taking trade-offs such as predictive accuracy versus computational requirements into account.
key_sources: Pelánek, R. (2025). Adaptive Learning is Hard: Challenges, Nuances, and Trade-offs in Modeling. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00400-6

article_title: Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability
citation: Tom Murray. (2015). Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:37–71. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0076-6
title: Match authoring tool complexity to the complexity capacity of the intended user community
description: The article's central design recommendation is that authoring tools should be designed for realistic user audiences by matching tool complexity to task complexity and user complexity capacity, rather than pursuing maximal power. It recommends a qualitative, comparative approach: "we can categorize system complexity and cognitive capacity qualitatively roughly into types or groupings that will provide sufficient insight" into matching decisions, using rough low/medium/high categories with more precise frameworks when needed.
requirements: Designers must assess the complexity capacity of intended users, weigh investment risk, and make usability/power tradeoffs appropriate to realistic use contexts
constraints: The article states effortful quantitative complexity analysis is not necessary for these goals, and that the frameworks are a beginning step pointing to additional operationalization work
target_learning_goals: authoring and customizing intelligent tutoring systems
examples: The article presents Table 1 as an example mapping of author roles to low, medium, and high complexity capacity levels

article_title: MArCo: Building an Artificial Conflict Mediator to Support Group Planning Interactions
citation: Patricia Azevedo Tedesco. (2003). MArCo: Building an Artificial Conflict Mediator to Support Group Planning Interactions. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, 117-155. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197314
title: MArCo: a prototype embedding an artificial conflict mediator for group planning interactions
description: MArCo is the article's prototype system: "MArCo, our prototype embedding the artificial conflict mediator, shows how our conceptual framework has been put to practical use." It operationalises the framework for detecting and mediating meta-cognitive conflicts, drawing on the model of strategic changes, the model of the group, and the history of the interaction. Its purpose is to support group planning interactions by mediating conflicts as they arise.
requirements: Embeds the artificial conflict mediator within the article's conceptual framework
constraints: Demonstrates practical use of the framework; the available text reports no evaluation outcomes

target_learning_goals: Detecting and mediating meta-cognitive conflicts to support group problem solving

article_title: Educational theories and computer game design: lessons from an experiment in elementary mathematics education
citation: Es-Sajjade, A., & Paas, F. (2020). Educational theories and computer game design: lessons from an experiment in elementary mathematics education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09799-w
title: MATHERIAL game design based on CLT and GDT
description: MATHERIAL is a two-player interactive math game in which players solve and create mathematical equations while competing in parallel games. The design drew on cognitive load theory to minimize extraneous load and maximize intrinsic load, and on game design theory principles (identity, immersion, interactivity, increased complexity, informed teaching, and instruction). The game avoided animations to draw more on working memory capacity and used player status development instead of sophisticated avatars.
requirements: Built in HTML5 with responsive website design for access on popular smartphone, tablet, and desktop platforms
constraints: Sophisticated avatars with advanced abilities were beyond the authors' financial capability
target_learning_goals: Math achievement
Math motivation

article_title: Orchestrating iVR technology in an authentic classroom setting and its effects on factual knowledge, comprehension and transfer
citation: P. Spangenberger, N. Matthes, F. Kapp, L. Kruse, J. L. Plass. (2025). Orchestrating iVR technology in an authentic classroom setting and its effects on factual knowledge, comprehension and transfer. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10409-2
title: MARLA: a curriculum-aligned iVR serious game for offshore wind energy troubleshooting
description: MARLA is an immersive VR serious game developed for Meta Quest in which apprentices take the role of a service technician who must "diagnose an error in the hydraulic brake pressure system and repair it". It was built over three years (2019–2022) by an interdisciplinary team using the ADDIE model, and includes a pedagogical agent (Alex), three miniature wind energy plant models, a help view with hypotheses and an interactive hydraulic plan, and game-based feedback. It implements a cognitive apprenticeship approach across a training level (~45 min) and a mission level (~25 min).
requirements: Developed in line with curricula from German vocational education in electrical engineering and two stated learning objectives (structural troubleshooting procedure; factual knowledge about offshore wind energy plants)
constraints: Design required close cooperation with stakeholders (researchers, game designers, teachers, technicians) and approximately 1.5 years of prototyping, testing and adapting scenarios
target_learners: apprentices in electrical engineering at German vocational schools
target_learning_goals: structural troubleshooting procedure
factual knowledge about offshore wind energy plants
sustainability-related learning objectives
examples: Players are accompanied by the pedagogical agent Alex in the training level and operate more independently in the mission level, reflecting modeling, coaching and exploration phases

article_title: Trends, tensions, and futures of maker education research: a 2025 vision for STEM+ disciplinary and transdisciplinary spaces for learning through making
citation: Ioannou, A., & Gravel, B. E. (2024). Trends, tensions, and futures of maker education research: a 2025 vision for STEM+ disciplinary and transdisciplinary spaces for learning through making. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10334-w
title: Four clusters structure the current state of maker education research
description: The editors organize the special issue's eighteen papers into four thematic clusters: STEM+ disciplinary and transdisciplinary learning spaces; digital technologies in making; assessment practices and frameworks; and representation, inclusion, and tensions around maker-centered initiatives. They state that "these clusters reflect the current state-of-the-art in the field as well as significant questions to guide near future research." The taxonomy serves as a map of the maker education research landscape.
requirements: The taxonomy reflects the editors' perceived dominant focus of each manuscript, as papers often span multiple clusters
target_learners: K-20 students in formal and informal maker contexts
target_learning_goals: Learning through making and design across STEM+ disciplines
key_sources: Ioannou, A., & Gravel, B. E. (2024). Trends, tensions, and futures of maker education research: a 2025 vision for STEM+ disciplinary and transdisciplinary spaces for learning through making. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10334-w

article_title: Trends, tensions, and futures of maker education research: a 2025 vision for STEM+ disciplinary and transdisciplinary spaces for learning through making
citation: Ioannou, A., & Gravel, B. E. (2024). Trends, tensions, and futures of maker education research: a 2025 vision for STEM+ disciplinary and transdisciplinary spaces for learning through making. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 1–14. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10334-w
title: Assessment in maker education requires new forms and tools suited to heterogeneous contexts
description: The editors argue that because makerspaces differ inherently in learning opportunities, processes, and challenges, traditional one-size-fits-all assessment is inadequate. They state that "a traditional, one-size-fits-all assessment tool or practice of assessment is unlikely to fulfill the expectation of capturing learning and skill development in these dynamic learning spaces." New forms of assessment and tools are needed to document learning outcomes.
requirements: Assessment tools must account for the heterogeneity of makerspaces and their intended outcomes
constraints: Heterogeneity in intended outcomes makes assessment difficult and makes context inseparable from findings
target_learners: Learners in formal and informal makerspaces
target_learning_goals: Documenting learning outcomes, skills, attitudes, and dispositions in maker contexts

article_title: Developing digital formative assessment for deep conceptual learning goals: Which topic-specific research gaps need to be closed?
citation: Hankeln, C., Kroehne, U., Voss, L., Gross, S., & Prediger, S. (2025). Developing digital formative assessment for deep conceptual learning goals: Which topic-specific research gaps need to be closed? Education Tech Research Dev, 73, 1953–1973. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10486-x
title: Mastering Math Online-Check: a DFA platform for assessing conceptual understanding of basic arithmetic
description: The Mastering Math Online-Check is a DFA administered on the alea.schule platform, developed within the 15-year-long Mastering Math project targeting Grade 5–7 students who struggle in mathematics. It uses closed formats (multiple-choice, single-choice, drag-and-drop) automatically coded regarding typical assets and misconceptions, plus open-ended items manually coded by teachers with item-specific categories. Evaluation outcomes are displayed on dashboards with varying degrees of detail.
requirements: Open answers need to be manually coded by teachers; item-specific categories entailing typical responses, assets, and errors are provided to support teachers in the manual coding
constraints: The validity of the evaluation relies strongly on the quality of teachers' coding
target_learners: Grade 5–7 students who struggle in mathematics
target_learning_goals: Understanding of multiplication and division, place value understanding

article_title: Understanding the educators’ practices in makerspaces for the design of education tools
citation: Turakhia, D., Ludgin, D., Mueller, S., & Desportes, K. (2024). Understanding the educators' practices in makerspaces for the design of education tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10305-1
title: A codebook framework of educators' competencies, strategies, and challenges in makerspaces
description: The article's thematic analysis of interviews with seven educators across five makerspaces produced a codebook organized into three macro-themes. The authors state that the analysis 'resulted in a codebook consisting of six sets of competencies that educators valued most, five sets of strategies they deployed, and three sets of challenges that educators encountered'. They offer it 'as a potential framework for further studying makerspace learning', with sub-themes linking strategies to the competencies they build.
requirements: Derived from semi-structured interviews with educators in makerspaces serving middle and high school students; the authors note it is 'not exhaustive or identical across educators or makerspaces'.
constraints: The authors caution the codebook 'gives an overview of the educators' perspectives and experiences and is possibly indicative of more prominent themes', not a complete taxonomy.
target_learners: middle and high school students in makerspaces
target_learning_goals: maker competencies including technical skills, communication, creative mindset, agency, and contextual reflection
examples: Six rounds of coding on over 240 response quotes from Zoom interviews, using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic coding process with inter-rater agreement over 80%.
key_sources: Turakhia, D., Ludgin, D., Mueller, S., & Desportes, K. (2024). Understanding the educators' practices in makerspaces for the design of education tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10305-1

article_title: Understanding the educators’ practices in makerspaces for the design of education tools
citation: Turakhia, D., Ludgin, D., Mueller, S., & Desportes, K. (2024). Understanding the educators' practices in makerspaces for the design of education tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10305-1
title: Scaffolding learning through problem scoping, project stages, concept progression, adapted support, and metaphors
description: The most prominent strategy theme in educators' interviews was scaffolding learning. The codebook lists five sub-strategies: widening project scope over time, incrementally teaching skills through project stages, introducing complex concepts over time, providing more support early and more autonomy as students learn, and teaching complex concepts using analogies familiar to individual learners instead of a one-size-fits-all approach.
requirements: Educators adapt scaffolding to project complexity and learner familiarity, e.g. starting with simple circuits before computer and laser cutter work.
target_learners: middle and high school students in makerspaces
target_learning_goals: technical skills and design concepts built incrementally
examples: One educator described a two-week skill-building phase with cardboard, glue, and paper before moving to digital fabrication and CAD, then 3D printing and games.
key_sources: Turakhia, D., Ludgin, D., Mueller, S., & Desportes, K. (2024). Understanding the educators' practices in makerspaces for the design of education tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10305-1

article_title: Understanding the educators’ practices in makerspaces for the design of education tools
citation: Turakhia, D., Ludgin, D., Mueller, S., & Desportes, K. (2024). Understanding the educators' practices in makerspaces for the design of education tools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10305-1
title: Strategies of fostering collaboration, building relationships, personalized assessment, and encouraging failure
description: Beyond scaffolding, the analysis identified four strategy categories: fostering collaboration through organizational and spatial interventions, building relationships through direct student-teacher engagement and a catalytic role, assessing performance through personalized metrics and learner-defined outcomes rather than fixed standards, and encouraging failure by teaching overcoming fear of failure and the importance of failing fast and early through tinkering.
requirements: Assessment of technical and soft skills relies on individual growth and improvement over time instead of fixed standards and metrics.
target_learners: middle and high school students in makerspaces
target_learning_goals: collaboration, interpersonal trust, resilience towards failure, and growth in technical and soft skills
examples: Group sizes were typically student pairs, with five as the largest group; educators re-designed seating and spatial setups to build organic collaborative interaction.

citation: Luca Botturi, Tiffany Fioroni, Chiara Beretta, Davide Andreoletti, Alessandro Ferrari, Felipe Cardoso, Anna Picco-Schwendener, Suzanna Marazza, Silvia Giordano. (2024). title: MAPAW privacy education materials (Emma video set and protectyourdata.ch resources)
description: Within the MAPAW project, a set of 4 short digital stop-motion video clips (duration 2–3 minutes) was developed and released under Creative Commons license, presenting Emma, a girl, and her use of a social network called Momentum. The videos address personal data collection, personalized advertising, the technical network infrastructure involved in data collection, and legal aspects, and can be used to wrap up discussion. All original materials are available at www.protectyourdata.ch in Italian and other Swiss national languages, along with pointers to other online privacy education resources.

understanding personalized advertising
legal aspects of data processing

article_title: Spatial versus normal audio guides in exhibitions: Cognitive mechanisms and effects on learning
citation: Manuela Glaser, Laura Hug, Stephan Werner, Stephan Schwan. (2025). Spatial versus normal audio guides in exhibitions: Cognitive mechanisms and effects on learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10424-3
title: The Model of Audio-Visual Cognitive Processing (MAVCP) extends multimedia learning theory with a non-verbal auditory representation built from acoustic and spatial codes
description: The MAVCP is the authors' own integration of auditory perception theories (auditory scene analysis, the association model) with multimedia learning theories (CTML, CATLM, ICALM). It posits three attentionally selected bases — sound base, word base and image base — organized into acoustic, verbal and visual mental representations that are integrated into a single mental model with prior knowledge. As the authors state, "this model emphasizes the integration not only of audio-textual (word base) and visual information (image base) but also of acoustic spatial codes (sound base) as a relevant aspect of multimedia learning." Learning quality depends on how clearly content is presented, extractable by attention, and attributable across bases.
requirements: Auditory and visual learning content must be clearly presented, extractable from surrounding information by attentional processes, and easily attributable to each other
constraints: The authors note the CTML mainly refers to two-dimensional learning material, and the MAVCP is proposed as a further development for spatial acoustic information
target_learning_goals: integration of audio explanations with exhibited visual content
memory of audio-explained exhibit content
examples: The MAVCP (Fig. 1) was used to derive the prediction that the spatial contiguity principle should extend to spatial acoustic information in exhibitions, tested in two experiments with a spatial audio guide
key_sources: Manuela Glaser, Laura Hug, Stephan Werner, Stephan Schwan. (2025). Spatial versus normal audio guides in exhibitions: Cognitive mechanisms and effects on learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10424-3

article_title: Insights on identifying potential types of guidance for supporting student inquiry when using virtual and remote labs in science
citation: Gamor, K.I. (2021). Insights on identifying potential types of guidance for supporting student inquiry when using virtual and remote labs in science. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09928-5
title: Apply guidance types matched to the inquiry phase and to how and when they are used for optimal effect
description: The principle holds that guidance in inquiry learning should be selected not only by type but by timing: the appropriate type of guidance should be leveraged during the relevant phase of inquiry. The article credits the reviewed framework with aptly describing "how and when to apply the types of guidance for optimal effect", making phase-matching a condition of optimal guidance effect.
requirements: Designers must know which guidance type is appropriate for each phase of inquiry before deploying it
constraints: Optimal effect depends on applying guidance at the right phase; mis-timed guidance is not addressed as beneficial
target_learners: students conducting inquiry with virtual and remote labs in science
target_learning_goals: effective support of student inquiry through appropriately timed guidance
examples: The reviewed framework describes how and when to apply guidance types such as prompts, heuristics, scaffolds, process constraints, and direct presentation of information across inquiry phases.

article_title: Multimodal analysis of interaction data from embodied education technologies
citation: Walkington, C., Nathan, M. J., Huang, W., Hunnicutt, J., & Washington, J. (2024). Multimodal analysis of interaction data from embodied education technologies. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 2565–2584. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10254-9
title: MAET: multimodal analysis for embodied technologies as a research method
description: MAET is a research method adapted from multimodal analysis for embodied, interactive educational technologies where learners collaborate. It tracks "learners' gestures, actions on physical and virtual objects, whole body movements and positions, and their talk moves" over time and space. Its distinguishing affordance is alignment with embodied cognition theories, valuing action itself as a conceptual tool, unlike social semiotics, conversation analysis, or multimodal (inter)action analysis approaches.
requirements: A networked system of audio, motion, and video data capture technologies are necessary for MAET to rigorously examine interactions across modalities
Video recordings, screen recordings, and motion capture data synced across perspectives
constraints: Relies on video camera feeds rather than automatic multimodal learning analytics such as automatic gesture detection
Syncing and coding video data from multiple perspectives for micro-interactions can be quite time-consuming
Cost, technical expertise, and setup may be prohibitive in some cases
target_learners: Learners using collaborative immersive educational technologies (K-12 students, teacher-learners)
target_learning_goals: Understanding embodied and collaborative mathematical reasoning
examples: Applied to a motion capture game (The Hidden Village), a shared VR environment for mathematics teachers, and shAR hologram conjecture tasks
key_sources: Walkington, C., Nathan, M. J., Huang, W., Hunnicutt, J., & Washington, J. (2024). Multimodal analysis of interaction data from embodied education technologies. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 2565–2584. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10254-9

article_title: Mapping student-AI interaction dynamics in multi-agent learning environments: Supporting personalized learning and reducing performance gaps
citation: Hao, Z.; Cao, J.; Li, R.; Yu, J.; Liu, Z.; Zhang, Y. (2025). Mapping Student-AI Interaction Dynamics in Multi-Agent Learning Environments: Supporting Personalised Learning and Reducing Performance Gaps. https://osf.io/preprints/eduRxiv
title: MAIC: a massive AI-empowered course system with an AI teacher, four AI peer roles, and analytical back-end agents
description: MAIC is an online learning platform that constructs LLM-driven agents to support teaching and learning. Interface agents include a teacher and four AI peer types — "Sparker, Questioner, Thinker and Notetaker" — each with distinct functions, while back-end analytical agents (Classroom Situation Analysis, Learning Situation Analysis, Classroom Director) decide pacing and which agent appears. Students can choose observation or interaction mode and adjust discussion intensity, speech intervals, and text display speed.
requirements: Instructors upload course materials so agents can draft teaching slides and lecture scripts using multimodal understanding and knowledge structure extraction
constraints: The study used one introductory course, Towards Artificial General Intelligence, at a single elite university in China
target_learners: university students from various academic disciplines
target_learning_goals: understanding of artificial general intelligence topics
interactive and personalized learning
examples: Students begin by selecting a course, customize classroom participants, and can interchange observation and interaction modes anytime

article_title: Students' perceptions of Facebook for academic purposes
citation: Arteaga Sánchez, R., Cortijo, V., & Javed, U. (2015). Students' perceptions of Facebook for academic purposes. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2013.08.012
title: The Mazman & Usluel (2010) structural model explains educational usage of Facebook through adoption and purposes of usage.
description: A structural equation model relating three latent variables — adoption, purposes of usage, and educational use of Facebook. Adoption is measured by usefulness, ease of use, social influence, facilitating conditions and community identity; purposes by social relations, work related and daily activity; educational use by communication, collaboration and resource/material sharing. The article states "educational use of Facebook is explained directly by purposes of Facebook usage and indirectly by Facebook adoption" and validates the model on a Spanish sample.
requirements: Survey measurement of the model's 11 observed variables using Likert-scale items adapted from Mazman & Usluel (2010)
constraints: Validated on a single-institution sample of business students at one Spanish university; the authors note the sample limitation and call for multi-institution and cross-country replication
target_learning_goals: adoption of social network tools for educational purposes
educational use of social networking sites

article_title: A peer assessment method to provide feedback, consistent grading and reduce students' burden in massive teaching settings
citation: Luaces, O., Díez, J., & Bahamonde, A. (2018). A peer assessment method to provide feedback, consistent grading and reduce students’ burden in massive teaching settings. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.08.006
title: Matrix factorization model of peer assessment with ordinal preference learning
description: The article proposes representing peer assessment as a sparse three-dimensional matrix (graders × answers × labels) and completing it via matrix factorization. Answers are encoded as bag-of-words vectors and graders and labels as one-hot vectors, all embedded in a shared k-dimensional Euclidean space. The model is trained using stochastic gradient descent on a maximum-margin loss over preference judgments (pairs of answers where one grader rated one higher than another), rather than by regression on raw grade values, reflecting an ordinal rather than cardinal view of grading.
requirements: Instructors must provide a rubric and a list of aspects (labels) to be assessed, with each label scored on an ordinal range of values.
constraints: The approach assumes an unknown relationship between grades given to different labels and relies on ordinal preference judgments rather than exact grade values.
target_learners: higher education students in massive courses
target_learning_goals: open-response assessment and feedback
key_sources: Luaces, O., Díez, J., & Bahamonde, A. (2018). A peer assessment method to provide feedback, consistent grading and reduce students’ burden in massive teaching settings. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.07.016

article_title: A comparison of structured and unstructured navigation through a CBT package
citation: Stanton, N. A. and Stammers, R. B. (1990). A comparison of structured and unstructured navigation through a CBT package. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ414518
title: Match navigation structure to trainee cognitive style rather than imposing one structure for all
description: The article concludes that the unstructured condition may be a better training environment for some individuals, whilst others may do better in the structured condition, dependent on the individual's own learning style and abilities. It recommends that further investigations should have the emphasis upon advice rather than control, as too much structure may make the environment inflexible and tedious. This principle supports offering learner-controlled sequencing with guidance rather than fixed pre-sequencing for all trainees.
requirements: Trainees must be able to relate the task goals to the learning environment clearly enough to organize a suitable learning environment of their own
constraints: A dislike of the lack of structure was reported by some subjects, and non-sequential presentation may be inappropriate for learning procedural skills
target_learning_goals: acquisition of procedural knowledge in hierarchical process-control tasks
examples: The unstructured group selected the modules to be viewed via an overview screen and returned to it after each module to select the next, while the structured group were presented with each of the modules in a fixed order
key_sources: Stanton, N. A. and Stammers, R. B. (1990). A comparison of structured and unstructured navigation through a CBT package. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ414518

article_title: Impact of Mobile Assisted Language Learning (MALL) on EFL: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Imtiaz Hassan Taj, Norrihan Binti Sulan, Muhammad Aslam Sipra, Waqar Ahmad. (2016). Impact of Mobile Assisted Language Learning (MALL) on EFL: A Meta-Analysis. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.2p.76
title: MALL as a ubiquitous, multimodal platform for EFL instruction fitting the PPP paradigm
description: The article frames Mobile Assisted Language Learning as instruction delivered through mobile phones, whose "user friendly interfaces, ubiquitous access and improved data storage and retrieval capacities offer a good platform for learning". It holds that MALL fits the Presentation–Practice–Production paradigm, that phones can present rich material in multimodal ways, and that instructors can provide initial scaffolding and gradually withdraw support, allowing learners to take charge of their learning.

constraints: The article notes MALL is a relatively young field, only a couple of decades old, with no dedicated journal and much literature in conference proceedings
target_learners: EFL learners from fifth grade through undergraduate level
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary acquisition
English as a foreign language instruction
examples: The meta-analysis included 13 studies in which content was delivered via mobile phones (12 studies) or a PDA (1 study), mostly through SMS or dedicated applications

article_title: Effectiveness of Problem-Based Learning on Secondary Students' Achievement in Science: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Funa, A. A., & Prudente, M. S. (2021). Effectiveness of problem-based learning on secondary students’ achievement in science: A meta-analysis. International Journal of Instruction, 14(4), 69-84. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2021.1445a
title: Maastricht Seven Step Model of PBL process
description: The article identifies the Maastricht Seven Step Model (Schmidt, 1983; Clouston et al., 2010) as "the best known and widely used process of PBL". Its steps are: clarifying the text and explaining unclear terms and concepts; defining the key problem; analyzing the problem and suggesting possible solutions; elaborating, testing, reviewing, and refining; formulating learning objectives; self-study; and integrating and testing new information. The article states most of the pooled studies used these processes along with the identified teaching strategies.
requirements: Implementation includes self-assessment and collaborative reflection alongside teachers’ evaluation, which the article calls important parts of PBL to evaluate students’ learning
constraints: The reflexive part of PBL was not given emphasis by the analyzed studies, possibly due to their quasi-experimental, quantitative research designs
target_learning_goals: problem solving
self-directed learning
science concept understanding
examples: Most studies obtained in this meta-analysis used the Maastricht Seven Step Model processes along with collaboration, probing questions, and student choice of solution method.

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence Linking Mathematics and Science Professional Development Interventions to Teacher Knowledge, Classroom Instruction, and Student Achievement
citation: Lynch, K., Gonzalez, K., Hill, H., & Merritt, R. (2025). A Meta-Analysis of the Experimental Evidence Linking Mathematics and Science Professional Development Interventions to Teacher Knowledge, Classroom Instruction, and Student Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584251335302
title: Meta-analytic dataset of 46 experimental mathematics and science PD studies with 200 teacher-outcome and 126 student-achievement effect sizes
description: The dataset comprises randomized experimental studies of PK-12 mathematics and science PD published 2001 or later, each reporting both teacher and student outcomes. As the article states, "The final meta-analytic sample includes 46 studies contributing 200 effect sizes for teacher outcomes and 126 effect sizes for student achievement outcomes." Teacher outcomes were coded as knowledge or classroom instruction; moderators coded intervention features, PD foci, and contextual features.
requirements: Studies must employ a randomized experimental design comparing a treatment group to a business-as-usual control group and report sufficient data to calculate effect sizes for both teacher and student outcomes
constraints: Excludes non-randomized designs and interventions not involving in-service classroom teachers, such as researcher-delivered instruction
target_learning_goals: mathematics and science achievement
teacher knowledge
classroom instruction
examples: Screening located 12,086 records from database searches plus 1,402 from other sources, reduced to 840 studies passing preliminary relevance criteria

article_title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Effect of Gamified Clinical Skill Learning on Learning Outcomes in Undergraduate Nursing Education.
citation: Chen W.-L., Winitchayothin S., Cheng C.-H., Tonapa S.I., Chou F.-H., & Zimmerman P.-A. (2026). A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of gamified clinical skill learning on learning outcomes in undergraduate nursing education. The Journal of Nursing Research. https://doi.org/10.1097/jnr.0000000000000772
title: Select gamification approaches by matching format to educational objectives, institutional technological capabilities, and implementation context
description: The review concludes that gamified learning's effectiveness depends critically on design characteristics, implementation quality, and alignment with objectives, so educators should "match formats to objectives, invest in faculty development, and pilot before scaling". Serious games are recommended where consistent knowledge gains are sought, gamified simulation for procedural skills, and scalable web/mobile formats in resource-constrained settings provided mastery goals, timely feedback, and assessment alignment are built in. The principle operationalizes the review's subgroup findings as implementation guidance for nursing curricula.
requirements: Institutional technology infrastructure, technical support, and educator preparation are needed for successful adoption, per the review's discussion
constraints: Formal statistical testing of between-subgroup differences was not conducted, so category-level guidance requires cautious interpretation
target_learning_goals: Knowledge acquisition
Clinical skill performance
Attitudes toward clinical skill learning
examples: The review's subgroup analysis differentiated serious games (SMD=0.84), gamified simulation (SMD=0.79), and gamified web/mobile formats (SMD=0.55) on knowledge outcomes to guide format selection
key_sources: Chen W.-L., Winitchayothin S., Cheng C.-H., Tonapa S.I., Chou F.-H., & Zimmerman P.-A. (2026). A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of gamified clinical skill learning on learning outcomes in undergraduate nursing education. The Journal of Nursing Research. https://doi.org/10.1097/jnr.0000000000000772

article_title: Computer-based surgical skill training: a systematic review.
citation: Morsund Lars Andreas Lars, Singh Shraddha, Patel Agastya, Lancellotti Francesco, Satyadas Thomas. (2026). Computer-based surgical skill training: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08830-7
title: Mastery learning as the pedagogical framework resonating with self-directed virtual teaching
description: The review connects self-directed virtual teaching to mastery learning, "wherein students take ownership of their own educational progression through individualized pacing and repeated practice." Rather than emphasizing final assessments alone, this approach "promotes continual learning through milestone-based evaluations." The review argues educational environments must be adaptable, offering structured opportunities for iterative practice and meaningful feedback to support such models.
requirements: An adaptable educational environment offering structured opportunities for iterative practice and meaningful feedback
target_learning_goals: self-directed progression of technical surgical skills through individualized pacing and repeated practice
key_sources: Morsund Lars Andreas Lars, Singh Shraddha, Patel Agastya, Lancellotti Francesco, Satyadas Thomas. (2026). Computer-based surgical skill training: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08830-7

article_title: Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review.
citation: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/
title: Match assessment methods to Miller's competency levels, using direct observation for higher levels
description: The review recommends that instructors understand the limitations of different assessment approaches and use a range of methods fitting the specific learning situations of Miller's four competency levels. It states that written examinations "tend to measure the potential to perform rather than actual work performance", so more advanced trainees should be assessed through direct observation in simulation scenarios or real practice for the higher competency levels.
requirements: Instructors must understand the limitations of different assessment approaches before selecting methods for each Miller level.
constraints: Written examinations tend to measure the potential to perform rather than actual work performance, limiting their use for higher competency levels.
target_learners: Physicians, residents, medical students, nurses, and nursing students in hospital settings
target_learning_goals: Patient safety competencies including knowledge, skills, and behaviour across Miller's four competency levels
examples: The review identified 20 tools for the 'shows how' and 'does' levels in the domains of managing safety risks, working in teams, and communicating effectively, including three suitable for emergency situations, two for surgery, and two for anaesthesiologists in training.
key_sources: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/

article_title: Effectiveness of simulation-based nursing education depending on fidelity: a meta-analysis.
citation: Kim Junghee, Park Jin-Hwa, Shin Sujin. (2016). Effectiveness of simulation-based nursing education depending on fidelity: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0672-7
title: Match the level of simulation fidelity to the educational goal rather than assuming higher fidelity is always better
description: The article's meta-analytic results show the effect of simulation-based nursing education is not proportional to simulator fidelity: medium-fidelity simulation led for psychomotor outcomes while high-fidelity simulation and standardized patients led for cognitive and affective outcomes. The authors conclude "it is important to use an appropriate level of simulation to meet all of the educational goals and outcomes" and that "educational interventions should be broad enough to satisfy educational goals". The principle directs educators to select simulation modality by intended learning outcome.
requirements: The required learning outcomes must govern the choice of simulation method, as the article states in its background
constraints: The analyses did not consider learning-related factors such as debriefing methods, reflection, and feedback at each fidelity level
Studies published in languages other than English or Korean were not included
target_learning_goals: cognitive outcomes
psychomotor outcomes
affective outcomes
satisfaction and learning attitudes
examples: The meta-analysis compared effect sizes across low-, medium-, and high-fidelity simulators, hybrid simulators, and standardized patients, finding the largest psychomotor effect for MFS (1.76) and the largest cognitive effect for HFS (0.50)
key_sources: Kim Junghee, Park Jin-Hwa, Shin Sujin. (2016). Effectiveness of simulation-based nursing education depending on fidelity: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0672-7

article_title: The Effectiveness of CPS-ALM Model in Enhancing Statistical Literacy Ability and Self Concept of Elementary School Student Teacher
citation: Takaria. J, Rumahlatu. D. (2016). The Effectiveness of CPS-ALM Model in Enhancing Statistical Literacy Ability and Self Concept of Elementary School Student Teacher. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.25. https://www.iiste.org
title: Mathematics blog viewership graphic as literacy media for statistical interpretation
description: The article illustrates its literacy media with a website display of a mathematics blog's viewership. "The display in figure above describe the numbers of  viewers of mathematic blog per days, per weeks, and per months." Students interpret the histogram and summary figures, e.g., the biggest viewership leap on January 18th 2012 reaching 337 persons, 84 viewers that day, and 32,900 total since establishment.
requirements: Media sources for statistical literacy can include print media, electronic media, journals, book reports, and the internet
target_learning_goals: interpreting graphs and tables
extracting quantitative information from media
examples: The article's worked interpretation reads the histogram's highest and lowest viewer levels (February 21st and 23rd) and the summary totals from the blog display

article_title: Errors of Students Learning with React Strategy in Solving the Problems of Mathematical Representation Ability
citation: Sari, D.P., Darhim, & Rosjanuardi, R. (2018). Errors of students learning with REACT strategy in solving the problems of mathematical representation ability. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 121-128. https://jme.ejournal.uns.ac.id
title: Test of mathematical representation ability with three indicators (visual, verbal, symbolic) and reliability coefficient 0.56
description: The study's instrument was a test to measure students' mathematical representation ability, with a reliability coefficient of 0.56, which the article classifies as "the medium reliability level". Following Mudzakir (2006), it measured three indicators: visual representation (making the image of a real world situation to clarify the problem), verbal representation (answering using words or written text), and symbolic representation (solving problems involving arithmetic symbols). The same items were used as a 60-minute posttest in both classes.
requirements: Expert validation of items, provided in this study by six named validators
constraints: Reliability of 0.56 is characterized by the article as only medium
target_learning_goals: mathematical representation ability
examples: Posttest items included the net of a cube (1a), a decorative lamp cube contextual problem (1b), a cuboid cake volume problem (2), and a pyramid surface area problem (3)
key_sources: Sari, D.P., Darhim, & Rosjanuardi, R. (2018). Errors of students learning with REACT strategy in solving the problems of mathematical representation ability. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 121-128. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1173659

article_title: Scaling Academic Planning in Community College: A Randomized Controlled Trial. REL 2017-204
citation: Visher, M. G., Mayer, A. K., Johns, M., Rudd, T., Levine, A., and Rauner, M. (2016). Scaling academic planning in community college: A randomized controlled trial (REL 2017–204). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Regional Educational Laboratory West. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs
title: My Academic Plan (MAP) system: nudging, guaranteed counseling, online planning tool, and integrated data system
description: The MAP system is a technology-based intervention the South Orange County Community College District developed to scale counselor-approved academic planning. It has four components: "Targeted nudging" delivered through Sherpa, a recommendation and personalization engine, via emails, texts, MySite portal notices, and robocalls; guaranteed counseling appointments in two-hour group workshops or one-on-one sessions; access for all students to the online MAP planning tool; and an integrated data system coordinating MAP, Sherpa, and the SARS scheduling software to deliver nudges, track responses, schedule sessions, and track attendance and plan completion.
requirements: Every student's academic plan must be reviewed and approved by a counselor, a requirement the counseling department added beyond the Student Success Act mandate
Counseling capacity must be organized so guaranteed appointments do not lengthen wait times for non-study students, using strategies such as greater use of adjunct counseling faculty
constraints: The study was not designed to assess which type of nudge worked best
In fall 2012, before the intervention, less than 10 percent of students opened the district's MAP tool
target_learning_goals: Semester-by-semester academic planning aligned to education goals, majors, and transfer or credential requirements
examples: Counselors conducted 57 two-hour workshops between September 29 and December 18, 2014, in a 19-computer lab; 523 (48.2 percent) of workshop-group students attended, and the district delivered up to 11 nudges per intervention student over the semester
key_sources: Visher, M. G., Mayer, A. K., Johns, M., Rudd, T., Levine, A., and Rauner, M. (2016). Scaling academic planning in community college: A randomized controlled trial (REL 2017–204). article_title: Effects of Digital Storytelling in Mathematics Instruction on Academic Achievement and Examination of Teacher-Student Opinions on the Process
citation: İlknur Özpinar, Semirhan Gö kç e, Arzu Aydoğan Yenmez. (2017). Effects of Digital Storytelling in Mathematics Instruction on Academic Achievement and Examination of Teacher-Student Opinions on the Process. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 5, No. 10. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i10.2595
title: Match digital story scenarios to the learners' grade level and keep stories focused rather than covering a whole subject
description: The article's student and teacher data indicate scenario quality determines whether digital stories engage learners. Students reported a story was boring because "it wasn’t suitable for our age group", and the teacher emphasized that "scenarios being suitable for the grade levels" is important and that stories covering a whole subject become long and boring. The principle is to design story scenarios at the learners' level and scope them to specific learning objectives.
requirements: Scenarios must be prepared in consideration of the grade level of the learners
constraints: The teacher reported storytelling would be long and boring if prepared for the whole subject rather than specific learning objectives
target_learners: eighth-grade mathematics students (teacher suggested applicability to 5th grade and lower)
target_learning_goals: mathematics topics such as triangles, transformational geometry, and probability of simple events
examples: In the study, 11 digital stories were prepared for 14 learning objectives across three sub-learning domains, and students criticized the Ece and Kerem story as too simple for their age group

Effects of Digital Storytelling in Mathematics Instruction on Academic Achievement and Examination of Teacher-Student Opinions on the Process. Journal of Education and Training Studies, Vol. 5, No. 10. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v5i10.2595

article_title: The 5E Instructional Model: A Constructivist Approach for Enhancing Students' Learning Outcomes in Mathematics
citation: Stephen Akinyemi Omotayo & Joshua Oluwatoyin Adeleke. (2017). The 5E Instructional Model: A Constructivist Approach for Enhancing Students' Learning Outcomes in Mathematics. JISTE, Vol. 21, No. 2, 2017.
title: Mathematics Achievement Test (MAT) and Mathematics Interest Inventory (MII) instruments
description: The study used two researcher-developed measures. The MAT was a 30-item multiple-choice test drawn from the SSII curriculum, with items selected for difficulty indices between .40 and .60 and discriminating indices .030 and greater; its reliability via the Kuder Richardson 20 Formula "yielded a reliability coefficient of .79". The MII, adapted from Bakare's Vocational Interest Inventory, contains 20 Likert-scale items and achieved a Cronbach Alpha of .92, which the authors say suggests the instrument was highly reliable.
requirements: Items vetted by experienced secondary school mathematics teachers and pilot tested on sixty senior secondary school II students
target_learners: senior secondary school II students in Nigeria
target_learning_goals: measuring mathematics achievement
measuring interest in mathematics
examples: The MAT was content validated at the first three levels of Bloom's taxonomy: knowledge, comprehension, and application

article_title: Effect of Mastery Learning on Senior Secondary School Students' Cognitive Learning Outcome in Quantitative Chemistry
citation: Telimoye Leesi Mitee and Georgina N. Obaitan. (2015). Effect of Mastery Learning on Senior Secondary School Students' Cognitive Learning Outcome in Quantitative Chemistry. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.5. https://www.iiste.org
title: Mastery learning instructional cycle of units, formative tests, and corrective instruction
description: A lesson/unit-level instructional pattern in which material is divided into smaller units with performance criteria, formative tests are administered during each unit, and results are checked against the mastery criterion. Students who attain mastery are commended and may serve as peer tutors, while those who do not receive "corrective instruction based  on the identified areas of difficulties" through re-teaching, peer tutoring, homework, or small group discussion, and are retested. The cycle continues "until virtually  all the students master the taught material before the teac her moves to the next unit of learning."
requirements: Formative tests administered during the teaching of each unit
Set criterion accepted as mastery level against which performance is checked
Corrective instruction targeted at identified areas of difficulty, followed by retesting
target_learning_goals: Mastery of unit content and improved cognitive learning outcome
examples: The experimental group in this study was taught with this cycle for two weeks before the post-test

article_title: Effects of Mathematics Integration in a Teaching Methods Course on Self-Efficacy of Preservice Agricultural Education Teachers
citation: Christopher T. Stripling and T. Grady Roberts. (2013). Effects of Mathematics Integration in a Teaching Methods Course on Self-Efficacy of Preservice Agricultural Education Teachers. Journal of Agricultural Education, 54(2), 114-129. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2013.02114
title: Mathematics Enhancement Teaching Efficacy Instrument (Jansen, 2007)
description: The Mathematics Enhancement Teaching Efficacy Instrument, developed and validated in a doctoral dissertation at Oregon State University, measures three constructs: mathematics teaching efficacy, personal mathematics efficacy, and personal teaching efficacy. "The instrument utilizes a different rating scale for each construct" — personal mathematics efficacy (1 = not at all confident to 4 = very confident), mathematics teaching efficacy (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree), and personal teaching efficacy (1 = nothing to 9 = a great deal of influence). Post-hoc reliabilities in this study were .93, .80, and .89 respectively.
requirements: Face and content validity established by an expert panel; construct and discriminate validity verified through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses; scores computed by averaging items after reverse coding items 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, and 13.
constraints: Validated originally with secondary agricultural teachers in Utah, Oregon, and Washington populations, not with preservice teachers.
target_learning_goals: measuring mathematics teaching efficacy
measuring personal mathematics efficacy
measuring personal teaching efficacy
examples: Administered three times during Fall 2011 (weeks 1, 12, and 15), taking participants approximately 8 minutes to complete.
key_sources: Christopher T. Stripling and T. Grady Roberts. (2013). Effects of Mathematics Integration in a Teaching Methods Course on Self-Efficacy of Preservice Agricultural Education Teachers. Journal of Agricultural Education, 54(2), 114-129. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2013.02114

article_title: Difference among Levels of Inquiry: Process Skills Improvement at Senior High School in Indonesia
citation: Hardianti, T. & Kuswanto, H. (2017). Difference among Levels of Inquiry: Process Skills Improvement at Senior High School in Indonesia. International Journal of Instruction, 10(2), 119-130. http://www.e-iji.net/dosyalar/iji_2017_2_8.pdf
title: Match the level of inquiry learning to students' scientific experience and competence, then raise levels gradually
description: The article recommends that teachers select the inquiry level fitting students' current competence and experience rather than defaulting to the highest level. It states "the teacher could apply inquiry learning of the levels that are appropriate for their scientific experience and competence, which are then to be raised to higher levels." The study's finding that Level 3 outperformed Level 4 for novice Grade X students grounds this recommendation.
requirements: Teachers must know students' level of competence and experience before choosing an inquiry level
constraints: The article notes students could not instantly keep up with ILL-4 because good inquiry learning is applied in sequence from lowest to highest level
target_learners: Grade X (first-grade) senior high school physics students in Indonesia
target_learning_goals: science process skills: observation, hypothesis construction, data interpretation, conclusion drawing, communication
examples: Three SMA classes were treated with ILL-2, ILL-3, and ILL-4; the ILL-3 group, whose competence matched that level, achieved the highest gain score (0.62)

title: Malaysia Critical Thinking Instrument (MACTI)

requirements: Prior validity and reliability testing, which the article reports was done by its developer
constraints: No new validity or reliability testing was performed in this study because the instrument was unchanged
target_learners: Technical Matriculation College students in Malaysia
target_learning_goals: Measuring critical thinking disposition
examples: Administered as pre-test before the 8-week intervention and as post-test to both groups, with data analyzed in SPSS

article_title: Depicting and Outlining as Pre-Writing Strategies: Experimental Results and Learners' Opinions
citation: Hung, B. P., & Van, L. T. (2018). Depicting and Outlining as Pre-writing Strategies: Experimental Results and Learners' Opinions. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 451-464. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11231a

requirements: When depicting is applied, training and instruction should be offered to students at the beginning
Teachers should make depicting friendly, fun and comfortable in the classroom
constraints: Depicting cannot suit all descriptive writing topics because some ideas are hard to depict
The study was conducted on a small sample size, which might have diminished generalization
target_learners: students at a low level of proficiency

idea generation
organization of ideas
examples: Participants wrote 8 descriptive paragraphs, 4 with outlining training and 4 with depicting training in a cross-intervention design

article_title: Application of Make a Match Model to Improve Geography Learning Outcomes
citation: Arisanty, D., Riyah. (2019). Application of make a match model to improve geography learning outcomes. Journal of Technology and Science Education, 9(1), 32-40. https://doi.org/10.3926/jotse.547

May interfere with the peace of learning in left-right classes

article_title: Gender-Related Effects of Group Learning on Mathematics Achievement among the Rural Secondary Students
citation: Hossain, M.A., & Tarmizi, R.A. (2012). Gender-related effects of group learning on mathematics achievement among the rural secondary students. Egitim Arastirmalari-Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 47, 1-22.

article_title: Bridging Gender Gap in the Physics Classroom: The Instructional Method Perspective
citation: Obafemi, D. T. A. (2015). Bridging Gender Gap in the Physics Classroom: The Instructional Method Perspective. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.20. http://www.iiste.org
title: Match the instructional method to the level of the educational objective being taught

article_title: Effects of Behavioural Objectives-Based Instructional Strategy on Senior School Students' Academic Performance in Mathematics in Omu-Aran, Nigeria
citation: M. F. Salman, L. A. Yahaya, A. Yusuf, M. A. Ahmed & J. O. Ayinla. (2012). description: The article describes the Mager model, which spread through 1960s teacher workshops, as the source of behavioural objectives in education. target_learning_goals: Clear specification of intended learning outcomes across cognitive, affective and psychomotor domains
examples: The article's worked ABCD example: after completing the unit, students will answer correctly 90% of posttest questions, decomposed into audience, behaviour, condition and degree

citation: Chesimet M. C, Githua B.N, Ng’eno, J. K. (2016). Effects of Experiential Learning Approach on Students’ Mathematical Creativity among Secondary School Students of Kericho East Sub-County, Kenya. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(23). http://www.iiste.org
title: Mathematical Creativity Test (MCT)
description: The Mathematical Creativity Test (MCT) was the instrument used to post-test all four groups after the treatment. It was "validated with the help of experts in the Department of Curriculum Instruction and Education Management of Egerton University and mathematics teachers from selected secondary schools", and was pilot tested for reliability using Cronbach alpha, which was found to be 0.778. The test measured the four dimensions of mathematical creativity the article defines.
requirements: Expert validation and pilot reliability estimation, as the article describes

article_title: The Effects of Arts-Integrated Instruction on Students' Memory for Science Content: Results from a Randomized Control Trial Study
citation: Mariale M. Hardiman, Ranjini Mahinda JohnBull, Deborah Carran. (2017). The Effects of Arts-Integrated Instruction on Students' Memory for Science Content: Results from a Randomized Control Trial Study. Paper presented at the annual meeting of the American Educational Research Association. https://www.aera.net
title: Matched-pairs crossover design pattern: equal content, dosage, order, and activity type across treatment and control units
description: This lesson-and-unit-level design pattern pairs an arts-integrated unit with a conventional unit matched in content, dosage, order of content presentation, and type of instructional activity, so that the only systematic difference is the arts-based versus conventional mode of demonstrating knowledge. Students are randomized to one condition for a first unit and cross over to the alternate condition for a second unit, with classroom pairs matched within sites for time of day and within-teacher effects. The article used this pattern to isolate the effect of arts integration on retention.
requirements: All teachers deliver both conditions; unit pairs must provide the same science content, dosage, and mode of delivery to assure active learning in both conditions
constraints: Randomization at the student level with IEP designations checked for even distribution across classes; condition reversal in the second session
target_learners: elementary students in matched classroom pairs
target_learning_goals: retention of academic content in non-arts subjects
examples: In the control condition students designed charts, wrote sentences with target vocabulary, and did choral reading; in treatment they sang songs, chanted raps, took visual notes, and performed dance and tableau

description: The article defines mathematical creative thinking skills through a set of indicators that a measurement instrument must cover: "original thinking, thinking in detail, thinking fluently, thinking flexibly." These indicators ground the study's posttest instrument, whose essay questions were aligned to the indicators of students' creative thinking abilities, and they frame the article's concern that Indonesian students' reasoning aspect scored lowest in the 2018 PISA cognitive-process comparisons.

article_title: Improving Numeracy and Literacy: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Worth, J., Sizmur, J., Ager, R. & Styles, B. (2015). Improving Numeracy and Literacy. Education Endowment Foundation. http://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN20621819
title: Mathematics and Reasoning programme
description: A Year 2 numeracy intervention developed by Professor Terezinha Nunes and Professor Peter Bryant at the University of Oxford, based on quantitative reasoning. As the report states, "Quantitative reasoning— understanding the relations between numbers and being able to use them to solve problems— formed the basis of the numeracy intervention." Four types of quantitative reasoning were explored: inversion; additive reasoning; multiplication and one-to-many correspondence; and division and sharing. Lessons covered two mathematical concepts each and used whiteboard presentations, worksheets, board games and online tasks.
requirements: Teachers attend one day of training plus a support visit from the Oxford research team; delivery requires one hour of instruction per week over 10 to 12 weeks
constraints: All teachers agreed there was too much content to deliver in one hour per week and made adaptations to delivery
target_learners: Year 2 pupils in primary and infant schools

understanding of the logical principles underlying mathematics
quantitative reasoning
examples: In the trial, 17 schools were allocated to the numeracy group and delivered the programme as weekly lessons replacing one normal numeracy lesson, at a cost of £21 per pupil over the evaluation year

The first was "a school program which involved daily routines in mathematics (1-Sudoku, 2-chess, 3- find an intruder in a group of objects, 4- match replacing, 5- solving adaptation of Raven's matrices)" lasting two months (N=48). school motivation

article_title: Kindergarten Impacts of a Preschool Language Focused-Intervention
citation: Megan Johanson, Laura M. Justice, and Jessica Logan. (2016). Kindergarten Impacts of a Preschool Language-Focused Intervention. Applied Developmental Science, 20(2), 94-107. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888691.2015.1074050
title: Matthew Effect in preschool language interventions
description: The Matthew Effect is the phenomenon in which an intervention benefits higher-skilled children more than lower-skilled children, such that "the ''rich get richer and the poor get poorer''" (Penno et al., 2002, as cited). The article uses it to interpret the finding that only children with high initial language skill showed long-term LLLI benefits on decoding and comprehension. The authors also distinguish a "true" Matthew Effect from one caused by teachers unintentionally providing fewer participation opportunities to lower-skilled children.
requirements: Interpretation requires measuring children's initial language skill before the intervention to test skill-by-treatment interaction
constraints: The article notes the observed pattern could reflect implementation bias rather than slower learning ability for children with initially low language
target_learning_goals: oral language skills
decoding
reading comprehension
examples: The study probed Language × Treatment interactions at the mean and one SD above and below the mean of the fall preschool language composite

article_title: The Effect of the Math Emporium Instructional Method on Students' Performance in College Algebra
citation: Cousins-Cooper, K., Staley, K. N., Kim, S., & Luke, N. S. (2017). The Effect of the Emporium Instructional Method on Students' Performance in College Algebra and Trigonometry. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 5(1), 1-13. https://ejournals.eu
title: Math emporium instructional method for college algebra
description: The math emporium is a nontraditional, interactive instructional method for learning math, first implemented at Virginia Tech in 1997 and since adopted at many colleges and universities. In the emporium classroom students spend time learning content and working problems using interactive software, getting immediate feedback by soliciting help from instructors and teaching assistants rather than watching an instructor work problems on the board. In this study it was delivered via Pearson's MyLabsPlus across six modules, each containing a pretest, instructional videos, workbook exercises, homework, a quiz, a practice test, and a module test, with staffing at a minimum ratio of one instructor or GTA for every twelve students.
requirements: Students must complete all problems in the corresponding workbook section before taking a module test
A minimum staffing ratio of one instructor or GTA for every twelve students
Students scoring 85 or higher on a module pretest may proceed directly to the next module
constraints: Some emporium instructors graded the workbook for accuracy while others graded for completion
Several faculty members perceived that some students did not understand the rules of the emporium until late in the semester
target_learners: undergraduate students in college algebra and trigonometry
target_learning_goals: algebraic thinking and college algebra achievement
examples: Students placed a cup on top of the desk to signal instructors and GTAs that they had questions, and were encouraged to ask each other questions while waiting

title: Researcher-built creative-thinking test and 30-item English achievement test
description: The study used two researcher-built instruments: a creative-thinking test measuring "the three basic creative capacities: fluency, flexibility and originality" in English, and a 30-item multiple-choice achievement test. Validity was checked by arbitrator review and internal consistency (all dimensions correlated with the total at significance 0.01); reliability was 0.751 by split-half (Spearman Brown) and 0.700 by Alpha Cronbach for the creative-thinking test, with split-half reliability for the achievement test.

constraints: The study's objective limit restricts measurement to three creative-thinking skills (fluency, flexibility, originality) and achievement levels

article_title: Scaffolding Middle School Students' Comprehension and Response to Short Stories
citation: Liang, L. A. (2011). Scaffolding Middle School Students' Comprehension and Response to Short Stories. RMLE Online, 34(8). ISSN 1940-4476.
title: Match the approach to teaching literature with the outcome desired
description: The study's central recommendation is that no single approach to teaching literature serves all purposes: teachers should "match their teaching approach with the outcome desired." Because the reader-response approach fostered response abilities and the cognitive-oriented approach fostered evidence-based comprehension, each is useful for particular purposes related to its theoretical bent but not all purposes. The article concludes both approaches should be used and that instructional decisions have lasting impact.
requirements: Teachers must identify the specific purpose for teaching a text before selecting an approach
constraints: The study examined only one text type, two weeks of instruction, a relatively small student group, and two teachers; replication is needed
target_learners: middle school students in secondary English classrooms
target_learning_goals: comprehension of narrative text
response to literature
examples: Teachers in the study planned to use both the cognitive-oriented and reader-response sets of SREs with all of their current and future classes and to share the plans with grade-level teachers

article_title: Use of Mobile Testing System PeLe for Developing Language Skills
citation: Titova, S. (2015). Use of mobile testing system PeLe for developing language skills. Critical CALL – Proceedings of the 2015 EUROCALL Conference, Padova, Italy. http://dx.doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2015.000387
title: MALL methodological framework combining mobile testing with enquiry-based learning and formative assessment
description: A methodological framework for implementing the PeLe mobile testing system into the language classroom, developed and pilot tested in the MobiLL project. It combines enquiry-based methods ("collaborative and peer learning post-test activities, brainstorming, problem solving activities, group discussions") with mobile learning opportunities such as "immediate feedback, formative assessment, interactivity and flexibility". The framework was implemented through eight in-class PeLe grammar and vocabulary tests followed by teacher-led post-test activity grids.

Instructor-led post-test activities after each test to realize the enquiry-based component
constraints: The study's conclusions are based on subjective and objective data with a small sample (N=35)
Data discussed cover only the first period of the MobiLL project and only the LMSU groups
target_learners: University students of English as a foreign language at B1 level in a preparatory course
target_learning_goals: English grammar and vocabulary skills
Collaboration skills
Learner motivation
examples: Students in three experimental groups took eight PeLe in-class grammar and vocabulary tests responding on their own smartphones or tablets, with 24 post-test activity grids completed by teachers after the tests

article_title: Application of Interactive Multimedia Tools in Teaching Mathematics--Examples of Lessons from Geometry
citation: Marina Milovanoviü, Jasmina Obradoviü, Aleksandar Milajiü. (2013). APPLICATION OF INTERACTIVE MULTIMEDIA TOOLS IN TEACHING MATHEMATICS – EXAMPLES OF LESSONS FROM GEOMETRY. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Cognitive theory of multimedia learning as the design basis for mathematics lessons
description: The article designs its lessons in accordance with Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning, which holds that in mathematics teaching "it is necessary to combine the picture method and the definition method in order to improve the existing knowledge and to enlarge it with the new facts". The multimedia material applies this by pairing textual definitions and theorems with dynamic and graphic presentations based on a step-by-step method with accent on visualization, alongside multimedia design principles from Atkinson and Merrill.
requirements: Combining picture and definition methods so students' existing pictures of terms are connected and developed further
target_learners: Students at different levels of education learning mathematics
target_learning_goals: Building conceptual understanding of mathematical definitions and theorems through visualization
examples: The authors state their lecturing material was created in accordance with the cognitive theory of multimedia learning (Mayer, 2001, 2005) and principles of multimedia teaching and design (Atkinson, 2005; Merrill, 2003).

citation: Shikuku Beatrice Nakhanu, Amadalo Maurice Musasia. (2015). Problem Based Learning Technique and its effect on Acquisition of Linear Programming Skills by Secondary School Students in Kenya. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.20. http://www.iiste.org
title: MAT 1 and MAT 2 mathematics achievement instruments
description: Two researcher-developed instruments measured entry ability and final performance: "MAT 1 had five items that tested linear programming prerequisites" (constructing linear graphs, forming and graphing inequalities, shading unwanted regions, solving simultaneous linear equations graphically), and MAT 2 had five items on linear programming and optimization. examples: MAT 1 was administered to both groups within one week before treatment; MAT 2 was administered within one week after the two weeks of teaching.

description: The study found nearly half of students rated CHLS English content difficult, and the authors argue that "excessively challenging content could quickly lead to students' loss of interest and motivation," so designers must consider content and tasks appropriate to learners' developmental levels. title: Math-enhanced micro-teaching with peer teaching and role-playing as secondary students
description: A lesson-level design pattern in which preservice teachers prepare and deliver agricultural lessons incorporating Stone et al.'s (2006) seven components of a math-enhanced lesson to their peers, who role-play as secondary students. A math-enhanced lesson is defined as "an agricultural lesson that incorporates Stone et al.’s (2006) seven components of a math-enhanced lesson". The pattern combines lesson preparation, peer micro-teaching, and observational learning through watching peers teach.

Assignment of specific cross-referenced NCTM sub-standards to each preservice teacher
constraints: The authors note it is unknown whether the value lies in preparing the lessons, teaching them, participating as students, or a combination of these activities

designing and delivering math-enhanced agricultural lessons

article_title: Magic Breakfast: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Crawford, C., Edwards, A., Farquharson, C., Greaves, E., Trevelyan, G., Wallace, E., & White, C. (2016). Magic Breakfast: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. http://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN14385822
title: Magic Breakfast: supported free, universal, before-school breakfast clubs in disadvantaged primary schools
description: Magic Breakfast is a charity-supported breakfast club intervention in which schools receive "free food, support from a Magic Breakfast school change leader, and a £300 grant towards up-front costs", with delivery by school staff and volunteers. The model tested was universal, free, and held before the school day, chosen because universal provision was thought more likely to raise take-up among disadvantaged pupils by changing norms and reducing stigma. The cost per pupil per year over three years is £11.86, averaged across all pupils in breakfast club schools.

constraints: In practice some schools deviated from the intended model: "some introduced a small charge for some or all pupils, some capped the number of places available, and some introduced a breakfast club during school hours."

target_learning_goals: academic attainment in English and maths
reduced pupil hunger
improved behaviour, concentration, attendance and punctuality
examples: 106 schools received free food, a school change leader, and a £300 grant between September 2014 and July 2015 in a waitlist RCT.

title: MathsFlip online learning environment (class site and learning zone on Microsoft Office 365)

It consists of two main parts: "the class site and (2) the learning zone".
