article_title: Mathematics Mastery: Primary Evaluation Report
citation: Anna Vignoles, John Jerrim, Richard Cowan. (2015). Mathematics Mastery: Primary Evaluation Report. Education Endowment Foundation. http://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/library/maths-mastery-primary
title: Mathematics Mastery programme: whole-school mastery curriculum with training, curriculum-embedded CPD and cross-school collaboration
description: Mathematics Mastery is a whole-school approach to teaching mathematics developed by Ark that aims to raise attainment for all pupils and close the attainment gap between pupils from low income families and their peers. Compared to traditional curricula, "fewer topics are covered in more depth and greater emphasis is placed on problem solving and on encouraging mathematical thinking". Its mastery curriculum has the large majority of pupils progress through content at the same pace, with differentiation through depth of exploration rather than accelerated content coverage. Support includes launch training, in-school development visits, cluster workshops, an online toolkit with mastery-aligned lesson designs, and face-to-face and online collaboration between schools.
requirements: Schools adopt the approach whole-school, rolling out to subsequent year groups year by year
Teachers and schools receive training and in-school support to make the shift to a mastery curriculum
constraints: The report notes no process evaluation was conducted, so the extent to which individual schools adhered to the programme could not be determined
target_learning_goals: Deep conceptual understanding of key mathematical concepts, particularly number
Problem solving and mathematical thinking
examples: In the trial, 83 schools from London and the South East participated, with treatment schools receiving training and resources delivered by the charity Ark
key_sources: Anna Vignoles, John Jerrim, Richard Cowan. (2015). Mathematics Mastery: Primary Evaluation Report. Education Endowment Foundation. http://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/library/maths-mastery-primary

article_title: Mathematics Mastery: Primary Evaluation Report
citation: Anna Vignoles, John Jerrim, Richard Cowan. (2015). Mathematics Mastery: Primary Evaluation Report. Education Endowment Foundation. http://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/library/maths-mastery-primary
title: Given its low per-pupil cost, Mathematics Mastery may represent a cost-effective change for primary schools to consider
description: The report concludes that, given the low per-pupil cost, Mathematics Mastery may represent a cost-effective change for primary schools to consider. First-year cost for a two-form primary school is approximately £7,460 including teacher training, giving an average per-pupil cost of around £131 in the first year, with cost per pupil likely to reduce in future years. The evaluators rate the evidence strength for the programme's effect as moderate and note the effect itself was not statistically significant in this trial.
requirements: Schools fund an upfront participation cost and staff training days in the first year
constraints: The effect detected in this Year 1 trial was not statistically significant, so the cost-effectiveness judgement rests partly on the combined meta-analytic finding
target_learning_goals: Raising mathematics attainment
examples: Costs were calculated from information provided by Ark: £6,000 upfront plus £1,248 of training time, with per-pupil cost falling below £30 for additional year groups

article_title: Physics Learning Achievement Study: Projectile, Using Mathematica Program of Faculty of Science and Technology Phetchabun Rajabhat University Students
citation: Artit Hutem, Supoj Kerdmee. (2013). Physics Learning Achievement Study: Projectile, using Mathematica program of Faculty of Science and Technology Phetchabun Rajabhat University Students. European J of Physics Education, Vol.4 Issue 3. https://www.europeanjournalofphysicseducation.com
title: Mathematica projectile-motion program with DSolve worksheets and trajectory plots
description: A set of Mathematica worksheets the authors used as the experimental instructional treatment. The worksheets solve the equations of motion symbolically with DSolve, substitute parameter values such as x1=350 and g=9.8, and plot trajectories for varying flight times and launch angles. The article states the program "can be experimented at home or at university", allowing students to learn and revise projectile motion at any time.
requirements: Access to the Mathematica program for individual experimentation at home or at university
target_learners: first-year Faculty of Science and Technology university students studying physics
target_learning_goals: understanding projectile motion, including trajectory, range, and velocity components
examples: Worksheets use DSolve on m x''[t]==0 and m y''[t]==-m g, then ListPlot trajectories for t1 = 5 to 20 and launch angles π/3 to 5π/12
key_sources: Artit Hutem, Supoj Kerdmee. (2013). Physics Learning Achievement Study: Projectile, using Mathematica program of Faculty of Science and Technology Phetchabun Rajabhat University Students. European J of Physics Education, Vol.4 Issue 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1052425

article_title: The Effect of Peer Teaching on Mathematics Academic Achievement of the Undergraduate Students in Oman
citation: Abdelkarim, R., & Abuiyada, R. (2016). The Effect of Peer Teaching on Mathematics Academic Achievement of the Undergraduate Students in Oman. International Education Studies, 9(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n5p124
title: Mathematics Achievement Test (MACT)
description: The Mathematics Achievement Test (MACT) is a 10-problem multiple-choice instrument built by the researchers to measure end-of-study mathematics achievement, with a maximum score of 10 and minimum of 0. It covered "Characteristics of Linear Equations, Two variable system of equations, Functions and their Domains and Characteristics of Exponential Functions". Validity was checked by three mathematics professors with an agreement degree of (89%) via the Cooper equation, and reliability via the Corder-Richardson (K, R-20) equation was found (0.83).
requirements: Content validity checked by three mathematics professors with agreement above the 75% acceptance threshold the article cites
constraints: Covers only two chapters of the textbook "Applied Mathematics for Business, Economics, and Social Sciences"
target_learners: Undergraduate female students in Mathematics for Social Sciences I at Dhofar University
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement in linear equations, systems of equations, functions and domains, and exponential functions
examples: Used as the posttest (O2) in the pretest-posttest control-experimental group design
key_sources: Abdelkarim, R., & Abuiyada, R. (2016). The Effect of Peer Teaching on Mathematics Academic Achievement of the Undergraduate Students in Oman. International Education Studies, 9(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n5p124

article_title: Effects of Mastery Learning Instructional Strategy on Senior School Students' Achievement in the Mole Concept
citation: Bashirat T. Lamidi, Oloyede S. Oyelekan and Adekunle S. Olorundare. (2015). Effects of Mastery Learning Instructional Strategy on Senior School Students’ Achievement in the Mole Concept. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 19(5). http://ejse.southwestern.edu
title: Teachers should consider using mastery learning instructional strategy for chemistry instruction to improve the performance of their students in chemistry examinations.
description: The study recommends that teachers should consider using mastery learning instructional strategy for chemistry instruction, based on findings that students taught the mole concept with it performed better than controls taught conventionally. School authorities should also create conducive environment for the use of the strategy by teachers.
requirements: Teachers divide subject matter into units with predetermined objectives, assess after each unit, and require students to demonstrate mastery on unit exams, typically 80%, before moving on to new material.
constraints: Intact classes are easier to organize and getting an intact class with fair representation of the samples along gender and scoring levels was difficult; the quasi-experimental design was not randomized.
target_learning_goals: Achievement in the mole concept in School Certificate Chemistry
examples: The experimental group was given the treatment over a period of two weeks while the control group was taught in the usual way, with revision lessons organized for students who failed to achieve mastery.
key_sources: Bashirat T. Lamidi, Oloyede S. Oyelekan and Adekunle S. Olorundare. (2015). Effects of Mastery Learning Instructional Strategy on Senior School Students’ Achievement in the Mole Concept. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 19(5). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1188287

article_title: Effects of Mastery Learning Instructional Strategy on Senior School Students' Achievement in the Mole Concept
citation: Bashirat T. Lamidi, Oloyede S. Oyelekan and Adekunle S. Olorundare. (2015). Effects of Mastery Learning Instructional Strategy on Senior School Students’ Achievement in the Mole Concept. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 19(5). http://ejse.southwestern.edu
title: Mastery learning is rooted in behaviourist principles of operant conditioning and presumes that all children can learn if provided with appropriate learning conditions.
description: The concept of mastery learning is rooted in the behaviourism principles of operant conditioning (Skinner, 1984). According to the operant conditioning theory, learning occurs when an association is formed between a stimulus and response, and mastery learning focuses on overt behaviours that can be observed and measured. The philosophy presumes that all learners can learn if given the appropriate amount of time and the appropriate instructional opportunities, with three basic indicators of learning output: cognitive introduction behaviours, emotional introduction features, and the quality of teaching activity.
requirements: Students are assisted by the teacher to master each learning unit before proceeding to the next which is more advanced.
constraints: Bloom observed that instructors typically had students take an assessment at the end of instruction which served to give a grade, but regardless of how students did, they continued into the next unit not minding their grade.
target_learning_goals: Maximum achievement in learning tasks
examples: Bloom (1968) came up with the learning for mastery method after examining what it was about individual tutoring that made it an effective instructional approach.
key_sources: Bashirat T. Lamidi, Oloyede S. Oyelekan and Adekunle S. Olorundare. (2015). Effects of Mastery Learning Instructional Strategy on Senior School Students’ Achievement in the Mole Concept. Electronic Journal of Science Education, 19(5). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1188287

article_title: Racing against the Vocabulary Gap: Matthew Effects in Early Vocabulary Instruction and Intervention
citation: Coyne, M. D., McCoach, D. B., Ware, S., Austin, C. R., Loftus-Rattan, S. M., & Baker, D. L. (2019). Racing Against the Vocabulary Gap: Matthew Effects in Early Vocabulary Instruction and Intervention. Exceptional Children, 85(2), 163–179. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402918789162
title: Matthew effect in vocabulary development: students with larger initial vocabularies learn more efficiently and benefit more from instruction
description: The Matthew effect, as described by Stanovich (1986) and applied in this article, is the self-perpetuating mechanism by which students with larger initial vocabularies get more exposure to new vocabulary and are better able to learn from it. The article states the "bottom-line impact of the Matthew effect is that students with larger initial vocabularies get more exposure to new vocabulary through increased oral language and reading experiences and are better able to learn from those experiences." This study extends the framework by showing Matthew effects also appear on experimenter-developed measures of response to vocabulary instruction.
requirements: A previously existing knowledge base that is rich and elaborated facilitates further learning
constraints: The article reports the Matthew effect was more pronounced on distal outcomes like listening comprehension than on target word learning, and that Tier-2 intervention substantially counteracted it for target words
target_learners: kindergarten students at risk for language and learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: vocabulary development
response to vocabulary instruction
key_sources: Coyne, M. D., McCoach, D. B., Ware, S., Austin, C. R., Loftus-Rattan, S. M., & Baker, D. L. (2019). Racing Against the Vocabulary Gap: Matthew Effects in Early Vocabulary Instruction and Intervention. Exceptional Children, 85(2), 163–179. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402918789162

article_title: Mathematics Mastery: Secondary Evaluation Report
citation: John Jerrim, Helen Austerberry, Cosette Crisan, Anne Ingold, Candia Morgan, Dave Pratt, Cathy Smith, Meg Wiggins. (2015). Mathematics Mastery: Secondary Evaluation Report. Education Endowment Foundation. https://doi.org/10.1186/ISRCTN70922140
title: Mathematics Mastery: a whole-school mastery curriculum with depth over accelerated coverage
description: Mathematics Mastery is a whole-school approach aiming to raise attainment for all pupils and close the attainment gap between low-income pupils and their peers. It uses a mastery curriculum in which "the large majority of pupils progress through the curriculum content at the same pace, with differentiation through depth of exploration rather than accelerated content coverage". Fewer topics are covered in more depth each year, with systematic mathematical language, frequent use of objects and pictures, and emphasis on high expectations. Support includes launch training, in-school development visits, cluster workshops and an online toolkit.
requirements: Training and in-school support including launch training days, development visits and cluster workshops
Curriculum-embedded CPD through mastery-aligned lesson designs adapted from an online toolkit
Collaboration and peer support across schools committed to the same curriculum framework
constraints: Unlike classic mastery learning, the class does not significantly delay new topics when some pupils have not achieved mastery; intervention is provided for pupils at risk of falling behind
target_learning_goals: Deepen pupils' conceptual understanding of key mathematical concepts
Build fluency alongside conceptual understanding
Close the attainment gap between low-income pupils and their peers
examples: The Year 7 programme includes 25 hours of work on fractions, with a task asking pupils which of sixteen expressions equal one-quarter, and generalisation tasks for higher-attaining pupils
key_sources: John Jerrim, Helen Austerberry, Cosette Crisan, Anne Ingold, Candia Morgan, Dave Pratt, Cathy Smith, Meg Wiggins. (2015). Mathematics Mastery: Secondary Evaluation Report. Education Endowment Foundation. https://doi.org/10.1186/ISRCTN70922140

article_title: Mathematics Mastery: Secondary Evaluation Report
citation: John Jerrim, Helen Austerberry, Cosette Crisan, Anne Ingold, Candia Morgan, Dave Pratt, Cathy Smith, Meg Wiggins. (2015). Mathematics Mastery: Secondary Evaluation Report. Education Endowment Foundation. https://doi.org/10.1186/ISRCTN70922140
title: Mathematics Mastery secondary implementation with training, resources and per-pupil cost of around £50 in year one
description: The evaluated implementation delivered the Mathematics Mastery programme to Year 7 pupils in 44 trial schools from London and the South East, with training and resources provided by the charity Ark. First-year cost is estimated at "approximately £7,460 in the first year for a secondary school, including teacher training costs", giving an average per-pupil cost of around £50 per year, likely to reduce in future years. The programme was later accredited by NCETM for CPD quality.
requirements: Schools must not already be receiving the Mathematics Mastery programme
Headteachers, maths coordinators and class teachers receive launch training, development visits and cluster workshops
constraints: Participating schools volunteered, so effects may not generalise to all schools; participating schools had lower-achieving, lower-income and more ethnic minority pupils than the country as a whole
target_learners: Year 7 pupils in participating secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Raise mathematics attainment for all pupils
examples: 88% of schools and 73% of pupils initially enrolled were successfully followed through to completion
key_sources: John Jerrim, Helen Austerberry, Cosette Crisan, Anne Ingold, Candia Morgan, Dave Pratt, Cathy Smith, Meg Wiggins. (2015). Mathematics Mastery: Secondary Evaluation Report. Education Endowment Foundation. https://doi.org/10.1186/ISRCTN70922140

article_title: Utilizing Instructional Media for Teaching Infrastructure Administration
citation: Ulfah Nur Fajriah, Madziatul Churiyah. (2016). Utilizing Instructional Media for Teaching Infrastructure Administration. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.6. https://www.iiste.org
title: Make a Match card-pairing activity following media-based presentation
description: A classroom activity pattern in which each student receives a card holding either a question or an answer and searches for the matching partner. In this study the teacher distributed question and answer cards after presenting material via the multimedia module, students worked in pairs on paper, and the exercise was followed by a posttest. The article defines it: "each studen ts received a card (can be question or answer), the n looks for the pair suited with the card being hold on as fast as possible".
requirements: A set of question and answer cards distributed to each student
target_learning_goals: Infrastructure administration content mastery
examples: The teacher applied Make a Match in both the experimental and control classes after the respective learning treatments.
key_sources: Ulfah Nur Fajriah, Madziatul Churiyah. (2016). Utilizing Instructional Media for Teaching Infrastructure Administration. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.6. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1092480

article_title: Learning How to Learn: A Student Success Course for at Risk Students
citation: Bowering, E. R., Mills, J., & Merritt, A. (2017). Learning How to Learn: A Student Success Course for At Risk Students. The Canadian Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 8(3). http://ir.lib.uwo.ca/cjsotl_rcacea/vol8/iss3/12
title: Mandate registration for at-risk students, pair diagnostic assessment with feedback, and build an academic toolbox honed through multiple application opportunities
description: The authors attribute the SSC's success to three design characteristics: compulsory registration (since students rarely seek out free support services voluntarily), diagnostic assessment with individual feedback that makes students aware of their own strengths and weaknesses, and an academic toolbox of cognitive, metacognitive, and self-governance skills practiced repeatedly. As they state: "We believe that the following characteristics of the SSC underlie its success as a student support tool: mandatory program registration, diagnostic assessme nt with feedback, and development of an “academic toolbox” of skills honed through multiple application opportunities." The assessment feedback also framed academic performance as changeable with effort, which the authors connect to Dweck's growth mindset.
requirements: Enough time for attitudes toward mandatory attendance to become positive (the article's program duration was 14 weeks)
Instructors who provide guidance and constructive feedback throughout the semester, allowing relationship building
constraints: Mandatory course registration and payment of associated fees were not initially well received by most students, though attitudes became more positive with time
target_learners: Undergraduate students on academic probation or otherwise at risk
target_learning_goals: Awareness of one's own learning strategy strengths and weaknesses
Adoption of more sophisticated cognitive and metacognitive strategies
Personal responsibility for learning
examples: All AP students were required to register for the SSC and pay its cost-recovery tuition fee
On course evaluations, at least 80% of students said they would recommend the course to friends, and students commented they wished they had taken it in first year
key_sources: Bowering, E. R., Mills, J., & Merritt, A. (2017). Learning How to Learn: A Student Success Course for At Risk Students. The Canadian Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 8(3). http://ir.lib.uwo.ca/cjsotl_rcacea/vol8/iss3/12

article_title: The Effect of Mathematics Instruction through Computer Algebra Systems on the Academic Achievements of Secondary Education Students: Turkey Example
citation: Mehmet Alper Ardıç; Tevfik İşleyen (2018). The Effect of Mathematics Instruction through Computer Algebra Systems on the Academic Achievements of Secondary Education Students: Turkey Example. Journal of Education and e-Learning Research, 5(3): 165-173. https://doi.org/10.20448/journal.509.2018.53.165.173
title: Mathematica computer algebra system as a CAMI tool for secondary mathematics
description: Mathematica is the computer algebra system used to deliver the experimental instruction. The article describes it as software that "can do symbolic calculation besides numerical calculation to solve mathematical problems", with abilities to plot advanced graphs in cartesian, polar and cylindrical coordinates and to visualize. Its notebook (.nb) files can be saved in numerous formats, and the freely installable CDF Player lets users examine prepared structures and "interfere as far as allowed" without Mathematica installed. Manipulable structures such as slides intersect with dynamic geometry software features.
requirements: Teachers received in-service training on CAS use before implementation; dynamic materials and worksheets were developed by the researchers beforehand
target_learning_goals: understanding graphs of quadratic functions (parabola)
examples: Figure 1 shows a three-dimensional graph plotted through Mathematica; experimental lessons used dynamic materials and worksheets over six lesson hours

article_title: Historic and Ethnic Music Found to Increase Geographic Understanding: A Quasi-Experimental Study
citation: Richardson, Ronald; Brouillette, Liane. (2013). Historic and Ethnic Music Found to Increase Geographic Understanding: A Quasi-Experimental Study. Journal for Learning through the Arts, 9(1). http://escholarship.org/uc/item/71g4x3cr
title: Mapping the Beat eighth-grade music-history workshop curriculum
description: Mapping the Beat is a supplementary American history curriculum developed with National Geographic Education Foundation funding via the ArtsBridge program, organized around "three concepts--environment, identity, and movement" modeled on the Geography for Life standards. The eighth-grade version studied here comprised nine 45-minute, two-period workshops (e.g., Instrument Migration, Work Songs, the Ngoni and the Atlantic Slave Trade, Underground Railroad, Civil War bands, Chinese in America, the Piano and the Industrial Revolution), taught with recorded music. Each unit opens with a conversation linking concepts to students' lives, then presents musical examples discussed as records of cultural migration, products of geographic environment, and cornerstones of identity.
requirements: Deliverable within regular class periods using recorded music when funding for live musicians is unavailable
constraints: Studied at one suburban California middle school with a high-achieving social studies curriculum; 15% of students could not be randomly assigned due to scheduling constraints
target_learning_goals: cultural and physical geography of the United States
geography-related attitudes and interest
understanding of cultural migration and identity
examples: Workshop 5 used African-American spirituals and coded quilt maps of the Underground Railroad; Workshop 9 traced the Steinway family and mass piano production to teach the Industrial Revolution
key_sources: Richardson, Ronald; Brouillette, Liane. (2013). Historic and Ethnic Music Found to Increase Geographic Understanding: A Quasi-Experimental Study. Journal for Learning through the Arts, 9(1). http://escholarship.org/uc/item/71g4x3cr

article_title: The Effect of Direct Instruction Strategy on Math Achievement of Primary 4th and 5th Grade Students with Learning Difficulties
citation: Ahmad Abdulhameed Aufan Al-Makahleh. (2011). The Effect of Direct Instruction Strategy on Math Achievement of Primary 4th and 5th Grade Students with Learning Difficulties. International Education Studies, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v4n4p199
title: 80-item mathematics achievement test and 20-item attitudes to mathematics scale
description: The author developed two instruments: an 80-item mathematics achievement test built from content analysis of fourth and fifth mathematics textbooks covering facts, concepts, and the four operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication and division), and a twenty-item attitudes to mathematics scale measuring attitudes to mathematical content, the mathematics classroom, and using mathematical skills in day-to-day life. Both were administered as pre-test and post-test with validity and reliability coefficients secured.
requirements: Validity and reliability coefficients secured for both instruments
target_learners: 4th- and 5th-grade students with mathematics learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: Basic mathematical skills achievement and attitudes toward mathematics
examples: The achievement test was administered as pre-test and post-test to both experimental and control groups

citation: Manesha Kaur Rajendra Singh, Manjet Kaur Mehar Singh, & Lin Siew Eng. (2015). Advances in Language and Literary Studies 6(6). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.6p.201
title: Ministry of Education speaking assessment scale for Form One
description: The speaking assessment scale was created by the Malaysian Ministry of Education based on the contexts and functions listed in the Course of Study and is used for Form One students. It "assesses students' ability to take part in social interaction to express ideas, opinions and thoughts", with assessment criteria for spoken interaction including personal response, fluency, language accuracy and pronunciation. It served as the scoring instrument for pre-tests and post-tests in this study.
requirements: Administered as identical pre-test and post-test forms of five questions, ten minutes per student, validated by three experienced English language teachers
target_learners: Form One secondary school students in Malaysia
target_learning_goals: Spoken interaction: expressing ideas, opinions and thoughts in English
examples: Pre-test and post-test scores on this scale were compared using an independent sample test

article_title: Successful Learning of Academic Word List via MALL: Mobile Assisted Language Learning
citation: Minoo Alemi, Mohammad Reza Anani Sarab & Zahra Lari. (2012). Successful Learning of Academic Word List via MALL: Mobile Assisted Language Learning. International Education Studies, 5(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n6p99
title: Mobile Assisted Language Learning (MALL) as learning that occurs any time and any place via mobile technology
description: MALL is a teaching method that uses mobile phone technology to stress learner centeredness and autonomy. The article defines mobile learning, citing O'Malley et al. (2003), as "any kind of learning that takes place when the learner is not in a fixed state" and, citing Geddes (2004), as learning "which takes place at any time and in any place," extending teaching beyond classroom walls. A key feature is that students feel responsible for their own learning. The study operationalises MALL through SMS delivery of vocabulary items.
requirements: Learners must have access to mobile phone technology capable of receiving SMS messages
constraints: The study used mobile learning in a nonreciprocal way, with materials pushed to learners rather than exchanged
target_learners: university freshmen learning English as a foreign language
target_learning_goals: academic vocabulary learning and long-term retention
examples: In the study, 320 Academic Word List headwords with Persian and English definitions and example sentences were sent to the experimental group twice a week over 16 weeks
key_sources: Minoo Alemi, Mohammad Reza Anani Sarab & Zahra Lari. (2012). Successful Learning of Academic Word List via MALL: Mobile Assisted Language Learning. International Education Studies, 5(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n6p99

article_title: Developing the Mathematics Learning Management Model for Improving Creative Thinking in Thailand
citation: Sriwongchai, A., Jantharajit, N., & Chookhampaeng, S. (2015). Developing the Mathematics Learning Management Model for Improving Creative Thinking in Thailand. International Education Studies, 8(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v8n11p77
title: Mathematics learning management model for improving creative thinking (six components grounded in five theoretical bases)
description: A learning management model for secondary mathematics designed to improve creative thinking, composed of six components: "1) principle, and concerned theoretical concepts, 2) lear ning objectives, 3) learning process, 4) social system, 5) principles of reflection, an d 6) a support system." It integrates constructivist theory, metacognitive strategy, problem solving strategy, inquiry approach, and Gestalt psychology principles, and was judged highly appropriate by expert evaluation before try-out with 9th-grade students over 30 hours of learning on Probability and Statistics content.
requirements: Expert evaluation of quality and appropriateness of the model, as done with a rating form in Phase 2
constraints: Developed and implemented with 9th-grade students in Khonsawan school, Thailand, on the Math 23102 Probability and Statistics content over thirty hours
target_learning_goals: Creative thinking (elaboration, flexibility, fluency, originality)
Mathematics learning achievement in probability and statistics
examples: The prototype was tried out with two groups of 9th-grade students in two schools for an overall 30 hours of learning, then adjusted for student abilities before implementation.

article_title: The Effects of Multimedia Learning on Thai Primary Pupils' Achievement in Size and Depth of Vocabulary Knowledge
citation: Mathukorn Jingjit. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia Learning on Thai Primary Pupils' Achievement in Size and Depth of Vocabulary Knowledge. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.32. https://www.iiste.org
title: Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning: dual channels and three cognitive processes
description: The article uses Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning as its explanatory framework. Information enters through separate audio and visual pathways, and knowledge construction involves three working-memory processes: "the selecting process", the organizing process, and the integrating process, which builds relations between verbal-based and visual-based models with prior knowledge from long-term memory. Because working memory capacity is limited, new knowledge must be transferred to long-term memory or it is lost. The author applies this framework, with cognitive load theory, to explain why integrated multimedia reduced load and improved size-of-vocabulary achievement.
requirements: Learning material must be processed by working memory and integrated with prior knowledge stored in long-term memory for learning to occur
constraints: Working memory capacity is limited, so total cognitive load cannot exceed available capacity
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary knowledge
examples: The researcher-designed multimedia program was built on four Mayer-derived factors: segmented modules, written and spoken instructions, integrated placement of pictures and texts, and attractive appearance.
key_sources: Mathukorn Jingjit. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia Learning on Thai Primary Pupils' Achievement in Size and Depth of Vocabulary Knowledge. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.32. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1083500

article_title: The Importance of Educational Marble Games in Teaching German
citation: Coşkun, H. (2013). The importance of educational marble games in teaching German. Egitim Arastirmalari – Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 53, 151-174. https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/ejer
title: Structured 120-minute game-based lesson flow with alternating group, individual, and plenary phases
description: The article presents a 16-step flow chart (Table 2) for a 120-minute socio-pedagogical activity built around the marble game, alternating game play, referee scoring, flash-card work, clothesline reading, puzzle solving, and plenary recitation. The article states that "the teaching and learning processes for the lesson in which the educational games are used should be planned in detail". The flow allocates 30 minutes to the marble game and 90 minutes to additional games and teaching materials.
requirements: A prepared table of proper names, pronouns, nouns, verbs, adjectives and expressions to facilitate communication in the lesson
constraints: The flow chart was developed for a specific socio-pedagogical activity with 16 physically handicapped students aged 11-16 in a dining hall of approximately 130 m2
target_learning_goals: foreign language vocabulary learning
participation and communication in the target languages
examples: Step 9 has referees write profession names in Turkish, English and German for won stones; step 13 has groups hang flash cards on a clothesline and explain them

article_title: Comparative Effectiveness of Contextual and Structural Method of Teaching Vocabulary
citation: Malik Behlol & Mohammad Munir Kaini. (2011). Comparative Effectiveness of Contextual and Structural Method of Teaching Vocabulary. English Language Teaching, 4(1). http://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: Match the vocabulary teaching method to achiever level: contextual method for high achievers, structural method for average and low achievers
description: The article's central design recommendation is differential assignment of vocabulary methods by learner ability. It states that "Contextual method may be applied for high achievers and structural method may be followed for teaching average and low achievers", because high achievers can exploit contextual clues while average and low achievers benefit from morphological analysis of root forms, prefixes and suffixes. The recommendation rests on the study's posttest and retention subgroup results.
requirements: Teachers trained in both methods; the article recommends workshops focusing on morphological analyses and use of words in different contexts
constraints: Based on one school, one grade (10th class), Urdu-medium public secondary students in Rawalpindi District; the article calls for further research controlling attitude, background, intelligence and gender
target_learners: secondary school English learners of varying achievement levels
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning and use in English as a second language
examples: The experiment split two matched sections into high (60+ marks), average (45-59) and low (<45) achiever categories and taught group A contextually and group B structurally
key_sources: Malik Behlol & Mohammad Munir Kaini. (2011). Comparative Effectiveness of Contextual and Structural Method of Teaching Vocabulary. English Language Teaching, 4(1). http://www.ccsenet.org/elt

article_title: Effectiveness of Demonstration and Lecture Methods in Learning Concept in Economics among Secondary School Students in Borno State, Nigeria
citation: Muhammad, A. U., Bala, D., & Ladu, K. M. (2016). Effectiveness of Demonstration and Lecture Methods in Learning Concept in Economics among Secondary School Students in Borno State, Nigeria. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(12). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1103097
title: Economics teachers should maximize use of the demonstration method when teaching selected economics concepts
description: The article recommends that "Economic teachers should maximize the use of demonstration method which learning some selected economic concepts among students, than lecture method." This follows directly from the finding that demonstration groups significantly outperformed lecture groups in both schools. The recommendation is scoped to selected concepts suitable for demonstration.
requirements: Concepts must be ones that can be demonstrated practically, as the study used topics like Theory of Demand, Theory of Supply, and the Price System
constraints: Demonstration method requires pre-preparation and may limit student participation, per the article's background section
target_learning_goals: Understanding of economics concepts such as demand, supply, and the price system
examples: Over four weeks, the demonstration group saw things practically and participated actively while the researcher and students demonstrated together
key_sources: Muhammad, A. U., Bala, D., & Ladu, K. M. (2016). Effectiveness of Demonstration and Lecture Methods in Learning Concept in Economics among Secondary School Students in Borno State, Nigeria. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(12). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1099610

article_title: Enhancing Argumentative Writing Skill through Contextual Teaching and Learning
citation: Hasani, A. (2016). Enhancing argumentative writing skill through contextual teaching and learning. Educational Research and Reviews, 11(16), 1573-1578.
title: Match writing instruction to students' critical thinking ability: contextual methods for high-ability students, explicit guidance for low-ability students
description: Based on the significant interaction between instructional model and critical thinking ability, the article recommends differentiated instruction. The authors conclude that "Students with high critical thinking ability will be better if we put into practice contextual model, as it follows students with low critical thinking ability may use non-contextual instructions." They further state that struggling students "need explicit instruction and fade it up toward contextual instruction."
requirements: Lecturers must assess or consider students' critical thinking ability when choosing writing instruction

citation: Frank DeSimone and John Buzza. (2013). Experiential Learning: Improving The Efficacy Of An Undergraduate Business Degree. American Journal Of Business Education, 6(1). http://www.cluteinstitute.com/
title: Marketing incubator experiential component

Student teams negotiate a scope of work with a client, act as a mock advertising agency with the professor as account executive, and are graded on deliverables against the agreed scope, with an informal end-of-semester presentation. It was worth 20% of the final grade, with extra credit available for exceeding scope. citation: Sonja Pečjak, Tina Pirc. (2018). Developing Summarizing Skills in 4th Grade Students: Intervention Programme Effects. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, June 2018, Volume 10, Issue 5, 571-581. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2018541306
title: Kintsch and van Dijk's macrorules framework for summarizing
description: The article frames summarizing through Kintsch and van Dijk's (1978) model, which "proposed three processes that are a part of summarizing–deletion, generalization and integration". Deletion covers excluding trivial and removing redundant information; generalization replaces individual specific terms with broader concepts (named selection and invention by Brown and Day); integration connects microstatements into a joint general statement by choosing a main-idea statement from the text or forming a keynote statement in one's own words (superordination). The intervention trained students in exactly these macrorules.
requirements: Students must monitor their comprehension of the text read and their understanding of the text structure
constraints: Younger students most commonly use a copy-delete strategy, applying one rule at a time and copying statements literally from the text
target_learning_goals: Producing summaries that reflect the macrostructure of expository texts
examples: The intervention's first part trained students in deletion of trivial and redundant information and in generalization and integration into coherent summaries

title: Design game-based interventions to match game complexity to learners' prior knowledge and cognitive load capacity
description: The article argues that game-based learning is not universally effective and that its impact depends on fit between the game and the learner. It warns that novice learners facing highly complex game scenarios may experience an "expertise reversal" effect, where the rich interactive format may hamper rather than help learning due to cognitive overload. The principle is to calibrate game difficulty, scenario complexity, and scaffolding (such as guided hints) to students' prior knowledge and cognitive load capacity, especially in specialised domains.

Scaffolding mechanisms such as the guided hints used in this study
constraints: The article states this concern arises from heterogeneous prior literature, including a meta-analysis reporting high heterogeneity (I² values up to 90%), not from a manipulation tested in this study

Knowledge retention
Self-regulated engagement
examples: The study's game offered three difficulty levels of multiple-choice questions selected by a labeled die and permitted up to three guided hints per session to support problem-solving without compromising autonomy

citation: Zhao Zhengqi, Wu Baijing, Tian Shuyuan, Hu Haigen, Hao Pengyi. (2026). Scaffolded AI-Supported Problem-Based Learning for Medical Interns: Exploratory Retrospectively Registered Randomized Controlled Evaluation With a Voluntary Feasibility Follow-Up. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/95039
title: MAPLE-CR process-oriented scaffolding framework: cognitive, social-interactional, and regulatory scaffolding for AI-supported PBL
description: The article proposes a process-oriented view of scaffolding for AI-supported PBL, defining scaffolding as "structured support embedded in the learning workflow to help learners perform reasoning, interaction, and reflection activities that would otherwise require sustained tutor facilitation." MAPLE-CR instantiates three complementary scaffolding forms: cognitive scaffolding (prompts for hypothesis generation, evidence justification, revision, and synthesis), social-interactional scaffolding (simulated tutor and peer roles sustaining dialogue and externalization), and regulatory scaffolding (workflow structuring, objective-coverage monitoring, phase transitions, and feedback loops). The framework treats scalability as preserving the cognitive, dialogic, and feedback-regulatory functions that make PBL educationally meaningful rather than merely automating human labor.
requirements: Requires an LLM-supported multiagent environment with tutor, peer, evaluator, and advisor roles, a shared data and knowledge layer, and case-linked pretests and posttests aligned with learning objectives.
constraints: The article notes the study did not isolate specific scaffolding effects, and simulated group-process behaviors varied across sessions, so AI is unlikely to fully reproduce the nuance of human facilitation.
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning
Diagnostic hypothesis generation and justification
Collaborative discussion and reflection skills
examples: MAPLE-CR implements the framework through 4 connected modules (recommendation, testing, PBL training, assessment with feedback) and transcript-based formative feedback across 5 dimensions (AP, CR, KA, CC, SR).

citation: Zhao Zhengqi, Wu Baijing, Tian Shuyuan, Hu Haigen, Hao Pengyi. (2026). JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/95039
title: MAPLE-CR: Multiagent PBL Environment for Clinical Reasoning
description: MAPLE-CR is a web-based, LLM-supported PBL environment for medical interns that "instantiates tutor, peer, evaluator, and advisor functions as distinct agents and uses multiagent orchestration to coordinate role interactions and workflow sequencing." Learners interact through 4 connected modules — recommendation, testing, PBL training, and assessment with feedback — supported by a shared data and knowledge layer. The PBL training module presents sequential case scenarios with a tutor agent and calibrated peer-agent personas; the assessment module generates transcript-based formative feedback across 5 dimensions (AP, CR, KA, CC, SR) on a 0-5 scale with dimension-specific justifications. Model inference used the Qwen-flash API with temperature 0.7.
requirements: A remotely accessed web platform (Streamlit interface on a cloud server) with LLM API access, a structured medical knowledge graph for CR and KA scoring, and case-linked assessment items reviewed by domain experts.
constraints: The article states MAPLE-CR is an educational tool rather than a clinical decision support system, intended for formative, low-stakes learning rather than summative decision-making, and is best positioned as a supplement rather than a replacement for faculty-facilitated PBL.
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning practice
Case-based knowledge application
Formative self-assessment
examples: In the randomized evaluation, interns completed up to 2 hours of scaffolded PBL on a standardized lung-mass case after a 40-minute orientation.

description: A computer vision-deep learning pipeline built on Mask R-CNN automatically detects areas of interest (objects and graspers) in eye-tracking recordings of the peg transfer task, then matches fixation points to AOI masks to compute fixation rates and tool speed. Visual attention allocation during surgical training
examples: Used to extract fixation rates on objects, object-tool interactions, not-moving objects, tools, and tool speed for 18 novices on adult and pediatric box trainers.

requirements: Learning objectives must be defined first so an appropriately matched (possibly low-fidelity) simulator can be chosen
Simulation contexts with decision-making demands to capture the fuller benefits of scenario-based practice
constraints: The authors note cost thresholds are relative: a low cost in developed countries can be a high cost in developing ones, and perishable biological materials can raise maintenance costs
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students learning basic procedural techniques
Health professionals in resource-limited training settings
target_learning_goals: Procedural skills such as thoracentesis and pleural drainage
examples: The team reserved high-fidelity reasoning for more advanced learners in the background literature while building and validating a US$18 simulator for basic undergraduate thoracentesis training

article_title: Evaluation of glasses-free 3D anatomy learning materials through a randomized control study with a puzzle-like method.

title: When evaluating 3D learning materials, match the evaluation method to the spatial nature of the material rather than relying solely on paper tests
description: This principle holds that assessment of 3D learning materials should directly measure the competency the materials target — spatial arrangement understanding — instead of relying only on multiple-choice and word-answer paper tests. The article argues that "the inconsistency in the outcomes of the effectiveness of 3D learning materials in previous RCTs might partly be due to the limitations of these traditional assessment methods", since paper tests can be passed by memorization or guessing without genuine spatial understanding. The study operationalized this with its 3D puzzle-like placement task.
requirements: Digital 3D content that permits recording of learner placements and computation of placement accuracy against correct positions.
constraints: Paper tests remain standard for most universities and suit terminology and verbalized-description outcomes; the puzzle method targets spatial arrangement specifically.
target_learning_goals: Accurate assessment of spatial anatomical understanding
examples: The study designed its RCT outcome measure as direct 3D organ placement rather than a multiple-choice or word-answer test.

psychological safety in team-based acute-care management

title: MAES: Self-Learning Methodology in Simulated Environments
description: MAES is a self-learning methodology for simulated clinical environments developed in 2013, built on problem-based learning, peer education, and clinical simulation in highly realistic environments. Its "structure of MAES is developed with 6 phases in a minimum of 2 sessions and the completion of homework by the student between sessions 1 and 2": establishing group identity, choosing a scenario, setting baseline learning objectives, designing the scenario at home, running the simulation, and a structured GAS debriefing. Students take an active role, reflecting in small working groups on their learning needs and seeking supporting evidence, guided by an expert facilitator. In this study MAES was applied for the first time to interprofessional CPR training with nursing and medical students.

Students complete homework between the two sessions, designing the scenario and searching scientific evidence
Participants need prior simulation experience and prior basic life support training
constraints: Students reported the short time for scenario design between sessions, especially in busy periods, as a limit
Some students feared the responsibility of leaving knowledge to their peers
target_learning_goals: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation technical skills
Nontechnical skills: teamwork, communication, role assignment, leadership
Interprofessional collaboration
examples: Two interprofessional CPR scenarios were designed by students: cardiac arrest secondary to myocardial infarct (CUV) and cardiac arrest secondary to drowning (UCAM)

citation: Karniej Piotr, Dissen Anthony, Pietrzykowski Łukasz, Juárez-Vela Raúl, Sabater Antonio Martinez, Kulińska Janina, Zieliński Jakub, Czapla Michał. (2025). title: Make LGBT-related content a mandatory, recurring component of medical curricula rather than relying on optional continuing education
description: The article recommends mandatory inclusion of LGBT-related content in broader medical curricula so that training reaches professionals who would not opt into it voluntarily. This rests on the observed association between training frequency and competency, with the authors citing a "positive dose-effect relationship between the number of trainings received and total LGBT-DOCSS scores" and concluding that ongoing, higher-frequency training is key. Training is framed as one component of a broader, multifaceted strategy rather than a standalone solution.
requirements: Ongoing and higher-frequency trainings pertaining to LGBT health and competence, embedded within a multifaceted approach that also includes systemic interventions, legislative measures, and institutional policies.
constraints: The article states the training-competency association does not imply causation, since professionals with pre-existing positive attitudes may be more inclined to attend training.
target_learners: health professionals and medical students in countries where LGBT topics are less integrated into medical education
target_learning_goals: clinical preparedness, attitudes, and knowledge for LGBT patient care
examples: The study found attendance at LGBT-related training 3 or more times associated with the largest preparedness gains in Spain and attendance 1–3 times with a total-score gain in Poland, supporting recurring rather than one-off training.

citation: Okuyama K, Lönn SL, Khoshnood AM, Assari S, Sundquist J, Sundquist K. (2025). School performance gap between non-immigrant and second-generation immigrant children in Sweden—time trends and contributing factors. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1521387
title: Marginalization-related diminished returns (MDRs): smaller beneficial effects of socioeconomic resources among minority and immigrant children
description: Marginalization-related diminished returns is the account that the protective effects of socioeconomic resources on children's outcomes are smaller for minority and immigrant groups than for majority groups. In this study it appears as the finding that "the potential effects of these factors on school performance were smaller among second-generation immigrant children", and the authors connect it to prior US research on parental education. They suggest that residential and school segregation as well as discrimination at educational settings may hinder second-generation immigrant children from performing well at school.
requirements: comparison of factor-by-immigration-status interaction effects between groups
constraints: the article states it is difficult to conclude whether the observed MDRs are caused by structural inequalities
target_learners: second-generation immigrant children in compulsory school
target_learning_goals: school performance in ninth grade
examples: The study's interaction terms (e.g., low parental education * second-generation immigrant = 32.79 for females) offset the main negative parental-education coefficients, implying weaker factor effects among second-generation children.

title: Management scripts: mental schemas that organize intervention options and decisions

constraints: Due to the complex nature of intervention in practice, clinicians must constantly adapt their management scripts to individual and contextual factors

intervention decision making

citation: Jantausch Barbara A., Bost James E., Bhansali Priti, Hefter Yosefa, Greenberg Isabella, Goldman Ellen. (2023). Assessing trainee critical thinking skills using a novel interactive online learning tool. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2023.2178871
title: Malaria Vignette Player (MVP): a case-based branching online simulation with avatars and immediate tailored feedback
description: The MVP is an online individualized learning tool built as a "case-based branching scenario for teaching malaria recognition, evaluation, and management". Trainees 'choose their own adventure' by selecting a world region and receive "immediate online feedback" on diagnostic, therapeutic and disposition choices, customized for animated virtual patients. Two custom animated avatars keep trainees engaged during the virtual simulation. It is delivered asynchronously through the hospital's online learning platform and was used with medical students, residents and fellows in global health education.
requirements: Trainees access the module via an online learning platform and complete a demographic questionnaire and pre-test before use
constraints: Applied specifically in global health education, specifically malaria diagnosis and management
target_learning_goals: malaria recognition, evaluation and management
critical thinking skills of interpretation, analysis and explanation
examples: Trainees commented that they liked the interactive nature of the vignettes, the immediate feedback on answer choices, the autonomy of the choose-your-adventure aspect, and the avatars
key_sources: Jantausch Barbara A., Bost James E., Bhansali Priti, Hefter Yosefa, Greenberg Isabella, Goldman Ellen. (2023). Assessing trainee critical thinking skills using a novel interactive online learning tool. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2023.2178871

article_title: A novel retraining strategy of chest compression skills for infant CPR results in high skill retention for longer.
citation: Gugelmin-Almeida Debora, Jones Michael, Clark Carol, Rolfe Ursula, Williams Jonathan. (2022). A novel retraining strategy of chest compression skills for infant CPR results in high skill retention for longer. European Journal of Pediatrics 181(12):4101-4109. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-022-04625-2
title: Mastery learning strategy applied to CPR skill retraining
description: The article grounds its competence-based retraining design in the 'mastery learning strategy,' in which learners 'have the opportunity to practice key skills, receive feedback and improve performance until mastery is achieved.' Retraining is individualized and based on the quality of performance against a predefined level of competence. The article cites evidence that 'repetition paired with feedback enables learners to consistently demonstrate a predefined level of competence for a specific skill' and operationalizes this with monthly assessments plus brief feedback-based practice until two consecutive passes.
requirements: Opportunity to practice key skills, receive directed feedback, and repeat performance until a predefined competence criterion is attained
constraints: The study applied it only to chest compression skills, not ventilation or the full iCPR cycle, and the authors note this may not reflect training times for the full cycle
target_learners: healthcare students and providers learning resuscitation skills
target_learning_goals: achieving and retaining a predefined standard of psychomotor skill competence
examples: Monthly iCC assessments on an instrumented mannequin with 1-minute real-time-feedback practice blocks after each failure, until two consecutive monthly passes
key_sources: Gugelmin-Almeida Debora, Jones Michael, Clark Carol, Rolfe Ursula, Williams Jonathan. (2022). A novel retraining strategy of chest compression skills for infant CPR results in high skill retention for longer. European Journal of Pediatrics 181(12):4101-4109. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-022-04625-2

article_title: A novel algorithm-driven hybrid simulation learning method to improve acquisition of endotracheal intubation skills: a randomized controlled study.
citation: Mankute A, Juozapaviciene L, Stucinskas J, Dambrauskas Z, Dobozinskas P, Sinz E, Rodgers DL, Giedraitis M, Vaitkaitis D. (2022). A novel algorithm-driven hybrid simulation learning method to improve acquisition of endotracheal intubation skills: a randomized controlled study. BMC Anesthesiology 22:42. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12871-021-01557-6
title: Mastery learning integrated with deliberate practice as the theoretical basis of hybrid simulation training
description: The article grounds its hybrid learning system in two frameworks: Ericsson's Deliberate Practice model, under which "practice with feedback is essential to improvement", including self-reflective feedback and feedback from others compared to a standard of performance; and Bloom's Mastery Learning model, which "includes breaking larger tasks into smaller elements and perfecting the performance of each element before moving on to the next element". The conclusions state the findings support the theoretical model of mastery learning integrated with deliberate practice, with the hybrid method breaking the complex intubation task into steps progressed one at a time, supported by peer-to-peer feedback.
requirements: Adequate time must be provided to achieve mastery at each step before moving on to the next step
target_learning_goals: acquisition of complex clinical procedural skills
correct sequencing of procedure steps
examples: The hybrid model broke endotracheal intubation into smaller steps that learners progressed through one at a time, with peer-to-peer feedback improving performance.
key_sources: Mankute A, Juozapaviciene L, Stucinskas J, Dambrauskas Z, Dobozinskas P, Sinz E, Rodgers DL, Giedraitis M, Vaitkaitis D. (2022). A novel algorithm-driven hybrid simulation learning method to improve acquisition of endotracheal intubation skills: a randomized controlled study. BMC Anesthesiology 22:42. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12871-021-01557-6

article_title: Feasibility, effectiveness and transferability of a novel mastery-based virtual reality robotic training platform for general surgery residents.
citation: Radi Imad, Tellez Juan C., Alterio Rodrigo E., Scott Daniel J., Sankaranarayanan Ganesh, Nagaraj Madhuri B., Hogg Melissa E., Zeh Herbert J., Polanco Patricio M. (2022). Feasibility, effectiveness and transferability of a novel mastery-based virtual reality robotic training platform for general surgery residents. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-022-09106-z
title: Mastery-based VR simulation curriculum with protected time and dedicated equipment
description: A reusable training design in which learners practice simulator tasks to a proficiency benchmark rather than a fixed number of repetitions, embedded in a rotation month with protected time. The article states that "Having dedicated training equipment that was accessible 24/7 in the simulation center made access readily available" and that "Having protected training time as well as a structured curriculum with clear expectations seemed pivotal." The design supports a high completion rate and lets trainees progress at their own pace.
requirements: Proficiency benchmarks defined for each task with automated performance metrics
Dedicated training equipment accessible without competing clinical use
Protected training time scheduled within a rotation with relatively light clinical duties
constraints: Some residents required more than 4 months when training was interrupted (e.g., a pandemic shutdown) or begun before the designated rotation
target_learners: Surgical residents learning basic robotic skills
target_learning_goals: Technical skill acquisition to a defined mastery standard
examples: UTSW scheduled training during a month-long rotation with light clinical duties, staggering trainees to maximize simulator access; most residents completed the curriculum in about one month
key_sources: Radi Imad, Tellez Juan C., Alterio Rodrigo E., Scott Daniel J., Sankaranarayanan Ganesh, Nagaraj Madhuri B., Hogg Melissa E., Zeh Herbert J., Polanco Patricio M. (2022). Feasibility, effectiveness and transferability of a novel mastery-based virtual reality robotic training platform for general surgery residents. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-022-09106-z

article_title: Distance and force visualisations for improved simulation of intracranial aneurysm clipping.
citation: Allgaier M, Neyazi B, Preim B, Saalfeld S. (2021). Distance and force visualisations for improved simulation of intracranial aneurysm clipping. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-021-02413-1
title: Mass–spring vessel deformation model with Verlet integration for clipping simulation
description: The simulation computes vessel deformation from clip-applied force using a mass–spring model with Verlet integration, chosen because it "is not that computationally expensive and still provides a plausible deformation". Mass points are vertices of the vessel triangle mesh; spring forces follow Hooke's law, positions are solved numerically with damping, collisions move points to 0.9 times the collision distance, and a stretching compensation limits errors from large time steps. Force visualisations derive from the vector between each vertex's initial and displaced position.
requirements: Parameters such as the spring constant must be set so deformation is plausible and calculation error minimised, as they are not obvious in a mass–spring model
constraints: Neurosurgeons do not require perfectly realistic deformation; a plausible deformation is sufficient, and plausibility was confirmed by one expert
target_learning_goals: understanding forces on vessels during clip application
examples: The expert confirmed the deformation was plausible and appropriate enough for such a clipping simulation
key_sources: Allgaier M, Neyazi B, Preim B, Saalfeld S. (2021). Distance and force visualisations for improved simulation of intracranial aneurysm clipping. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-021-02413-1

article_title: Nursing Students' Satisfaction: A Comparison between Medium- and High-Fidelity Simulation Training.
citation: Alconero-Camarero, A.R., Sarabia-Cobo, C.M., Catalán-Piris, M.J., González-Gómez, S., & González-López, J.R. (2021). Nursing Students’ Satisfaction: A Comparison between Medium- and High-Fidelity Simulation Training. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18020804
title: Match simulation fidelity to students' level of knowledge and clinical experience rather than defaulting to high fidelity
description: The article concludes that "high-fidelity is not always better than medium-fidelity as this depends on the student’s level of knowledge and clinical experience". For beginners with little clinical experience, medium-fidelity simulation produced higher satisfaction at lower cost, and the literature it cites suggests simple scenarios adapted to the student's level favour achievement. The principle recommends selecting the fidelity level appropriate to the learner's stage, using HFS especially for advanced or postgraduate training.
requirements: Educators must know students' current knowledge and clinical experience level to select appropriate scenario complexity.
constraints: The supporting evidence covers beginner students with little previous clinical experience; the authors state results cannot be extrapolated to students with more clinical experience.
target_learners: beginner undergraduate nursing students with little clinical experience
target_learning_goals: acquisition of basic clinical skills and competencies such as CPR and critical-patient assessment
examples: Second-year students at Seville practised CPR on medium-fidelity mannequins in 30-minute group sessions and reported higher satisfaction than the Cantabria HFS group.
key_sources: Alconero-Camarero, A.R., Sarabia-Cobo, C.M., Catalán-Piris, M.J., González-Gómez, S., & González-López, J.R. (2021). Nursing Students’ Satisfaction: A Comparison between Medium- and High-Fidelity Simulation Training. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18020804

article_title: TEACHING MUST GO ON: flexibility and advantages of peer assisted learning during the COVID-19 pandemic for undergraduate medical ultrasound education - perspective from the "sonoBYstudents" ultrasound group.
citation: Nourkami-Tutdibi N., Hofer M., Zemlin M., Abdul-Khaliq H., Tutdibi E. (2021). TEACHING MUST GO ON: flexibility and advantages of peer assisted learning during the COVID-19 pandemic for undergraduate medical ultrasound education – perspective from the “sonoBYstudents” ultrasound group. GMS Journal for Medical Education 38(1). https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2021-38/zma001401.shtml
title: Maintain established PAL programs rather than suspending them, because suspension interrupts tutor-generation continuity and restarting is time- and cost-intensive
description: The article argues that PAL depends on sustained educational strategies: practical and didactical trainings and ongoing recruitment of new student tutors. "PAL courses rely on a continuity from one generation of student tutors to the other", and suspending them would interrupt this tradition, "requiring a start from the beginning, which is a time and cost intensive procedure". The authors therefore recommend prioritizing continuation of PAL skill teaching, adjusting formats as needed rather than pausing.
requirements: Ongoing recruitment and training of new student tutors each semester
Regular real-life teaching performance by tutors, since simulations and didactical training cannot replace the real life setting
constraints: The argument is the authors' perspective from one ultrasound PAL program; no comparative data on suspension versus continuation are presented
target_learning_goals: advanced practical skills such as ultrasound and echocardiography
teaching skills of student tutors
examples: The sonoBYstudents group continued teaching during the pandemic with an adjusted format instead of suspending the program
key_sources: Nourkami-Tutdibi N., Hofer M., Zemlin M., Abdul-Khaliq H., Tutdibi E. (2021). TEACHING MUST GO ON: flexibility and advantages of peer assisted learning during the COVID-19 pandemic for undergraduate medical ultrasound education – perspective from the “sonoBYstudents” ultrasound group. GMS Journal for Medical Education 38(1). https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2021-38/zma001401.shtml

article_title: The acceptance and impact of Google Classroom integrating into a clinical pathology course for nursing students: A technology acceptance model approach.
citation: Huang Tzu-Hao, Liu Fen, Chen Li-Chen, Tsai Ching-Ching. (2021). The acceptance and impact of Google Classroom integrating into a clinical pathology course for nursing students: A technology acceptance model approach. PLoS ONE 16(3): e0247819. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0247819
title: Design blended e-learning environments to maximize the playfulness and usefulness of the platform
description: The article's discussion states that "The key to the successful application of GC lies in teachers' ability to design and construct a teaching environment which maximizes the playfulness and usefulness of the platform to fully leverage their role as teacher and guide." This follows from the regression finding that playfulness and usefulness predicted intention to use. The principle directs educators building blended courses to include playful, gamified activities and clearly useful, practice-oriented content, and to give students additional time to explore and learn to operate the new platform.
requirements: Teachers must be able to design and construct the environment; students need sufficient time to learn how to operate the software and become familiar with it
constraints: Attention should be paid to concerns surrounding privacy, data protection, and users' intellectual rights, especially on free platforms; barriers such as poor motivation and inability to operate the platform remain
target_learners: nursing and higher-education students using blended e-learning platforms
target_learning_goals: sustained intention to use the platform and improved learning satisfaction and achievement
examples: The GC course integrated gamified software (Quizlet, Quizizz, Quizalize) with competitive, time-limited games and linked news and exam-paper resources to make knowledge feel useful
key_sources: Huang Tzu-Hao, Liu Fen, Chen Li-Chen, Tsai Ching-Ching. (2021). The acceptance and impact of Google Classroom integrating into a clinical pathology course for nursing students: A technology acceptance model approach. PLoS ONE 16(3): e0247819. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0247819

article_title: Assessment of the knowledge level and experience of healthcare personnel concerning CPR and early defibrillation: an internal survey.
citation: Spinelli G., Brogi E., Sidoti A., Pagnucci N., Forfori F. (2021). Assessment of the knowledge level and experience of healthcare personnel concerning CPR and early defibrillation: an internal survey. BMC Cardiovascular Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12872-021-02009-2
title: A certified BLS-D course should be mandatory for every healthcare personnel working in every hospital, with periodic refreshing and testing
description: Because the survey evidenced inadequate baseline knowledge and significant training needs among medical and nursing staff, the authors argue that "BLS-D course should be mandatory for all the hospital personnel, not only for healthcare professionals involved in critical area". They add that skills and knowledge regarding lifesaving techniques should be refreshed and tested periodically, since skills tend to decline over time.
requirements: Certified courses organized by instructors dedicated to CPR training
Periodic review and updates to reduce skill decay
constraints: Skills tend to decline over time (i.e., 3–12 months after training), per the 2020 International Consensus cited by the article
target_learners: all hospital personnel, including staff in non-critical areas
target_learning_goals: correct performance of the BLS-D sequence, CPR maneuvers and defibrillator use
examples: The study's 2-hour informative meeting with manikin practice in groups of 5, each group spending more than 1 hour of training, significantly raised knowledge and self-assessed adequacy
key_sources: Spinelli G., Brogi E., Sidoti A., Pagnucci N., Forfori F. (2021). Assessment of the knowledge level and experience of healthcare personnel concerning CPR and early defibrillation: an internal survey. BMC Cardiovascular Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12872-021-02009-2

article_title: How Can We Make Active Learning Work in K-12 Education? Considering Prerequisites for a Successful Construction of Understanding.
citation: Garvin Brod. (2021). How Can We Make Active Learning Work in K–12 Education? Considering Prerequisites for a Successful Construction of Understanding. Psychological Science in the Public Interest. https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100621997376
title: Choose active-learning practices by matching them to students' developmental prerequisites and provide guidance at an appropriate level
description: The article's central pledge is to "consider prerequisites in order to choose those active-learning practices that are likely to work best for a particular group of students." Because prerequisites differ between practices and a lack of them "can often be counteracted with additional guidance," instructors should select practices whose cognitive and metacognitive demands fit the group and calibrate guidance level, since active learning "can prove effective throughout K–12" when guidance is at an appropriate level.
requirements: Knowledge of the developmental trajectories of the relevant prerequisites and of their developmental status in the target students.
constraints: Age is only a crude proxy for a student's cognitive and metacognitive capacities, with substantial differences among children of the same age; typical trajectories are "only a rough heuristic."
target_learning_goals: improved learning outcomes from active-learning practices
tailoring instruction to learner characteristics
examples: The commentary recommends prediction-observation cycles, which are part of successful STEM curricula for elementary- and secondary-school students, and advises against practices requiring advanced analogical reasoning (generating examples, constructing drawings) until late secondary school unless guidance is high.
key_sources: Garvin Brod. (2021). How Can We Make Active Learning Work in K–12 Education? Considering Prerequisites for a Successful Construction of Understanding. Psychological Science in the Public Interest. https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100621997376

article_title: Intelligent Tutoring Systems: Re-Envisioning Surgical Education in Response to COVID-19.
citation: Mirchi N, Ledwos N, Del Maestro RF. (2020). Intelligent Tutoring Systems: Re-Envisioning Surgical Education in Response to COVID-19. Can J Neurol Sci. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7642506/
title: Let trainees practice to mastery with continuous iterative feedback and decreasing reliance on educator supervision
description: The article recommends that "Trainees could practice technical skills on the simulator to the level of mastery and obtain continuous feedback on performance in an iterative manner, with decreasing reliance on educator supervision." This learning-focused environment offers immersive, engaging practice while permitting social distancing. It extends educators' capacity by providing almost unlimited repetitive practice unconstrained by supervisor availability.
requirements: Intelligent tutoring systems integrated with simulation platforms providing continuous automated feedback
constraints: The authors state human interaction is vital to learning and that automated systems should complement, not replace, present educational paradigms
target_learning_goals: mastery of surgical technical skills
examples: The article describes trainees practicing on simulators in an iterative feedback loop within the proposed learning centers
