article_title: The association between early career informal mentorship in academic collaborations and junior author performance.
citation: AlShebli Bedoor, Makovi Kinga, Rahwan Talal. (2020). The association between early career informal mentorship in academic collaborations and junior author performance. Nature Communications. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-19723-8
title: Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG) dataset used to identify mentor–protégé pairs
description: The study draws on the Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG) dataset, which the article describes as containing "detailed records of scientific publications and their citation network". From it the authors analyzed 215 million scientists and 222 million papers, deriving discipline, impact, gender (via Genderize.io) and affiliation rank, and identified 3 million mentor–protégé pairs across ten disciplines. Data generated for the study were made available by the authors.
requirements: Name disambiguation and external sources for gender and affiliation rank, as described in the Methods and supplementary notes
constraints: Analysis restricted to US-based affiliations, same-discipline pairs, and papers with 20 or fewer co-authors
target_learning_goals: studying informal mentorship relationships in academic collaborations
examples: The use sample spans Biology, Chemistry, Computer Science, Economics, Engineering, Geology, Materials Science, Medicine, Physics, and Psychology, containing over 97% of identified pairs
key_sources: AlShebli Bedoor, Makovi Kinga, Rahwan Talal. (2020). The association between early career informal mentorship in academic collaborations and junior author performance. Nature Communications. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-19723-8

article_title: Are we training psychiatrists to develop skills in intellectual disability psychiatry? Current European context and future directions.
citation: Casanova Dias M., Perera B., Riese F., De Picker L., Pinto da Costa M., Petricean A., Kanellopoulos A., Krysta K., Baessler F. (2020). Are we training psychiatrists to develop skills in intellectual disability psychiatry? Current European context and future directions. European Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1192/j.eurpsy.2020.102
title: Make intellectual disability psychiatry a mandatory part of training curricula and exams in all European countries
description: The authors recommend that ID psychiatry be compulsory in postgraduate psychiatric curricula, explicitly invoking the assessment principle that "assessment drives learning". They argue that without improvements in postgraduate ID training, psychiatric care for people with ID will not fundamentally improve, and call for an active push for curriculum reform across Europe based on their survey findings.
requirements: National training bodies would need to incorporate ID content into curricula and examinations
constraints: The authors acknowledge different challenges faced by different countries related to economic power, organization of services and training, provision of social care, and societal expectations
target_learning_goals: psychiatric assessment and care of people with intellectual disabilities
examples: The survey found only 56% of 41 responding countries provided postgraduate ID training, motivating the recommendation for mandatory curricula
key_sources: Casanova Dias M., Perera B., Riese F., De Picker L., Pinto da Costa M., Petricean A., Kanellopoulos A., Krysta K., Baessler F. (2020). Are we training psychiatrists to develop skills in intellectual disability psychiatry? Current European context and future directions. European Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1192/j.eurpsy.2020.102

article_title: Developing an Evidence-Based Technical Assistance Model: a Process Evaluation of the National Training and Technical Assistance Center for Child, Youth, and Family Mental Health.
citation: Olson Jonathan R., Coldiron Jennifer Schurer, Parigoris Ryan M., Zabel Michelle D., Matarese Marlene, Bruns Eric J. (2020). Developing an Evidence-Based Technical Assistance Model: a Process Evaluation of the National Training and Technical Assistance Center for Child, Youth, and Family Mental Health. The Journal of Behavioral Health Services & Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11414-020-09686-5
title: Match TA content and dosage to the individual needs of TA recipients when supporting implementation
description: The article's discussion recommends that TA provision match what recipients need: "factors such as matching TA content and dosage to the individual needs of TA recipients may contribute to successful TA provision that ultimately promotes improved behavioral health systems, services, and treatments." This follows from findings that high-level users were those struggling to meet goals, implying need-level rather than uniform dosing. It also stresses attending to outer setting factors such as the political environment, funding resources, and cross-agency connections when tailoring TA.
requirements: TA providers must assess grantees' current implementation processes and adjust support to unique needs
constraints: high levels of TA provision were not consistently associated with better outcomes; the relation is complex and likely mediated by recipient need
target_learners: technical assistance providers supporting behavioral health systems implementation
target_learning_goals: effective, need-aligned TA provision that promotes improved systems and services
examples: NTTAC consultants assess grantees' current implementation processes and adjust support; data-driven approaches deliver TA to those who need it, not only to those who formally request support
key_sources: Olson Jonathan R., Coldiron Jennifer Schurer, Parigoris Ryan M., Zabel Michelle D., Matarese Marlene, Bruns Eric J. (2020). Developing an Evidence-Based Technical Assistance Model: a Process Evaluation of the National Training and Technical Assistance Center for Child, Youth, and Family Mental Health. The Journal of Behavioral Health Services & Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11414-020-09686-5

article_title: Conference Didactic Planning and Structure: An Evidence-based Guide to Best Practices from the Council of Emergency Medicine Residency Directors.
citation: Wood D. Brian, Jordan Jaime, Cooney Rob, Goldflam Katja, Bright Leah, Gottlieb Michael. (2020). Conference Didactic Planning and Structure: An Evidence-based Guide to Best Practices from the Council of Emergency Medicine Residency Directors. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2020.5.46762
title: Mayer's 12 principles of multimedia learning for slide design
description: The article tabulates Mayer's 12 principles of multimedia learning (Table 3) as design guidance for conference slides, stating that "Multimedia learning theory informs principles of slide design and is one effective method that can be used to increase the long-term retention of taught material." The enumerated principles include coherence (avoid extraneous words, pictures, and sounds), signaling, redundancy, spatial and temporal contiguity, segmenting, pre-training, modality, multimedia, personalization, voice, and image principles. Each is stated as a design rule, e.g., learning is more effective when words are presented as narration rather than on-screen text.
requirements: Slide and multimedia design must follow the principles, e.g., corresponding words and pictures presented near each other and simultaneously
constraints: The image principle states learning is not necessarily more effective when the speaker's image is added to the screen
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of lecture material
effective slide design by presenters
examples: The review's best-practice recommendation ties lecture effectiveness to compliance with multimedia learning theory (Level 1a; Grade B)
key_sources: Wood D. Brian, Jordan Jaime, Cooney Rob, Goldflam Katja, Bright Leah, Gottlieb Michael. (2020). Conference Didactic Planning and Structure: An Evidence-based Guide to Best Practices from the Council of Emergency Medicine Residency Directors. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2020.5.46762

article_title: Improved care and survival in severe malnutrition through eLearning.
citation: Choi Sunhea, Yuen Ho Ming, Annan Reginald, Monroy-Valle Michele, Pickup Trevor, Aduku Nana Esi Linda, Pulman Andy, Portillo Sermeño Carmen Elisa, Jackson Alan A, Ashworth Ann. (2020). Improved care and survival in severe malnutrition through eLearning. Archives of Disease in Childhood. https://doi.org/10.1136/archdischild-2018-316539
title: eLearning course 'Caring for infants and young children with severe malnutrition'
description: A free, interactive, scenario-based eLearning course developed by the University of Southampton and the International Malnutrition Task Force, "designed around a hypothetical nutrition community in which children and their care are the focus for learning". It "has three modules, each taking about 2–3 hours to complete, and is based on WHO guidelines for the management of severe acute malnutrition". Since being made freely available in 2010 it has been taken by over 16 000 health professionals, trainees and educators in over 120 countries, and in 2018 it was re-implemented for access on mobile devices.
requirements: An introduction of approximately 1 hour covering how to access the course and its navigation structure
Internet access for online use, or a CD version installed on laptops where internet access is limited
constraints: Participation in Latin America was constrained by proficiency in the course language (English); the main challenge in delivering the course in Latin America is its unavailability in the local language
target_learners: In-service doctors, medical officers, nurses and nutritionists
target_learning_goals: Assessing children for chronic and acute malnutrition
Managing malnourished children using the WHO Ten Steps
Inpatient and community-based management of severe acute malnutrition
Supporting mothers and carers to prevent recurrence of malnutrition
examples: In Ghana, few participants had internet access, so a CD version was installed on laptops and the course was taken over 2 days; in Latin America participants completed it online within 3 weeks
key_sources: Choi Sunhea, Yuen Ho Ming, Annan Reginald, Monroy-Valle Michele, Pickup Trevor, Aduku Nana Esi Linda, Pulman Andy, Portillo Sermeño Carmen Elisa, Jackson Alan A, Ashworth Ann. (2020). Improved care and survival in severe malnutrition through eLearning. Archives of Disease in Childhood. https://doi.org/10.1136/archdischild-2018-316539

article_title: A non-randomised trial of video and written educational adjuncts in undergraduate ophthalmology.
citation: Hogg H. D. Jeffry, Pereira Michael, Purdy Julian, Frearson Richard J. R., Lau Gordon B. (2020). A non-randomised trial of video and written educational adjuncts in undergraduate ophthalmology. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1923-1
title: Select the pre-learning material format to match the target learning outcome: written for knowledge, video for skills
description: The article concludes that judicious format selection optimises educational efficiency: "Written materials better facilitate knowledge acquisition while video materials preferentially promote skill acquisition." Teachers distributing pre-placement or pre-learning resources should therefore assign written materials when the outcome is knowledge-test performance and video materials when the outcome is clinical skill development. The recommendation rests on the trial's direct comparisons between formats.
requirements: Learners must be willing to complete the assigned pre-learning work; materials were sent one week in advance with a request for 90 minutes of preparation
constraints: The video advantage for skills appeared only in as-treated analysis, not intention-to-treat
Some reported significance did not survive Bonferroni correction
Findings are from a single-centre ophthalmology placement with limited exposure time
target_learners: final-year undergraduate medical students on short clinical placements
target_learning_goals: ophthalmology knowledge acquisition
clinical skill development such as visual acuity assessment
examples: Consecutive cohorts were sent welcome packs with either links to specified written materials or links to educational videos covering the same core ophthalmology content, alongside a no-materials cohort
key_sources: Hogg H. D. Jeffry, Pereira Michael, Purdy Julian, Frearson Richard J. R., Lau Gordon B. (2020). A non-randomised trial of video and written educational adjuncts in undergraduate ophthalmology. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1923-1

article_title: A Gamification-Based Intervention Program that Encourages Physical Activity Improves Cardiorespiratory Fitness of College Students: 'The Matrix rEFvolution Program'.
citation: Mora-Gonzalez Jose, Pérez-López Isaac J., Esteban-Cornejo Irene, Delgado-Fernández Manuel. (2020). A Gamification-Based Intervention Program that Encourages Physical Activity Improves Cardiorespiratory Fitness of College Students: 'The Matrix rEFvolution Program'. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17030877
title: The Matrix rEFvolution gamification-based physical activity program
description: A 15-week, 42-lecture gamified university course set in the film 'The Matrix Revolutions', in which students act as 'rebels' of 'The Resistance' against Matrix and must become 'The Chosen Ones'. It consisted of "5 different phases taken from the original film: 1. Recruitment; 2. Rehabilitation; 3. Training; 4. Incursion in Matrix; 5. Final Mission", each with learning missions, plus a PA component of running or cycling 3–5 days per week to escape 'The Sentinels'. Scoring via a classification awarded points for meeting weekly PA recommendations (registered by mobile phone applications) and for overcoming learning missions.
requirements: Students register weekly PA via mobile applications (Runtastic or Endomondo) to verify meeting recommendations
A lecturer experienced in the gamification approach implements the narrative faithfully to the film's script
constraints: Implemented in a natural university teaching context with students of the degree in Physical Activity and Sport Sciences at the University of Granada
target_learning_goals: meeting weekly physical activity recommendations
physical education content: innovation and programming in physical education
designing innovation projects in Physical Education
examples: Students followed a QR-code 'White rabbit' trail to find the professor playing Morfeo and chose the red pill; the course ran from 2 March to 17 June 2016

article_title: Ready student one: Exploring the predictors of student learning in virtual reality.
citation: Madden J., Pandita S., Schuldt J. P., Kim B., S. Won A., Holmes N. G. (2020). Ready student one: Exploring the predictors of student learning in virtual reality. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0229788
title: Match instructional technology to learning goals and affordances, since the technology itself does not guarantee learning gains
description: The article argues that what matters for learning is not the technology but how and why it is used, noting that "what is important for learning is not the technology itself, but how and why it is used". It therefore designed three conditions expressing identical Moon-phase content while varying embodiment and real-world complexity, and tested whether VR's affordances produced learning advantages. They did not, though attitudes improved.
requirements: Instructional activities should be designed so the technology's affordances (embodiment, controlled simplification of real-world complexity) target the specific demands of the concept, as the VR simulation was designed to mimic the hands-on activity while exploiting VR's unique affordances.
constraints: The study's null learning results are limited to Moon phases in physics/astronomy; the authors caution against applying findings to other subjects, and note VR's technological obstacles (control responsiveness, motion sickness, limited resolution and field of view) and participants' unfamiliarity with VR may change results as technology and familiarity progress.
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory science courses
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of spatially and temporally dynamic science phenomena such as Moon phases
examples: Participants were randomly assigned across VR, desktop, and hands-on conditions with identical content and guiding questions; learning was equivalent but 78% preferred VR.

article_title: Quantifying the medical student learning curve for ECG rhythm strip interpretation using deliberate practice.
citation: Waechter Jason, Reading David, Lee Chel Hee, Walker Mathieu. (2019). Quantifying the medical student learning curve for ECG rhythm strip interpretation using deliberate practice. GMS Journal for Medical Education 36(4):Doc40. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001248.shtml
title: Mandate a baseline practice module and pair deliberate practice with a dedicated summative exam to drive practice volume in skill-based learning
description: The article recommends that responsibility for providing practice and feedback belongs to the school, and shows that requiring one practice module plus a dedicated summative exam drove students far beyond the minimum: they completed "a mean of 59 practice rhythm strips when only 14 were required". The authors argue the summative exam was likely a strong motivator and that summative feedback should be strongly considered for skill retention.
requirements: A dedicated summative exam on the practiced skill, and at least one mandatory practice module embedded in coursework.
constraints: The 9-fold comparison rests on the authors' own previously unpublished local data with no control group; the study was observational.
target_learning_goals: ECG rhythm strip interpretation competency
examples: Students at two Canadian medical schools were required to complete one practice module and a mandatory rhythm strip exam counting 5% of the course grade, and voluntarily practiced well beyond the requirement.

The MATLAB script "takes the talk-turn data in the question-and-response format and generates an edge list and a corresponding weight list for the edges," which serve as inputs for an R script using the igraph package to calculate the graph theory parameters. All scripts and source code at the time of publication are available online in the Supplemental Material.

article_title: Perceptions about the Self-Learning Methodology in Simulated Environments in Nursing Students: A Mixed Study.
citation: Díaz Agea J.L., Ramos-Morcillo A.J., Amo Setien F.J., Ruzafa-Martínez M., Hueso-Montoro C., Leal-Costa C. (2019). Perceptions about the Self-Learning Methodology in Simulated Environments in Nursing Students: A Mixed Study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16234646
title: MAES©: self-learning methodology in simulated environments combining PBL, simulation-based learning, peer education and self-directed learning
description: MAES© (Metodología de Autoaprendizaje en Entornos Simulados) is an active learning methodology for nursing simulation implemented at UCAM since 2013–2014. The article states that "MAES© is structured through the synergistic union of other active learning methodologies such as problem-based learning (PBL), SBL, peer education, and self-directed learning." Students are protagonists of the whole process, from choosing and designing a case to the simulated experience and debriefing, developing competences such as communication, reasoning, advanced technical skills and empathy through intrinsic motivation and autonomy.
requirements: Students must be driven by intrinsic motivation and greater autonomy in their skill acquisition process
The educator must stand back, abandon the role of transmitter of knowledge, and become a facilitator of learning
constraints: Some believe that self-learning by itself cannot replace guided learning, per the article's account of the debate
target_learning_goals: communication skills
reasoning skills
advanced technical skills
empathy
teamwork
examples: At UCAM, nursing students learn with MAES© alongside facilitator-designed simulation-based learning (SBL); the article reports MAES© grants students a better degree of performance in learning with simulation when compared to SBL

article_title: Perceptions about the Self-Learning Methodology in Simulated Environments in Nursing Students: A Mixed Study.
citation: Díaz Agea J.L., Ramos-Morcillo A.J., Amo Setien F.J., Ruzafa-Martínez M., Hueso-Montoro C., Leal-Costa C. (2019). Perceptions about the Self-Learning Methodology in Simulated Environments in Nursing Students: A Mixed Study. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16234646
title: MAES© six-element session structure: autonomous teams choose a case, design a scenario for another team, experience it, and close with a structured debriefing including an expository phase
description: The article states that "MAES© consists of six elements and is structured in a minimum of two sessions." In the first session a psychologically safe environment is created, autonomous work teams with a defined group identity are formed (Element 1), each team freely chooses a topic presented by the facilitator as a bait or hook (Element 2), and a brainstorming establishes what students know and want to learn (Element 3). Teams then commit to designing a scenario another team will experience within a week (Element 4). In the second session a different team runs the simulation with a simulated patient (Element 5), followed by a structured debriefing (Element 6) that includes an expository phase in which the designing team teaches the skills the whole group chose to learn, supported by reliable scientific evidence.
requirements: A minimum of two sessions
Six work teams per session, with three teams designing and presenting and three teams experimenting and reflecting
Debriefing must be guided by a facilitator and supported with reliable and quality scientific evidence
constraints: Each session deals with three scenarios and involves six work teams, with an average duration of four hours including breaks
target_learning_goals: clinical and non-technical skills chosen by the teams
teamwork
self-directed learning
examples: An average of 12–16 students participate in MAES simulation sessions distributed in six work teams; debriefing is considered a key component of the methodology

article_title: Bachelor of Nursing students' HIV and AIDS knowledge in KwaZulu-Natal province: An evaluation study.
citation: Ngcobo, S.J. & Mchunu, G.G., 2019, 'Bachelor of Nursing students' HIV and AIDS knowledge in KwaZulu-Natal province: An evaluation study', Curationis 42(1), a1928. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v42i1.1928
title: Make preservice HIV and AIDS healthcare management training mandatory for all nursing students and require HIV and AIDS training for nursing educators
description: The article recommends that preservice HIV training be made mandatory for all nursing students irrespective of college or university training already provided, and that nursing educators should undergo mandatory HIV and AIDS training in order to effectively impart knowledge of this subject. The rationale is that preservice training reaches students before graduation, whereas in-service training reaches only those whose employers deploy them, and that educators 'can only teach what they have been taught'.
requirements: Nursing educators themselves trained in HIV and AIDS content; curriculum review and revision by training institutions and curriculum developers.
constraints: Evidence base is a single-university descriptive evaluation whose findings the authors state are not generalisable to other institutions or programmes.
target_learning_goals: HIV and AIDS healthcare management knowledge and clinical competencies
examples: The article's recommendations section states there is a need to ensure preservice HIV training is mandatory for all nursing students across the country, and that enhanced HIV training programmes should be provided for postgraduate students with similar outcome research.

It "simulates a postpartum uterus (up to 48 h after delivery)" and can be "used alone as a desk-top simulator or placed inside the Mama Natalie". Trainers valued its low cost, light weight, portability, and abstract shape, which reduced embarrassment.

article_title: How to choose an evidence-based medicine knowledge test for medical students? Comparison of three knowledge measures.
citation: Buljan Ivan, Jerončić Ana, Malički Mario, Marušić Matko, Marušić Ana. (2018). How to choose an evidence-based medicine knowledge test for medical students? Comparison of three knowledge measures. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1391-z
title: Match the EBM knowledge test to the course's content and learning objectives, and prefer the Berlin test over the ACE test in most settings
description: The article recommends that EBM knowledge assessment be chosen deliberately rather than by convention: "EBM knowledge assessment should be based on the course's content and learning objectives." Because the three common tests differ in format, guessing risk, discrimination and reliability, the authors suggest "in the majority of educational settings, the Berlin test is preferred over the ACE test", while the Fresno test, though most discriminative, is "probably best suited for smaller groups or smaller classes" due to teacher effort.
requirements: Assessment should use measures that assess both previously acquired knowledge and further application of that knowledge.
constraints: The Fresno test needs the most effort and investment by the teacher; no single tool exists for assessing higher dimensions of EBM knowledge according to Bloom's taxonomy.
target_learners: third-year graduate medical students in an EBM course
target_learning_goals: evidence-based medicine knowledge: question formulation, searching, appraisal and application of evidence
examples: After a 25-hour EBM course, students scored highest on the ACE test (median 73% of maximum), lower on the Berlin (60%) and lowest on the Fresno (45%), showing the same students receive different verdicts depending on the test.
key_sources: Buljan Ivan, Jerončić Ana, Malički Mario, Marušić Matko, Marušić Ana. (2018). How to choose an evidence-based medicine knowledge test for medical students? Comparison of three knowledge measures. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1391-z

citation: Chu Tsung-Lan, Wang Jeng, Monrouxe Lynn, Sung Yu-Chih, Kuo Chen-li, Ho Lun-Hui, Lin Yueh-E. (2019). The effects of the flipped classroom in teaching evidence based nursing: A quasi-experimental study. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0210606
title: Mandarin version of the SE-EBP scale (12 items) for measuring self-efficacy in evidence-based practice
description: A 12-item, 10-point Likert scale measuring nurses' self-efficacy across the 5A steps of EBN, adapted from Chang and Crowe's 2011 SE-EBP scale. The article reports that three TEBMA-qualified experts reduced the scale from 28 to 12 items, achieving "the CVI value of 0.97and the internal consistency (Cronbach's α) of 0.97." Scores range from 12 to 120 in 1-point increments.
requirements: Administration by Mandarin-speaking facilitators with the translated and expert-modified 12-item version
constraints: Content validity and reliability figures (CVI 0.97, Cronbach's α 0.97) were established for the modified 12-item version in this study's Taiwanese nursing context
target_learning_goals: Self-efficacy in evidence-based practice across the 5A steps
examples: Used to measure self-efficacy at pre-course, post-course, and one-month follow-up in the 151-nurse quasi-experiment

article_title: High-fidelity is not superior to low-fidelity simulation but leads to overconfidence in medical students.
citation: Massoth C, Röder H, Ohlenburg H, Hessler M, Zarbock A, Pöpping DM, Wenk M. (2019). High-fidelity is not superior to low-fidelity simulation but leads to overconfidence in medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1464-7
title: Match simulator fidelity to trainee level: for novice trainees, low-fidelity simulation achieves equal learning without inducing overconfidence
description: The article recommends caution about investing in high-fidelity simulation for novice learners: "no advantage in learning success is achieved by a higher degree of realism of the simulator", and HF training induced "misconceived self-assessments in terms of actual abilities and consequently overinflated self-confidence". Because overconfidence is linked to risk-taking and diagnostic error, LF simulation is the safer choice for medical students, with HF's added cost justified only if superior outcomes are demonstrated.
requirements: Selection of simulator fidelity should consider the trainee's educational level and the competency level targeted
constraints: Findings come from fourth-year medical students; transferability to medical professionals remains unclear per the authors
target_learning_goals: advanced life support skills
realistic self-assessment and confidence calibration
examples: The trial randomized 135 students to HF (SimMan 3G) or LF (Rescue Anne) ALS training and found equal knowledge gains, comparable or worse HF practical performance, and overconfidence only in the HF group

citation: Woodham Luke A., Round Jonathan, Stenfors Terese, Bujacz Aleksandra, Karlgren Klas, Jivram Trupti, Riklefs Viktor, Poulton Ella, Poulton Terry. (2019). Virtual patients designed for training against medical error: Exploring the impact of decision-making on learner motivation. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0215597
title: Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning and its triarchic cognitive-load processes as applied to virtual patients
description: The article applies Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning, a specialist application of Cognitive Load Theory, describing three learning processes: extraneous processing caused by poor instructional design, essential processing set by material complexity, and generative processing devoted to germane load. The article stresses that "Generative processing is directly dependent upon the levels of motivation of the student towards the learning task", which motivates its focus on motivation when adding branched decision-making to virtual patients.
requirements: Instructional design should "minimise unnecessary cognitive load in the form of extraneous processing" whilst fostering generative processing
constraints: Essential processing is "beyond the control of the instructional designer", being determined by the complexity of the material
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning in simulated patient encounters
engagement in generative processing of learning material
examples: The study treats VP cases as worked examples that minimise extraneous processing, with branched decision-making and feedback promoting generative processing via the guided activity principle.

article_title: The effects of graduate competency-based education and mastery learning on patient care and return on investment: a narrative review of basic anesthetic procedures.
citation: Bisgaard Claus Hedebo, Rubak Sune Leisgaard Mørck, Rodt Svein Aage, Petersen Jens Aage Kølsen, Musaeus Peter. (2018). The effects of graduate competency-based education and mastery learning on patient care and return on investment: a narrative review of basic anesthetic procedures. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1262-7
title: Mastery learning as a rigid form of competency-based education with high mastery standards and formative evaluation
description: The review defines mastery learning as "a more rigid form of CBE" in which "a high level of mastery, originally defined as 90% correct answers, is needed for the learner to progress to a more advanced level of training or to be asserted as proficient". Educationalists such as Keller, Carroll and Bloom proposed that up to 90% of all learners could reach mastery given appropriate method and time. Continuous formative evaluation identifies parts needing remedial teaching before the desired mastery level is achieved. Unlike fixed-duration curricula, training time to the fixed competence outcome varies with learner aptitude and teaching.
requirements: Continuous formative evaluation of learning to identify parts still needing remedial teaching
A predefined mastery standard (originally 90% correct answers) that learners must reach before progressing
constraints: Potentially increased costs due to enhanced supervision, education of supervisors, and variable duration of training, as critics note
target_learners: Residents and interns in graduate medical education
target_learning_goals: Reaching a predefined high mastery standard in procedural skills before independent practice
examples: The Barsuk/Cohen CVC studies used pretesting and training with immediate feedback until a predefined mastery level was reached in a four-hour simulation-based course

examples: The paper details metabolic risk factors, dietary patterns such as 51% of participants in one cited study eating in no longer than 15 min, and the nursing role in preventing medication side effects

article_title: Ten years of simulation-based shoulder dystocia training- impact on obstetric outcome, clinical management, staff confidence, and the pedagogical practice - a time series study.
citation: Dahlberg Johanna, Nelson Marie, Dahlgren Madeleine Abrandt, Blomberg Marie. (2018). Ten years of simulation-based shoulder dystocia training- impact on obstetric outcome, clinical management, staff confidence, and the pedagogical practice - a time series study. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12884-018-2001-0
title: Sustain mandatory simulation training on a fixed recurring schedule integrated into clinical working time to maintain rare-event emergency preparedness
description: The article recommends introducing and sustaining training for rare emergent events that staff cannot learn through frequent clinical work: "To introduce and sustain a shoulder dystocia training program for delivery staff improved clinical outcome". A putative adherence factor the authors name was that staff were scheduled for the 3-hour sessions as an integral part of clinical work with no other tasks planned. Recurring mandatory sessions at fixed intervals kept skills current over a decade despite the rarity of the event.
requirements: Sessions scheduled during working hours without competing clinical tasks
Long-term organizational commitment with a recurring interval (1.5 years) and fixed frequency (six times yearly)
constraints: The article reports one unit's decade-long experience; other settings reported inconsistent clinical outcomes from shorter or one-off training programs
target_learning_goals: Preparedness and confidence for rare, emergent obstetric complications
examples: PROBE sessions held six times per year with mandatory attendance at a 1.5-year interval, with midwives and doctors scheduled from introduction without other tasks planned for the 3 hours.

title: Manikin-based simulation (MBS) debrief sessions as needs assessment data sources
description: MBS debriefs are video-recorded 20 min sessions following manikin-based simulation scenarios, facilitated by an expert using focused facilitation and teaching. The article reports MBS debriefs were "Streamlined to uncover system level barriers" compared with other methods.

constraints: Higher cost than VPS due to manikin rental and transport
One case per scenario
Greater technical risk than traditional methods
